title: Waiting For Non-Monetary Motivation

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: Once again, you have failed to motivate me.

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: You said we shouldn't be motivated by money, so I'm waiting for the new thing to kick in.

transcript.speaker: Balding Employee
transcript.text: I'm not good at reading faces, but I think there's something happening over in this region.

situation: At a meeting, a balding employee tells the boss that he has once again failed to motivate him. When the boss has told staff not to be motivated by money, the employee says he is still waiting for the replacement motivator to kick in. The boss grows visibly angry, and the employee gestures at his face and remarks that something seems to be happening there.
punchline: Having removed money as a motivator, the boss has nothing to offer in its place, and the employee sarcastically points out the boss's obvious anger while claiming he can't read faces.
summary: A worker mocks his boss for offering no motivation other than money, then pretends not to notice the boss's furious expression.

title: Too Happy Means Overpaid

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm getting reports that your morale is too high.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Happiness is nature's way of informing human resources that you're overpaid.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Nature wants me to be unhappy?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't blame me. Go yell at the clouds.

setting: Catbert's office in the human resources department
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, summons an employee and tells him that reports show his morale is too high. He claims that happiness is a sign the employee is overpaid. When the employee asks if nature wants him unhappy, Catbert shrugs off responsibility and tells him to yell at the clouds.
punchline: HR treats an employee's happiness as evidence that he is paid too much, and then dodges all blame by pinning it on nature.
summary: An HR cat reprimands a worker for being too cheerful, reasoning that contentment must mean his salary is excessive.

title: Rented Tuna Can Ruins Mood

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If my self-esteem seems low, that's because I drove here in a rented tuna can on wheels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was such a bad automotive experience that I can't even pretend you should care what I have to say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I loathe myself and the company that pays me. Who's with me on this?

situation: Dilbert stands at the head of a meeting table and explains that his low self-esteem comes from driving a tiny rented car to get there. He then admits he can't pretend anyone should care what he says, and finally announces that he loathes himself and his employer, asking who agrees. Two seated coworkers eagerly raise their hands in agreement.
punchline: Dilbert's grumbling about a bad rental car turns into a call for solidarity in company-hating, and his coworkers enthusiastically join in, showing how widespread the disgruntlement is.
summary: After a miserable rental car trip, a dejected Dilbert invites his meeting to share his disdain for himself and the company, and his colleagues gladly volunteer.

title: Doing Email in the Parking Lot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're two hours late.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was doing e-mail in the parking lot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to bang out a few hours of work before some idiot starts asking me dumb questions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It would be funny if the next thing you say is in the form of a question.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert for arriving two hours late. Dilbert says he was answering email in the parking lot, and explains that he likes to get work done before some idiot starts asking him dumb questions. He then taunts the Boss, who stands grimacing with clenched teeth, by suggesting it would be funny if his next remark were a question.
punchline: Dilbert sets a trap by calling question-askers idiots, daring his boss to prove the point by asking a question, while his boss silently seethes.
summary: An employee who shows up hours behind schedule blames his tardiness on a parking-lot work session and then goads his irritated manager into proving himself a question-asking fool.

title: Pension Fund Invested In Garfield Posters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Studies show that a rat with a dartboard can manage your pension fund as well as experts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I invested your entire pension fund in Garfield posters.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm bad at darts.

situation: The Boss, seated at a table with Dilbert and Dogbert, cites studies claiming a rat throwing darts at a dartboard can manage a pension fund as well as experts. Dogbert, acting as the financial adviser, reveals he put the entire pension fund into Garfield posters. When the others look at him, he explains he is simply bad at darts.
punchline: Dogbert took the 'rat with a dartboard' investing idea literally and, because he's a poor dart thrower, ended up with an absurdly worthless investment like Garfield posters.
summary: A financial adviser mocks the idea that random picks match expert fund managers by staking everyone's retirement savings on cat-cartoon merchandise thanks to his lousy aim.

title: Inefficiency Is Kingly Leadership

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Empire Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Make your employees less productive. That way your CEO will let you hire more of them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Inefficiency is the same thing as leadership. A king needs an entire country just to wipe his. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brow?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was going to say windshield.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brow is catchier.

situation: Dogbert, working as an empire-building consultant and wearing a crown, advises the Boss to make his employees less productive so the CEO will approve hiring more people. He says inefficiency equals leadership and starts to say a king needs a whole country to wipe his something, but the Boss guesses 'brow' instead. Dogbert says he meant windshield, and the Boss decides brow sounds better.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical advice rewards inefficiency with bigger headcount, and the joke lands when the clueless Boss picks the more 'catchy' but wrong word, preferring a good-sounding phrase over the actual meaning.
summary: A crowned consultant teaches his boss to build a bigger kingdom by encouraging sloppy work, then the boss cheerfully mangles the lesson's punchline.

title: Rushing for Pointless Deadline Sarcasm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I'll need that by the end of day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will gladly rush to meet your arbitrary deadline so my work can sit in your e-mail inbox until next week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm still within hearing distance.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops. You usually scurry away faster.

situation: The Boss walks up to Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and demands work by the end of day. Dilbert sarcastically mutters that he will rush to meet the arbitrary deadline only for the work to sit unread in the Boss's inbox. The Boss is still standing nearby and overhears, and Dilbert dryly remarks that he normally scurries off faster.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic complaint about pointless deadlines is overheard because the Boss, who normally flees before hearing any pushback, lingered a moment too long.
summary: An employee grumbles about a made-up deadline and his manager catches every word because he failed to hurry away as usual.

title: The Worthless Dumb Guy Designation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And Russell will act as the WDG for our project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: WDG?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Worthless Dumb Guy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Every project has one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a different context, Russell might seem totally competent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But in any small group, the dumbest person always seems extra worthless.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone else on the project is brilliant. That makes Russell seem like a chimp.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's helpful to identify the WDG so we can discourage him from trying to contribute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it hurt his feelings?

transcript.speaker: Russell
transcript.text: Me want banana!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's hard to know.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: At a project meeting, Dilbert announces that Russell will serve as the project's WDG, or Worthless Dumb Guy. Dilbert and Alice explain that every group has one, and that identifying him lets the team discourage him from contributing. When Dilbert asks whether this hurts Russell's feelings, Russell shouts a chimp-like demand for a banana.
punchline: Russell responds to being labeled the worthless dumb guy by acting like a chimp, so it is genuinely unclear whether he understands or is hurt by the insult.
summary: A team formally names its least capable member as the one to keep out of the way, and his ape-like outburst leaves everyone unsure how he feels.

title: Declining Spit-Frosted Birthday Cake

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're having a birthday cake for Scott in the break room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks. I prefer cake that isn't frosted with the spit of recent candle-blowing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oooh, look at the Queen of England who likes her cake without spit. What's it like to be fancy?

situation: A coworker stops by Dilbert's cubicle to invite him to a birthday cake celebration for Scott in the break room. Dilbert declines, objecting to the germs spread when the birthday person blows out the candles. The coworker responds by sarcastically mocking him for being fancy.
punchline: The coworker treats Dilbert's perfectly reasonable hygiene objection as snobbery, mocking him as royalty for not wanting to eat cake covered in spit.
summary: A cubicle invitation to office cake is refused on sanitary grounds, and the inviter answers with mock admiration for the refuser's supposed royal tastes.

title: Dilbert Concludes He Is a Ghost

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The status of my project is that apparently I died and became a ghost.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't remember dying, but the evidence of my untimely demise is clear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the past week, no one has returned my phone calls or replied to my emails.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I try to print a document, I get nothing but error messages.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now all of you are looking at your phones and reading materials as if no one is speaking to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will now test my ghost theory by running through a living person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Boooo!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good news: I'm alive but unworthy of attention.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to watch a show.

setting: Conference room during a presentation, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert gives a project status presentation to The Boss and a coworker, arguing that he must be a ghost because nobody answers his calls or emails, his printer fails, and everyone ignores him in the meeting. He tests the theory by running into a living person and knocks The Boss over. At home, bandaged, he reports that he is alive but ignored, while Ratbert watches TV.
punchline: Dilbert's ghost theory is disproved only by a collision, and the real explanation is that he's a living employee whom everyone simply ignores.
summary: Convinced he has died because nobody pays him any notice, Dilbert barrels into his boss to prove he is solid and learns he is merely overlooked.

title: Mom's Scheme to Avoid Moving Back

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Dilbert, could you help me fill out this rebate form the next time you visit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Also, my laptop keeps crashing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take a look at it.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: My TV is acting up again too.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: And maybe you could show me how to change my ringtone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you really need all of that help?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or is this an elaborate scheme to inoculate against me ever wanting to move back home?

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: We have a bad connection! What? What? What?

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: That should buy me another six months.

transcript.speaker: Mom
transcript.text: Click

setting: Phone call between Dilbert's home and his mother's house
situation: Dilbert's mother phones him with a growing list of tech chores: a rebate form, a crashing laptop, a misbehaving TV and a ringtone change. Dilbert agrees at first, then suspects she is overloading him on purpose. She fakes a bad connection, hangs up, and reveals she did it to keep him from wanting to move back home.
punchline: Dilbert's suspicion was right: his mother deliberately burdens him with tech support requests so he will never want to live with her again, and she cleverly ends the call by faking a bad connection.
summary: A mother piles tech chores onto her son during a phone call, and when he catches on, she fakes static and hangs up, satisfied her plan will keep him away.

title: Coordinating With Everyone Means Giving Up

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make sure you coordinate with the brand manager and the category manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And also the clients, the account execs, the project leaders, strategic planning, facilities management, product managers, marketing, and I.T.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I heard was "give up."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's meet again in a year.

situation: The Boss instructs Dilbert to coordinate a project with a brand manager and category manager, then keeps adding more and more departments and stakeholders to the list. Dilbert says all he took from it was to give up, and the Boss cheerfully suggests they meet again in a year.
punchline: The list of people to coordinate with grows so absurdly long that the task is clearly impossible, and the Boss is content to treat total failure as a year-long timeline.
summary: A manager piles an impossible number of stakeholders onto a simple assignment, and the employee concludes that quitting is the only reasonable response.

title: Collecting Birthday Money For Ted

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting money for Ted's birthday.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Pass. I can't stand that idiot.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: His face looks like a ferret eating a lemon.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He makes my skin crawl.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: He tells racist jokes, and I think he's embezzling.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've been dating him for a month.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'd be lying if I said that wasn't worth a dollar.

situation: A coworker asks Carol to contribute to a birthday collection for Ted. Carol refuses and escalates her insults about Ted, calling him an idiot, ugly, creepy, racist and a suspected embezzler. The coworker then reveals she has been dating Ted for a month, and Carol sheepishly hands over a dollar.
punchline: After trashing Ted at length, Carol learns the person asking is his girlfriend, and her grudging dollar is an awkward, face-saving apology.
summary: A woman unloads a stream of insults about a colleague to someone who turns out to be dating him.

title: Strategy Recipe: Just Add Leadership

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I collected optimistic data, put it in the context of bad analogies, seasoned it with saliency bias. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . added herd instinct, a pinch of confirmation bias. . . and here's your strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just add leadership.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do I always get the hard part?

situation: Dilbert describes his strategy as if it were a recipe, listing flawed ingredients like optimistic data, bad analogies, saliency bias, herd instinct and confirmation bias. He hands the finished papers to the Boss and says all that's left is to add leadership. The Boss complains that he always gets the hard part.
punchline: Dilbert has built a strategy out of cognitive biases and flawed reasoning, and then leaves the Boss to make it work through leadership, which the Boss complains is the hard part, ignoring that the foundation is rotten.
summary: An employee serves up a strategy cooked from biased thinking and tells his boss to finish it off with some leadership.

title: Wally Sabotages Death Ray Success

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company wants to turn my invention into a death ray. How can I stop them from succeeding?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: There is one natural force that can stop any form of success. It goes by the name. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How may I be of disservice?

setting: Outdoors by a trash bin, then the office coffee station
situation: Dilbert asks a garbage man for advice on how to prevent his company from turning his invention into a death ray. The garbage man says one natural force can stop any success and trails off with a name. Dilbert then goes to Wally, who is at the coffee maker, and Wally offers his services as a saboteur.
punchline: Wally's laziness and knack for undermining projects is so reliable that he is the known cure for any success, and he cheerfully advertises himself as offering 'disservice' instead of service.
summary: Seeking to keep his invention from becoming a weapon, Dilbert is pointed toward the one person guaranteed to ruin any project: the coffee-nursing slacker Wally.

title: Carol's Calls Make Dilbert Wait

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Carol, would you. . .

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Rrring!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's an interesting experiment. . .

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Rrring!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Watch what happens to your blood pressure when I take this call and make you wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah? What's the problem now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell your brother I said to stop biting the heads off your dolls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-huh. . . Well, if the man was wearing a postal uniform, he wasn't the bogeyman.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You did what to him?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Listen carefully. I want you to tear up the carpet in the fancy bathroom. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can come back.

setting: Office cubicle area; the strip opens with a presentation slide
situation: Dilbert tries to ask Carol for something, but her phone keeps ringing and she answers it. Dilbert points out that this is an experiment in making someone wait, then takes a call of his own, which turns out to be a personal call about a sibling biting the heads off dolls and a mail carrier mistaken for the bogeyman. Carol then resumes her own call, giving instructions about a bathroom renovation, and Dilbert offers to come back later.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to make Carol wait on a call is undercut by the fact that her calls are never-ending, and his own call is absurd, so he gives up and leaves.
summary: After being ignored while his coworker takes calls, a man tries the same tactic on her, only to be stuck in an absurd family-crisis call before retreating.

title: Alice Fights Poltergeist Inside Copier

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can almost reach the paper jam, but a poltergeist is trying to drag me to the afterworld.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe I can blind him with the toner cartridge. Ha ha! Take that! And that!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I can't feel my arms!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only have one.

situation: Alice is stuck head-first inside a copy machine trying to clear a paper jam, with only her legs sticking out. She narrates that a poltergeist is dragging her toward the afterworld and that she plans to blind it with toner, while Dilbert stands by holding a sheet of paper. When she shouts that she can't feel her arms, Dilbert replies that he only has one.
punchline: Dilbert responds to Alice's life-or-death panic with a deadpan, irrelevant reply about his own arm count, showing he is oblivious or indifferent to her plight.
summary: A coworker lodged upside down in a photocopier battles an imagined ghost while her colleague offers a baffling, unhelpful remark.

title: Boss Returns With Demonic Consultant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Technically, I was dead for a week. But I was evicted from the afterlife and had to come back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The afterlife has a lot to teach us about management. I brought home a consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might be late with my status report.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Do you know what locusts taste like?

setting: Office, in the Boss's cubicle and at his desk
situation: The Boss tells a red furry creature and then Dilbert that he died for a week but was kicked out of the afterlife and returned to work. He claims the afterlife taught him about management and that he brought back a consultant. The consultant is a small red devil, who menacingly asks Dilbert about eating locusts when Dilbert mentions a late status report.
punchline: The Boss's new consultant is literally a devil from the afterlife who uses threats of torment to enforce deadlines, implying that hellish management methods are exactly what he wants to impose on his employees.
summary: After being thrown out of the afterlife, the boss returns with a little red devil as his management consultant, who promptly threatens a worker over a late report.

title: Alice's Two-Phase Plan for Controlling Men

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I learned to control men by exaggerating the importance of my projects and overextending myself.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Our most important customer is coming and I won't be ready on time unless you fetch me some coffee!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In phase two, I make you enjoy it.

situation: Alice sits at a conference table with Dilbert and Asok and explains how she manipulates men: she inflates the importance of her projects and overloads herself. She demonstrates by frantically demanding coffee, claiming a key customer visit will be ruined otherwise. She then adds that the second phase of her plan is making them enjoy serving her.
punchline: Alice reveals that her manufactured panic is a deliberate manipulation tactic, and that she plans to take it further by making her victims enjoy being controlled.
summary: Alice lays out her method for manipulating male coworkers through staged crises and hints that her real goal is making them happily comply.

title: Dilbert Insults Accounting Over Expense Report

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Groan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to see someone about my rejected expense report.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Monster
transcript.text: The problem is that you didn't submit a receipt for your bridge toll.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe the problem is that you have a joyless, dead-end job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And your boss doesn't allow you to use your own judgment because working here is proof that you don't make good decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Rejecting my expense report gives you the illusion of power, and nourishes your shriveled and dying ego.

transcript.speaker: Accounting Monster
transcript.text: Actually, I was going to approve it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't have to get an attitude about it.

setting: Office wall with a hole leading into the Accounting department
situation: Dilbert crawls through a hole in the wall marked Accounting to complain about his rejected expense report. The green monster in Accounting explains that he forgot a bridge toll receipt, and Dilbert responds by savagely insulting the monster's job, boss and ego. The monster then reveals it was going to approve the report anyway.
punchline: Dilbert launches a needless tirade of insults at the clerk, who was about to approve his claim, and then scolds the monster for having an attitude.
summary: A man tunnels into the accounting department to protest a denied reimbursement and berates the clerk, only to learn the approval was already coming.

title: Bad Product, Big-Mouthed Spokesman

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Our marketing campaign depends on word of mouth. Unfortunately, our product is bad.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: So we found a guy with poor judgment and a huge mouth to say good things.

transcript.speaker: Loud Mouth Guy
transcript.text: Present.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Market-ing isn't a real thing, is it?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: It's mostly guessing.

situation: A marketing manager tells a meeting that their campaign relies on word of mouth, but the product is bad, so they hired a man with poor judgment and an enormous mouth to praise it. The man raises his hand and announces he is present. Dilbert then asks whether marketing is even a real discipline, and the manager admits it's mostly guessing.
punchline: The marketing team's strategy is to hire someone gullible and loud to promote a bad product, and they cheerfully admit that marketing is basically just guesswork.
summary: Faced with a lousy product, a marketing team hires a loudmouthed fool as a spokesman and then concedes that their whole profession is educated guessing.

title: Ombudsman Is a Soul-Buying Devil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new ombudsman

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: How can you be impartial in my dispute with management when they are the ones paying you?

transcript.speaker: Ombudsman
transcript.text: Perhaps you have something of value that would allow me to see your side.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He's creepy without his soul, but I envy his carefree attitude.

setting: Ombudsman's office and a hallway at the office
situation: An employee asks the new ombudsman, a red devil, how he can be impartial in a dispute with management when management pays him. The devil hints that the employee could sway him by handing over something of value, implicitly his soul. Afterward, the soulless employee stands with Dilbert and Wally, and Wally remarks that he is creepy but enviably carefree.
punchline: The ombudsman is a literal devil whose price for taking your side is your soul, and the soulless employee ends up creepy but strangely carefree, so Wally envies him.
summary: A devilish workplace mediator trades his impartiality for the complainant's soul, leaving a vacant but untroubled colleague.

title: Debunking Her Beliefs on Date Two

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After our first date, I pulled together some links to studies that debunk every belief you have.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I alphabetized them. For example, here's Feng Shui, then Homeopathy, then Horoscope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's okay. I always budget a little extra for second dates.

situation: Dilbert is out walking with a woman on a second date and proudly tells her he compiled alphabetized links to studies debunking all of her beliefs. He shows her the list on his phone, citing feng shui, homeopathy and horoscopes. She angrily stomps on the phone, smashing it, and he calmly says he budgets extra for second dates.
punchline: Dilbert's tactless, pedantic gesture predictably enrages his date, who destroys his phone, and his deadpan remark shows he has come to expect to pay for such damage on every second date.
summary: A man on a date hands over a tidy list of research disproving everything his companion believes in, and she responds by smashing his phone underfoot.

title: Social Media Manager Banned From Social Media

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Beth is our new marketing manager for social media.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By the way, company policy forbids the use of Facebook and Twitter at work. And we don't trust you to work from home.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you blog about how lame we are, you're fired!!!

transcript.speaker: Beth
transcript.text: First day, not so good.

situation: The Boss introduces Beth, a new employee, as the company's marketing manager for social media. He then tells her that Facebook and Twitter are banned at work and that she can't be trusted to work from home. He finishes by pointing at her and threatening to fire her if she blogs about how lame the company is.
punchline: A social media manager is hired but forbidden from using social media at work or from home, and is threatened with firing for criticizing the company, which makes her first day grim.
summary: A new hire in charge of social media learns on day one that the company bans social media and threatens her with dismissal if she criticizes it.

title: Wolfgang the Mythical Software Genius

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked Wolfgang to join us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's a software genius, if not a legend.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He knows more than all of you put together.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Plus his name is Wolfgang.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Some say his talent is a genetic mutation. Others say that God speaks to him in Unix.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All we know for sure is that he glows, and he never needs to eat.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel a chill. It means he's approaching.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Please don't reprogram my DNA and make me a monkey-man!!!

transcript.speaker: Wolfgang
transcript.text: People make a lot of assumptions when you change your name to Wolfgang and stop shaving.

situation: The Boss and a coworker hype up a new software expert named Wolfgang to the team, spreading wild rumors about his genetic mutation, glowing, and divine connection to Unix. When Wolfgang walks in carrying a coffee mug, a frightened coworker begs him not to reprogram his DNA. Wolfgang calmly reveals the legend is just assumptions based on his name and beard.
punchline: Wolfgang's supposed superhuman programming legend is built entirely on people's assumptions about a man who simply changed his name to Wolfgang and stopped shaving.
summary: Colleagues build up a bearded newcomer into a glowing, DNA-altering coding deity, only for him to admit it's all just his name and scruffy look.

title: Managing Means Labeling Things

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We've pieced together the fragments of your poor communication and believe we have deduced your strategy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It appears that you are trying to get paid for doing little more than giving stupid labels to things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's called managing!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good one.

situation: Alice, Dilbert and Wally confront the Boss, saying they have decoded his strategy from his muddled communication. Alice concludes he is just collecting a salary for attaching pointless labels to things. The Boss defensively replies that this is what managing is, and Dilbert sarcastically says 'Good one.'
punchline: The Boss unwittingly confirms the accusation by defining management as labeling things, and Dilbert's sarcastic praise treats it as a joke.
summary: A trio of employees decode their boss's strategy as paid name-tagging, and his defensive reply only proves their point.

title: Blame the Network for Wooden Phone

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our new product is a useless block of wood.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When customers complain that it won't make phone calls, we'll blame the network.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who would want... Whoa, this is cool.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'd be lucky to have one.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells a meeting that the company's new product is a useless block of wood and that customers who complain it can't make calls will be told the network is at fault. The Boss scoffs at who would want one, then picks up the block and is immediately taken with it. Dogbert tells him he'd be lucky to get one.
punchline: Even an obviously worthless block of wood becomes a coveted gadget once someone treats it like a trendy phone, mocking hype-driven consumer tech and the habit of blaming the network for a product's failings.
summary: A consultant plans to sell a wooden block as a phone and pin the complaints on the carrier, and the boss ends up wanting one himself.

title: Gray Area Bugs Mock Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We start shipping in two weeks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not enough time to fix the known bugs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you say "bugs," that's sort of a gray area.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um. . .I don't think it is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, a user might need several steps to do something that should only take one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or perhaps the interface is a bit unclear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or perhaps it can only be operated by a robot from the future who jacks into it and sends commands in zeros and ones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're agreeing with me or mocking me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's sort of a gray area.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: The Boss announces that shipping starts in two weeks, and Dilbert objects that there isn't time to fix the known bugs. The Boss claims that what counts as a bug is a gray area, so Dilbert escalates with increasingly absurd examples of defects. When the Boss admits he can't tell if Dilbert is agreeing or mocking him, Dilbert answers with the Boss's own phrase.
punchline: Dilbert turns the Boss's "gray area" excuse back on him, leaving it deliberately unclear whether he is agreeing or mocking, which is exactly what he was doing all along.
summary: When his manager waves away software defects as a matter of interpretation, an engineer sarcastically pushes the logic to absurd extremes and then throws the vagueness right back.

title: Focus Group Gets Gassed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the focus group coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They don't like us. They're plotting to storm our observation room.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Release the sleeping gas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Chair!

setting: Outside a focus group observation room with a one-way window
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how the focus group is going while holding a coffee mug. Dilbert says the participants dislike the company and are plotting to storm the observation room. The Boss casually orders sleeping gas to be released, and Dilbert is suddenly knocked out or startled and yells 'Chair!'.
punchline: The Boss responds to negative customer feedback by drugging the focus group with sleeping gas, showing he would rather silence unhappy customers than listen to them.
summary: When test participants turn hostile toward the company, management's answer is to knock them out with gas instead of heeding their complaints.

title: Carol Plans Martial Law Over Project

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Guess what, Ted? I volunteered to run a critical project while knowing I don't have enough resources.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: When it becomes a crisis, I will declare martial law and order you to become my flunky.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: In your face, puppet boy!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: This day is turning out to be a little extra sucky.

situation: Carol stands beside Ted's desk and gleefully announces that she volunteered to lead a critical project despite knowing it is under-resourced. She says she will declare martial law when it becomes a crisis and force Ted to be her flunky, then taunts him in triumph while he glumly takes it.
punchline: Carol deliberately takes on a doomed, under-resourced project because she knows the inevitable crisis will give her the power to boss Ted around, and Ted can only note that his day just got worse.
summary: A coworker cheerfully sets herself up for a predictable failure so she can later conscript a colleague as her servant.

title: Dogbert Dehumanizes Customers as Data

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Customer data is an asset that you can sell.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's totally ethical because our customers would do the same thing to us if they could.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds fair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In phase one, we'll dehumanize the enemy by calling them "data."

setting: Conference room during a consulting meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss that he can sell customer data as an asset. He justifies it as ethical because customers would supposedly do the same to the company. When the Boss accepts this, Dogbert outlines a first phase of calling customers "data" to dehumanize them.
punchline: Dogbert casually reveals that the plan to exploit customers begins by dehumanizing them as 'the enemy', satirizing corporate rationalizations for unethical data practices.
summary: A consultant dog talks a gullible manager into selling customer information by framing clients as adversaries who deserve no moral consideration.

file: 2010/2010-04-28_customer service_credit card expense_reimbursement_late fees_punish_devil_hell_rock_sit at computer.gif
title: Dilbert Penalized for Slow Reimbursements

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It takes you two months to process my company credit card expense reimbursement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I get in trouble every month for incurring late fees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why must I be punished for your incompetence?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Apparently I'm awesome.

setting: Desert-like landscape with a computer on a rock, representing the expense processing department
situation: Dilbert complains to a green dinosaur sitting at a computer that it takes two months to process his company credit card expense reimbursement. Because of the delay, Dilbert is the one who gets in trouble for the resulting late fees. When he asks why he is punished for the dinosaur's incompetence, the dinosaur replies that apparently it is awesome.
punchline: The dinosaur has no incentive to improve because the penalty for its slowness falls on Dilbert, so it concludes from the lack of consequences that it must be doing a great job.
summary: A slow-moving prehistoric clerk faces no repercussions for delayed paperwork while the employee waiting on his money takes the blame.

file: 2010/2010-03-28_pants_hole_favorite_plan b_idea_stand on bed_surprise_arms out_pants witness tracking app_cell phone_picture_walk to work_lots of holes_take photo_technology.gif
title: Pants Witness Tracking App

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your pants have a tiny hole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These are my favorite pants!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have to go with Plan B.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wear other pants?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll wear these and act as if the hole just happened.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone knows you can't go home and change in the middle of the day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll use a pants witness tracking application on my phone to keep track of who has seen the hole.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I play my cards right, I can get two or three more wearings out of my favorite pants.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: All of this just happened.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same here.

situation: Dogbert points out that Dilbert's favorite pants have a tiny hole. Rather than change into other pants, Dilbert decides to wear them and pretend the hole just appeared, using a phone app to track who has seen it. At the office, a coworker with a similar hole in his own pants and Dilbert both claim it just happened.
punchline: Dilbert goes to absurdly elaborate technological lengths to avoid the simple fix of changing pants, and everyone else is apparently running the same ridiculous scheme.
summary: A man refuses to retire his beloved trousers and instead engineers a phone-based plan to hide the damage from onlookers.

title: Angry Jack and the Bent Fork

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Carol, this is my new boyfriend, Angry Jack.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I met him in a restaurant after he beat up a busser for bringing a bent fork.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: In the white trash community, we call that a red flag.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: You weren't there. That fork was a mess.

situation: Tina introduces her new boyfriend, Angry Jack, to her coworker Carol. She explains that they met when he beat up a restaurant busser over a bent fork. Carol points out that this is a warning sign, but Tina dismisses her concern and defends the violence.
punchline: Tina is so smitten that she brushes off an obvious red flag, defending her boyfriend's violent outburst by insisting the fork really was that bad.
summary: A woman proudly presents her volatile new beau, whose violent origin story with a restaurant worker alarms her coworker but not her.

title: Cleaning Up After Deadly Product

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a new job for you. Our product is defective and it's killing customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want me to organize a recall?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Engineer a fix?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll need overalls, several barrels of bleach and some sort of scrubby brush.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert the company's defective product is killing customers and he has a new job for him. Dilbert guesses he wants a recall or an engineering fix, but the Boss rejects both. Instead, the Boss lists cleaning supplies, implying Dilbert is to remove evidence of the deaths.
punchline: Rather than fixing or recalling the lethal product, management wants Dilbert to clean up the crime scenes and cover up the evidence.
summary: Instead of repairing a lethal product flaw, the boss assigns his employee the grim task of scrubbing away the traces.

title: Doomed Plan, Even Earlier Deadline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our project plan is so complicated that failure is assured.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But complexity is too abstract for you to manage, so instead you will spray my energy into the vortex of failure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to finish it six weeks sooner for a trade show.

situation: Dilbert presents a diagram of a hopelessly convoluted project plan and warns that it is guaranteed to fail. The boss dismisses the problem as too abstract and tells Dilbert to simply direct the boss's energy into failure, then orders him to go. He adds that the project must now be finished six weeks earlier for a trade show.
punchline: Instead of fixing a plan that is already doomed, the boss ignores the warning and makes the impossible project even harder by moving the deadline up.
summary: A project presenter admits his tangled plan cannot succeed, yet his manager shrugs off the warning and slashes the schedule anyway.

title: Doing Only Things That Matter

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Another division needs your help for a six-month project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who will do my work here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll keep doing this job too, but only the things that matter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long have I been doing things that don't matter?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: Office hallway or workspace, with the Boss holding a coffee mug
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that another division needs him for a six-month project. When Dilbert asks who will cover his current work, the Boss says he'll keep doing both jobs but only the things that matter. Dilbert then asks how long he has been doing things that don't matter, and the Boss realizes he has revealed too much.
punchline: By saying Dilbert can drop the work that doesn't matter, the Boss accidentally admits that Dilbert has been wasting time on pointless tasks that management assigned or tolerated.
summary: A manager dumps extra work on an employee by telling him to skip the pointless parts, inadvertently confirming that those parts were pointless all along.

title: Complaining About Doing Two Jobs

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Did I tell you I'm doing two jobs now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: About a million times.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've complained about it so much that it's like a song I can't get out of my head.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I only found out yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to get ahead of it.

situation: A female coworker stands holding papers and asks Dilbert if she has mentioned that she is now doing two jobs. Dilbert, seated in his chair, says she has told him about a million times and that it's stuck in his head like a song. She points out she only learned of it yesterday, and Dilbert says he is trying to get ahead of it.
punchline: Dilbert is so sure he'll be hearing her complaints about the double workload constantly that he is preemptively tuning them out and acting like he's already sick of them.
summary: A coworker's grumbling about her doubled workload is already so tiresome to Dilbert that he claims to be bracing for it before it has even properly started.

title: Keeping the Regulator as a Pet

transcript.speaker: Executive 1
transcript.text: Have you met the new head regulator for our industry?

transcript.speaker: Executive 1
transcript.text: At first it was inconvenient to feed him.

transcript.speaker: Executive 1
transcript.text: Luckily I started lactating.

transcript.speaker: Executive 2
transcript.text: Have you tried kibble?

setting: A cocktail party or industry social event
situation: Two executives stand talking with drinks in hand. One of them has a tiny man, introduced as the industry's new head regulator, tucked in his shirt pocket. He explains he feeds the regulator himself and casually mentions he began lactating, and the other executive suggests kibble instead.
punchline: The executive has literally shrunk and domesticated the regulator and treats him like a pet, a stand-in for companies capturing and controlling the agencies that are supposed to oversee them.
summary: At a party, a businessman keeps a miniature government overseer in his pocket and nurses him like a baby animal, while his colleague offers pet-feeding advice.

title: Consultants Turn Liars Into Thieves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe someone can help you quantify the value of your research and development work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only people who can quantify the value of research are liars and morons.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we could hire a consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That just turns a liar into a thief.

situation: The Boss suggests someone could quantify the value of Dilbert's research and development work. Dilbert replies that only liars and morons claim they can do that. When the Boss proposes hiring a consultant, Dilbert says that would merely make the liar a thief.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies consultants are dishonest people who also charge money for their made-up valuations, turning a mere liar into a thief.
summary: Dilbert dismisses his boss's attempt to put a number on R&D value and mocks the idea of paying a consultant to do it.

title: Matrix Management Initiation Via PowerPoint

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is where you jack into matrix management, Neo.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Insert these iPod ear buds and fire up PowerPoint. The reality you once knew is gone.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: One more thing: if your computer dies during PowerPoint, your career dies in the real world.

characters: Coworker (bald with glasses and coffee mug)
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug parodies the Matrix by 'initiating' a new employee into matrix management. He has the newcomer put in iPod ear buds and open PowerPoint, then warns that a computer crash mid-presentation will kill his career. The new employee grows increasingly terrified.
punchline: Matrix management is likened to the Matrix, where the only 'reality' is endless PowerPoint presentations, and a technical glitch is as deadly to your career as dying in the film is to the character.
summary: A veteran employee mockingly inducts a newcomer into matrix management like a sci-fi movie hero, warning that a PowerPoint crash spells career death.

title: Catbert Weighs Alice's Economic Value

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Alice broke my arm. You need to do something about this.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Okay. I'll compare Alice's economic value to yours and decide who to fire.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: No fair! She's an engineer!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You got beat up by someone who is also better at math?

setting: Catbert's desk in the human resources office
situation: A bandaged, bearded employee complains to Catbert, the HR director, that Alice broke his arm and demands action. Catbert says he will compare their economic values and fire whoever is worth less. When the employee protests that Alice is an engineer, Catbert points out she is also better at math.
punchline: The employee's complaint about Alice being an engineer only confirms she is worth more to the company, so he is the one likely to be fired; he was both beaten up and outclassed at math.
summary: A man hurt in a scuffle with a coworker asks HR for justice, only to learn that the company's idea of fairness is a cold calculation of who is more valuable.

title: Dogbert's App Zaps Coworker's Head

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Look at this app!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look at this app.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow! Zap! Pow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said the Dogbert app is supposed to make a funny noise.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll bet it did.

situation: A coworker shows Dilbert a phone app, and Dilbert responds by showing his own phone app, which fires a zapping blast that blows the coworker's head apart. Dilbert then complains that the Dogbert app was only supposed to make a funny noise. Dogbert, sitting at his computer and wagging his tail, smugly says he bets it did, revealing he rigged the app.
punchline: Dogbert's app was secretly a weapon rather than a novelty noisemaker, and Dogbert's smug reply shows he knew exactly what it would do.
summary: A harmless-seeming novelty phone app turns out to be a lethal gadget, and its mischievous creator couldn't be prouder.

file: 2010/2010-07-27_statue of liberty_destroy_pr_responsibility_clean up_new york harbor_light show_weapon demo_podium_speech_fish food.gif

Ratbert suggests taking full responsibility and promising to clean up the harbor, which the Boss never did. A flashback shows the Boss at a podium telling the press the statue was old and made entirely of fish food.
punchline: The Boss sought PR advice only after already giving a ridiculous, irresponsible excuse, blaming the destruction on the statue being made of fish food rather than accepting responsibility.
summary: After blaming a national monument's demolition on edible construction materials, a clueless executive belatedly asks for crisis-communications help.

file: 2010/2010-06-02_meeting_presentation_slide show_names_trademarked_hand motion_crotch area_wide eyes_shocked_gross_point_war criminals_nicknames_partnerless loving_business.gif
title: Product Naming Leaves Only Awful Options

transcript.text: This next slide shows all of the possible names for our product that are not already trademarked.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are there any that don't remind people of this general area of the human body?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That narrows it down to the names of accused war criminals, and the funnier nicknames for partnerless loving.

situation: Dilbert presents a slide of product names that are not already trademarked. The Boss gestures toward his own crotch and asks for names that don't evoke that part of the body. Dilbert replies that the remaining choices are accused war criminals and slang for masturbation.
punchline: Every decent product name is already trademarked, so the only ones left are either offensive or crude, a sarcastic comment on how impossible it is to name a product.
summary: A presenter discovers that once trademarks and embarrassing anatomy are ruled out, the only product names left are terrible ones.

file: 2010/2010-04-23_write press releases_investors_sitting on coal_diamonds_annoyed_angry_too much description_clenching_eyes closed_mouth open.gif
title: Coal Into Diamonds Press Release

transcript.text: By clench-ing.

transcript.speaker: Tina

The Boss starts to explain the method, 'by clenching', and Tina angrily realizes the crude metaphor he is describing.
punchline: The Boss's investor-friendly spin is an unintentionally crude image of squeezing coal into diamonds with one's buttocks, and Tina's furious 'I got it!' shows she understands exactly how absurd and insulting the assignment is.
summary: A manager hands his employee a press-release job built on a vulgar metaphor about turning coal into diamonds, and she gets the joke with visible disgust.

title: Boss Denies Promising Funding

transcript.text: I finished the business case.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably said something that sounded like "I will get funding" and you heard it wrong.

transcript.text: What exactly sounds like "I will get funding"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Landfill wet hunting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not even a good try!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shake it off.

setting: Office, Dilbert's cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert delivers a finished business case and reminds his boss that he promised to seek funding if the numbers looked good. The boss flatly denies ever saying it, then claims Dilbert misheard him, and when pressed offers a nonsensical phrase that supposedly sounded like the promise. Dilbert loses his temper and the boss tells him to shake it off. The strip opens with a banner of Dogbert on a stool and Dilbert presenting a slide.
punchline: The boss's absurd excuse that "landfill wet hunting" could be misheard as "I will get funding" shows he will say anything to dodge a commitment, then brushes off Dilbert's justified anger.
summary: A manager wriggles out of a funding promise by blaming an implausible mishearing, leaving his employee fuming.

title: Admiring Your Consistently Bad Decisions

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Would you like my opinion on how you should handle that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure, I'll just try to ignore the fact that your entire career has been a colorful tapestry of bad decisions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So... yes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I admire your consistency.

situation: A coworker stands at Dilbert's cubicle and offers his opinion on how Dilbert should handle a problem. Dilbert sarcastically says he will try to ignore the coworker's long record of bad decisions. The confused coworker asks if that means yes, and Dilbert replies that he admires his consistency.
punchline: Dilbert backhandedly compliments the coworker's reliability at making bad decisions, implying his advice is worthless while sounding polite enough to leave the coworker unsure whether he was insulted.
summary: A well-meaning colleague offers advice and gets a sarcastic reply that turns his history of blunders into a left-handed compliment.

title: Wally Previews the Lion's Pecs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, did you review the client's specs like I asked you to?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Wally
