transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would I ask you to preview a lion's pecs?!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So... now you want me to question everything you say?

setting: Conference table in an office meeting
situation: Dilbert asks Wally whether he reviewed the client's specs, and Wally claims he misheard the request as 'preview the lion's pecs.' Dilbert angrily points out how absurd that request would be. Wally turns it around by suggesting Dilbert now wants him to question everything he says.
punchline: Wally uses an absurd fake mishearing as an excuse for not doing his work, then deflects blame by turning Dilbert's outrage into a criticism of Dilbert's own instructions.
summary: A coworker dodges accountability for skipping an assignment by blaming a ridiculous mishearing and then flipping the blame onto the person who asked.

title: Feng Shui Excuse Backs Employee Into Corner

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I couldn't work this week because my workspace has bad feng shui.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know feng shui is a real thing because our CEO hired a feng shui consultant to design his office.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you agree, or are you saying that our CEO is a superstitious simpleton?

situation: At a meeting, an employee claims he couldn't work all week because his workspace had bad feng shui. The Boss accepts the excuse as legitimate because the CEO hired a feng shui consultant for his own office. He then holds out a microphone and asks the employee to either agree or call the CEO a superstitious simpleton.
punchline: The Boss turns a flimsy excuse into a trap by making any challenge to it an insult to the CEO, so the employee has no safe way to disagree.
summary: A worker's mystical excuse for skipping work gets validated by his boss through a rhetorical trap that ties the idea's legitimacy to the CEO's reputation.

title: Cabbage Blamed for Computer Trouble

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was it human error?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I doubt it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No human would be that stupid. My best guess is that a cabbage got access to your computer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cabbages can't use computers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can they tell when they're being mocked?

situation: The Boss sits at his computer and asks Dilbert, who stands behind him, whether a computer problem was caused by human error. Dilbert says no human would be that stupid and suggests a cabbage got access to the computer. When the Boss objects that cabbages can't use computers, Dilbert asks if they can tell when they're being mocked.
punchline: Dilbert is really insulting the Boss by implying that he, the person who used the computer, is stupider than a cabbage, and he covers the insult with a fake explanation.
summary: Dilbert diagnoses a computer fault by absurdly blaming a vegetable, while actually calling his boss dumber than produce.

title: Block of Wood Needs Pitchman

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your product is nothing but a piece of wood. You need a charismatic pitchman to make gullible consumers buy it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Normally that would be your job as CEO. Unfortunately, you remind people of a giant...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leader?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the CEO that his product is just a piece of wood and needs a charismatic pitchman to sell it to gullible consumers. He says the CEO would normally be that pitchman but is unsuitable because he resembles a giant something. The CEO hopefully guesses 'leader' and Dogbert agrees, though the unspoken word is clearly different.
punchline: Dogbert cuts off before saying the insulting word, and the CEO naively fills in a flattering one, with Dogbert's 'Exactly' sarcastically confirming the flattery while implying the real insult, a giant phallus.
summary: A consultant dog explains why a wooden product's vain executive can't be its own salesman, letting him hear a compliment where an insult was meant.

title: Salesman Wants Engineer Cross-Training

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I hate sales. Can you cross-train me to be an engineer?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absolutely. All you need is a time machine and a brain with twice as many folds as your current model.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Maybe I could try marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's just liquor and guessing.

situation: A salesman tells Dilbert he hates sales and asks to be cross-trained as an engineer. Dilbert, working on computer cables, says it would take a time machine and a much more complex brain. The salesman then suggests marketing, and Dilbert dismisses that as just liquor and guessing.
punchline: Dilbert insults the salesman's intelligence by saying engineering is impossible for him, then cynically describes marketing as nothing but drinking and guessing.
summary: A discontented salesperson hopes to switch careers, but an engineer mocks both his brainpower and the marketing field he considers next.

title: Researching on a Painfully Slow Phone

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: I can research that question with my phone's browser.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Much time passes.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: I found the Google!

situation: During a meeting, the boss offers to look up the answer to a question using his phone's browser. After a caption says much time passes, Alice, Dilbert and the boss have all aged into withered, cobwebbed old people. The boss finally announces he has found Google.
punchline: The boss's phone browser is so painfully slow that the meeting attendees age and practically die before he manages to reach Google's homepage, which he treats as a triumph.
summary: A manager's sluggish phone browser makes a simple lookup take so long that everyone at the table grows ancient waiting for it.

title: Shoulder Phone Scares Off Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a shoulder phone shaped like an old man's head. I invented it myself.

transcript.speaker: Shoulder phone (Dogbert)
transcript.text: Let's make soup from her bones, just like the others!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I shouldn't have told Dogbert it has auto-answer.

transcript.speaker: Shoulder phone (Dogbert)
transcript.text: Kiss me! Now!

setting: A crowded party with guests in the background, holding drinks
situation: At a party, Dilbert shows a woman his homemade shoulder phone shaped like an old man's head, hoping to impress her. The phone auto-answers a call from Dogbert, who shouts a creepy threat about making soup from her bones and then demands a kiss. The frightened woman runs away.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to impress a woman with his invention backfires when the auto-answer feature lets Dogbert's menacing prank call terrify her.
summary: A nerdy inventor's novelty phone gadget turns into a horror show when a prankster friend's call connects automatically in front of his date.

title: Software Can't Wear a Hat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to get our customers more involved in the product design cycle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We only have customers who are too dumb to check product reviews online.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Can it wear a hat like a monkey?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For the millionth time, software can't wear clothes.

setting: Conference room, then Dilbert's desk at the office
situation: In a meeting, Dilbert suggests involving customers in product design, then admits their customers are too dumb to even read online reviews. The Boss orders him to do it anyway, so Dilbert sits with a customer who asks absurd questions, such as whether the software can wear a hat like a monkey.
punchline: Involving clueless customers in design just produces ridiculous feature requests, and Dilbert has had to explain the same impossible demand over and over.
summary: Management insists on customer input into product design, and the result is a customer asking whether a program can dress up like a primate.

title: Placebo Questions Protect Secret Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need answers to these questions for a confidential project. I can't tell you more.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm a complete idiot and even I can deduce from your questions what the project must be.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I anticipated that, so some of you idiots are getting placebo questions.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well played.

setting: Office desk, in a meeting or interview
situation: Dilbert hands a coworker a sheet of questions for a confidential project without explaining its purpose. The coworker boasts that even an idiot could work out the secret project from the questions alone. Dilbert reveals that he gave some people decoy placebo questions, so the coworker's deduction may be wrong.
punchline: Dilbert outsmarts the coworker who thinks he has cracked the secret by having already planted fake questions, leaving the coworker unsure whether his deduction is correct.
summary: A man who proudly guesses a secret project from a questionnaire learns he may have been handed a deliberately misleading decoy version.

title: Patience As Excuse For Idleness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think my single point of contact died.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I haven't heard from him for three months. I don't know the name of his project or any other people on it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What have you been doing for three months?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you implying that patience is not a virtue?

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the Boss that his only contact on a project has apparently died. He admits he hasn't heard from the man in three months and doesn't know the project's name or anyone else involved. When the Boss asks what he has been doing all that time, Wally claims he was simply being patient.
punchline: Wally dresses up three months of doing nothing as the virtue of patience, deflecting blame by turning the Boss's question into a moral challenge.
summary: An employee who has gone months without work excuses his idleness by framing his inaction as admirable patience.

title: Scheduling a Meeting to Repeat Forgotten Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We agreed on about fifty things today, but you didn't take any notes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's schedule our next meeting to rehash all the stuff you'll forget from today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have your calendar with you?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No. Why do you ask?

setting: Conference table in an office meeting room
situation: Dilbert sits across a table from a coworker after a productive meeting and points out that the coworker took no notes on the fifty items they agreed on. He proposes a follow-up meeting to repeat everything the coworker will forget, then asks if the coworker has a calendar. The coworker, oblivious, says no and asks why.
punchline: The coworker's cheerful cluelessness proves Dilbert's point, since he won't remember to attend the meeting meant to cover what he'll forget.
summary: After a meeting full of agreements, Dilbert sarcastically suggests a repeat session for the note-less coworker, who blithely admits he has no calendar to schedule it.

title: Launching the Boss's Carcass Skyward

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss is stuck in our building's ductwork and presumed dead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can alert the proper authorities, or we can design a totally cool device to increase the duct pressure and propel his carcass into the stratosphere.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You had me at "carcass."

situation: Dilbert tells Alice, across a conference table, that the Pointy-Haired Boss is stuck in the building's ductwork and presumed dead. He offers two options: call the proper authorities, or build a cool device that uses duct pressure to blast the boss's carcass into the stratosphere. Alice enthusiastically picks the second option.
punchline: Alice parodies Jerry Maguire's "You had me at hello" to show that she is far more excited by the prospect of launching her dead boss into the sky than by any sensible, lawful response.
summary: Faced with their boss's apparent death in the air ducts, two coworkers eagerly choose to turn the situation into a fun engineering project rather than call for help.

title: Sarcastic Pottery Class Date Suggestion

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Maybe we could take a pottery class together.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. I love acquiring unattractive dishware in an expensive and inefficient way.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: It's called art.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we could whittle some art spoons too.

setting: Restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert and his date sit at a restaurant table holding menus. She suggests they take a pottery class together, and Dilbert sarcastically dismisses it as a costly, roundabout way of getting ugly dishes. When she says it's art, he sarcastically proposes whittling spoons to go with them.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the idea of pottery as art by sarcastically suggesting they also whittle spoons, continuing his dismissive take on handmade crafts.
summary: A dinner date proposes a shared hobby and Dilbert responds with deadpan sarcasm about homemade dishware and carved utensils.

title: Consultant-Assisted Corporate Suicide

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're a third-rate company in a dying industry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend consultant-assisted corporate suicide.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Will it hurt?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It might sting a little when you announce you're going to be a web-only company.

setting: Conference room during a consulting meeting
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells The Boss at a conference table that his company is third-rate and in a dying industry. He recommends 'consultant-assisted corporate suicide,' and The Boss nervously asks if it will hurt. Dogbert says the only sting will come from announcing a web-only strategy.
punchline: Going web-only is treated as the corporate equivalent of suicide, mocking trendy digital-transformation advice that consultants sell to struggling companies.
summary: A consultant dog bluntly tells a doomed company that its salvation is a painful, fashionable pivot to the internet.

file: 2010/2010-07-26_new product_military_weapon demo_new york harbor_light show_statue of liberty_stump_newspaper_entertainment.gif
title: Wally's Light Show Destroys Liberty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're planning to introduce our new military product with a light show in New York Harbor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, can you handle the weapon demo and the light show?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sure. What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're calling it "The Stump of Liberty."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No one is saying it was a boring show.

setting: Conference room, then the office a week later
situation: The Boss announces a military product launch with a light show in New York Harbor and hands the weapon demo and light show to Wally. Wally cheerfully accepts, asking what could go wrong. A week later Dilbert reads a newspaper reporting that the Statue of Liberty has been reduced to a stump, and Wally defends the outcome by noting the show was not boring.
punchline: The weapon demo evidently destroyed the Statue of Liberty, and Wally's only takeaway is that at least the show was entertaining.
summary: A lazy employee is trusted with a weapons demonstration over a famous harbor and the result is national embarrassment that he spins as a success.

file: 2010/2010-05-27_fired_pink slip_cleaned out desk_hold box_letter of reference_loser sign_angry_grit teeth_tease.gif
title: Letter of Reference: Just the L

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I cleaned out my desk. Would you be willing to give me a letter of reference?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How about the letter "L"? That seems about right.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Must... not... burn... bridges.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Too soon?

situation: A departing employee, holding a box of his belongings, asks the Boss for a letter of reference. The Boss holds up an "L" sign to his forehead and offers to give him the letter "L", calling him a loser. The employee grits his teeth, thinking he must not burn bridges, while the Boss smugly asks if the joke came too soon.
punchline: The Boss literally offers a letter, the letter "L" for loser, as the reference, mocking the employee who is forced to swallow his anger to preserve his professional reputation.
summary: A man leaving his job asks his superior for a recommendation and gets a cruel, literal joke instead, which he has to suppress his rage over.

title: Soulless Employee Seeks Marketing Transfer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our ombudsman took my soul in exchange for a favorable view.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like a transfer to marketing, where having no soul is widely considered an asset.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: I need someone who can make our product sound competitive without vomiting on his own copy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh!

setting: Office, then a marketing department meeting room
situation: Dilbert stands before The Boss and explains that the ombudsman took his soul in exchange for a favorable view. He asks for a transfer to marketing, where lacking a soul is an advantage. In a marketing meeting, a manager says he needs a writer who can make the product sound competitive without being sickened by his own copy, and Dilbert eagerly raises his hand.
punchline: Losing his soul makes Dilbert the ideal marketing candidate, implying marketing copy requires dishonesty that anyone with a conscience couldn't stomach.
summary: After selling his soul to the company's ombudsman, an employee discovers that this makes him perfectly qualified for a job writing marketing copy.

title: Objective: Enrich Parasitic Stockholders and Managers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You wrote that your objective for the year is to...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "...obscurely toil to increase the unearned wealth of our parasitic stockholders."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll add "and managers."

setting: The Boss's office, during an annual objectives review
situation: The Boss reads aloud from Dilbert's written yearly objective, which cynically says he will obscurely toil to increase the unearned wealth of parasitic stockholders. Dilbert sits silently with a phone to his ear while the Boss, instead of objecting, calmly writes in an addition. The middle panel shows an office building as the quote is read.
punchline: The Boss isn't offended by Dilbert's insulting description of stockholders; he simply wants managers added to the list of those who benefit from employees' toil.
summary: A manager reviewing an employee's brutally honest goal statement shrugs it off and merely amends it to include himself and his fellow managers as beneficiaries.

file: 2010/2010-05-02_work from home_bathrobe_distractions_challenge_determined_gas leak_sparks_baby in wall_ears up_frustrated_yell_mouth open.gif
title: Dogbert Distracts Dilbert Working From Home

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm working at home today so I can concentrate without any distractions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please don't disturb me. Nothing is so important that it can't wait.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I take that as a challenge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, please. . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you smell that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's nothing. I have to work now.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure it's a gas leak.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed that the lamp makes huge sparks every once in a while?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wouldn't worry. What's the worst thing that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I hear a baby trapped in the wall!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Get out of my head!

setting: Dilbert's home, where he works in a bathrobe at a desk and computer
situation: Dilbert, in his bathrobe, says he is working from home to avoid distractions and asks not to be disturbed. Dogbert takes this as a challenge and escalates, claiming first a smell, then a gas leak, then sparking lamps, and finally a baby trapped in the wall. Dilbert tries to ignore each one until he finally snaps.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately invents ever-worse emergencies to break Dilbert's concentration, proving that working at home does not protect you from distraction, and Dilbert ends up screaming at him.
summary: A man trying to work in peace at home is driven mad by his dog's increasingly alarming fake emergencies.

file: 2010/2010-03-11_eat donut_doughnut_feng shui_workflow energy_project_stack of papers_design specs_angry_superstition_science.gif
title: Feng Shui Workflow Energy Dump

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It's good feng shui to stand next to you because you absorb the workflow energy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I need someone to check all of these design specs before tomorrow morning.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Some people call it superstition, but I'm pretty sure it's a science.

situation: A bald coworker eating a donut tells Alice she is good to stand next to because she absorbs the workflow energy. A manager then arrives with a huge stack of design specs and hands them to Alice to check by tomorrow. The coworker, now safely out of the way, smugly says his feng shui theory is really a science.
punchline: The coworker's 'feng shui' claim is a cover for dodging work, since standing next to Alice lets her absorb all the incoming tasks instead of him.
summary: A donut-eating coworker praises a colleague's knack for soaking up workload, then watches her get buried in paperwork as his theory proves itself.

title: First Unit Lacks Boxed Features

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As lead software engineer, I give you the first unit of our ten thousand copy production run.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! I wish we'd designed it with the features listed on the box. That would have been awesome.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll put this with the other reminders of how my life could have been excellent.

setting: Office, with a final panel showing the exterior of the office building
situation: The Boss ceremonially hands Dilbert, the lead software engineer, the first finished unit from a production run of ten thousand. Dilbert examines the product and wistfully remarks that it doesn't have the features advertised on its box. The Boss is confused, and Dilbert says he will file it with his other reminders of lost potential.
punchline: The product shipped without the features promised on its packaging, and Dilbert deadpans that it joins his collection of reminders of how much better his life could have been.
summary: A manager proudly presents a freshly manufactured gadget to its engineer, who sadly notes that the real thing falls far short of what the packaging promises.

title: Magic Button Replaces Cost Estimates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a magic button.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any time you ask for cost estimates, I push the button and it guides me.

transcript.speaker: Button
transcript.text: Pull the numbers out of your...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only says the one thing.

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a handheld gadget he calls a magic button. He explains that whenever the Boss asks for cost estimates, he presses it and follows its guidance. In the last panel the button, which the Boss is now holding, issues a bold, cut-off instruction, and Dilbert notes it only ever says that one thing.
punchline: The button's only advice is the rude phrase 'pull the numbers out of your...' which exposes that cost estimates are really just made-up guesses.
summary: Dilbert hands his boss a gadget that supposedly guides his budgeting, but its single canned reply reveals how arbitrary his figures really are.

file: 2010/2010-02-10_boss_stuck_ductwork_device_pressure_push_shoot_foom_fly into the air_rocket_airplane_hang onto wing_koi pond.gif
title: Boss Launched From Ductwork Onto Airplane

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our device will create enough pressure to gently push our boss's carcass out of the ductwork.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: FOOM!

transcript.speaker: Pilot
transcript.text: This is Captain Sullenberger. Don't worry about the wing; I see a koi pond down there.

setting: Office ductwork, a rooftop, and the sky near an airliner
situation: Dilbert and Alice (with a tool belt) explain that their pressure device will gently free the stuck boss from the ductwork. Instead, the device blasts him out of the building's roof high into the air. In the final panel the pilot, Captain Sullenberger, announces over the intercom that he is ignoring the wing, where the boss is clinging, because he sees a koi pond to land in.
punchline: The 'gentle' push turns out to be a violent rocket launch that lands the boss on an airliner's wing, and the pilot, famous for ditching a plane in the Hudson River, cheerfully plans a water landing regardless of the boss clinging to the wing.
summary: A supposedly gentle pressure device fires the trapped boss skyward like a rocket, and he ends up clinging to the wing of a passenger jet piloted by a famous emergency-landing hero.

file: 2010/2010-10-19_evil_cat_director of human resources_sales bonus_raise target_boss_laugh_point_bend over_tail_annoyed_support_animals.gif
title: Catbert Mocks Moving Bonus Target

transcript.speaker: Employee

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I was hoping for some support.

When the employee says he was hoping for support, Catbert makes a crude joke by telling him to buy a cane and talk to his tail while bending over.
punchline: The employee asks for support and Catbert responds with a rude pun, literally offering a cane for support and sending him to talk to his rear end.
summary: A worker seeking sympathy about an ever-rising bonus goal gets laughter and an insulting gag from the feline HR chief.

title: Wally Blames Laziness on the Bible

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: The Bible says, "Good things come to those who wait."

transcript.text: So it's basically you against God. Let me know when you two get it sorted out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? There was thunder when he doubted you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I synchronize my excuses to weather forecasts.

setting: Boss's office, then the coffee area
situation: The Boss tells Wally to work with more urgency, and Wally replies by quoting the Bible about good things coming to those who wait. The Boss sarcastically tells him to take it up with God. Afterward Dilbert asks Wally whether lightning or thunder followed his doubt, and Wally admits he times his excuses to the weather forecast.
punchline: Wally cynically picks his excuses to coincide with predicted weather, so any thunder appears to be divine reaction rather than coincidence.
summary: Wally cites scripture to dodge working faster, then reveals he only does it when stormy weather is predicted.
keywords: good things come to those who wait

title: Idiots All The Way Down

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A technical writer misinterpreted the acronyms in my draft technical paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that's okay because my Pointy-Haired Boss will turn it into content-free bullet points and show it to idiots.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like stories with lots of idiots in them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Glad to help.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hillside, sitting on rocks
situation: Dilbert sits on a rock with Dogbert and explains that a technical writer garbled the acronyms in his technical paper. He says it won't matter because his boss will reduce it to empty bullet points and present it to other idiots. Dogbert says he enjoys stories full of idiots, and Dilbert replies that he's glad to help.
punchline: Dilbert's story about a chain of incompetence, from the writer to the boss to the audience, is exactly the kind of idiot-filled tale Dogbert enjoys, so Dilbert dryly says he's glad to supply it.
summary: A resigned engineer relays how his paper gets mangled at every stage by clueless people, much to his canine friend's amusement.

title: Hot Contract From Hell

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a Confusopoly consultant to help us design an extended warranty plan.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our goal is to scare people into buying insurance that doesn't cover anything.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can't tell you where the contract was designed, but be careful because it's still hot.

situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert, a Confusopoly consultant, to help design an extended warranty plan. Dogbert cheerfully states the goal is to frighten customers into buying insurance that covers nothing. He then hands over the contract with tongs and warns that it is still hot, with smoke rising from it.
punchline: The warranty contract was apparently drafted in hell, which is why it is still hot and fitting for a scam insurance product.
summary: A consultant dog delivers a deceptive insurance contract that is literally smoking from its fiery origins.

title: Technology Hospice Brings a Bazooka

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired the Dogbert Technology Hospice Service to ease the suffering of our dying technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dogbert will use compassion and. . . what was the other thing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bazooka.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Step away from the Windows XP!

setting: Conference room, then an office cubicle
situation: In a meeting, the Boss announces he has hired Dogbert's Technology Hospice Service to ease the suffering of obsolete technology. Dogbert says the service relies on compassion and a bazooka. In the final panel Dogbert aims a bazooka at an employee sitting at his old Windows XP computer and orders him to step away.
punchline: The 'compassionate' hospice for aging technology is really a bazooka-wielding euthanasia service that forcibly destroys old software and hardware, such as Windows XP, which users refuse to give up.
summary: A consultant dog offers end-of-life care for outdated computers, and his method turns out to be heavy weaponry.

file: 2010/2010-05-06_evil director of human resources_email_funny videos_angry_yell_mouth open_privacy_guess_hurts.gif

punchline: The employee's outrage over lost privacy was unnecessary, since Catbert's accusation was a lucky guess, yet the employee's embarrassment at being so predictable still hurts.
summary: A cat in charge of HR accuses a worker of wasting email on video links, then confesses he merely guessed it right.

title: Dilbert Camps Out at Phone Store

transcript.text: I'd like to waste the better part of my afternoon trying to upgrade my phone.

transcript.text: I'll just set up my sport chair, and use my laptop while you mumble and stare at your monitor for what seems like forever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look at me! I'm beating your system!

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: Quiet! I'm trying to stare.

situation: Dilbert walks into a cell phone store carrying a backpack and announces he expects to spend his whole afternoon upgrading his phone. He sets up a folding sport chair and opens his laptop to keep himself busy while the clerk stares at a monitor. The clerk, unamused, tells him to be quiet so he can keep staring.
punchline: Dilbert tries to outwit the slow, painful phone upgrade process by being productive while he waits, but the clerk's only concern is protecting his time-wasting staring.
summary: A customer arrives prepared for a marathon wait at a phone store, only to be shushed by a clerk who treats his sluggish computer stare as serious work.

title: Lunch Date Crashed By Bob

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Amber, would you like to go to lunch with me?

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: Sure!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!!! I'm in!

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: Do you mind if we bring Bob? I need to talk to him about his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that would be...

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: Hey, Bob. Meet us in the lobby.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Look at us! We're like the two Musketeers, plus Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There were three Musketeers.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'm pretty sure there were two.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... I just remembered I have a conference call at noon. You two go ahead without me.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: We're like the one Musketeer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just eat.

situation: Dilbert gleefully asks coworker Amber to lunch, thinking it is a date, but she invites Bob along to discuss his project. Bob jokes that they are the two Musketeers plus Dilbert, and Dilbert makes an excuse and bows out. In the last panel Dilbert ends up eating lunch alone with Bob after all, and Bob jokes that they are the one Musketeer.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to get a lunch date with Amber is ruined, and in the final panel he is stuck at lunch with just Bob, who cheerfully jokes about the shrinking number of Musketeers.
summary: A hoped-for lunch date turns into a third-wheel disaster for Dilbert when his coworker brings along an oblivious colleague.

title: Raising Bonus Threshold After Success

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ken, you've almost reached your sales bonus level with time to spare.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Obviously I set your bonus threshold too low. I'll need to adjust it upward retroactively.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Maybe I'm just a great salesperson!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the spirit! Stay hungry!

situation: The Boss tells a smiling salesman, Ken, that he is about to reach his sales bonus early. Rather than rewarding him, the Boss decides the target was set too low and says he will raise it retroactively. Ken protests that he may simply be a great salesperson, and the Boss cheerfully tells him to stay hungry.
punchline: Management treats an employee's strong performance as proof the goal was flawed, moving the bonus target so the reward is never paid out, while spinning it as motivation.
summary: A manager responds to a salesman's near-success by moving the goalposts so the promised bonus stays out of reach.

title: Deleting Data Based on Flawed Logic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to delete all of the unnecessary data from our servers to make room.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically it's ALL unnecessary because our decisions are always based on flawed logic anyway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you pretend some of it is necessary?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. Can you pretend I deleted the stuff that isn't?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to free up server space by deleting unnecessary data. Dilbert points out that all of the data is unnecessary because the company's decisions are always based on flawed logic. The Boss asks him to pretend some of it matters, and Dilbert agrees as long as the Boss pretends he actually did the deletion.
punchline: Both men agree to a mutual pretense, with Dilbert sarcastically implying that the data is useless and that no real cleanup will happen.
summary: A manager wants server space freed up, and the engineer offers a deal where both of them simply pretend the job was done properly.

title: Alice's Boyfriend Angry Jack

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet my new boyfriend, Angry Jack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People say my high level of engineering skill comes at the cost of good social judgment.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dilbert, his name is Angry Jack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he wants to hold my hand now.

situation: Alice introduces Dilbert to her new boyfriend, a scowling man with clenched fists named Angry Jack. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, comments that his engineering skill comes at the cost of social judgment, then misreads Jack's furious posture as a wish to hold hands. Alice has to point out that Angry Jack's name is a description of his mood.
punchline: Dilbert proves his own point about lacking social judgment by interpreting an obviously furious man's clenched fists as a friendly gesture.
summary: A socially clueless engineer fails to notice that his coworker's glowering new boyfriend is about to hit him.

title: Outsourced Afterlife at Helven

transcript.speaker: Dead Man
transcript.text: I think I died. Am I in Heaven or Hell?

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: You're in Helven. My name is Raj.

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: Heaven and Hell have been outsourcing souls to us since the demons and angels unionized.

transcript.speaker: Dead Man
transcript.text: So... is this place good or bad?

transcript.speaker: Raj
transcript.text: Well, you get a harp, but you won't like how we give it to you.

setting: A desert-like afterlife office with a desk and computer
situation: A newly deceased man with small horns asks whether he is in Heaven or Hell. Raj, a call-center-style worker wearing a halo and sitting at a computer, explains that he is in Helven, an outsourced afterlife processing center. Raj says Heaven and Hell outsource souls because their angels and demons unionized, and hints the harp comes with an unpleasant delivery.
punchline: Even the afterlife has been outsourced to a cut-rate offshore operation, and the 'reward' of a harp comes with the same poor service and hidden catches as any outsourced customer experience.
summary: A confused new arrival learns the afterlife has been farmed out to a third-party processor after the celestial and infernal workforces formed unions.

file: 2010/2010-04-03_plan_transfer_missile guidance engineering division_pour coffee_face front_unimportant tasks_destroy_fishing village_lazy.gif
title: Unimportant Tasks Protect Fishing Villages

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I asked for a transfer to our missile guidance engineering division.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Once they get to know me, they'll only give me unimportant tasks so I won't accidentally destroy a fishing village.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The great thing about unimportant tasks is that no one really cares if you do them.

setting: Office break area beside the coffee maker
situation: Wally pours coffee while chatting with Dilbert and explains that he has requested a transfer to the missile guidance engineering division. He expects the company to quickly learn his reputation and assign him only trivial work. He concludes that the real perk of unimportant tasks is that nobody minds whether they get done.
punchline: Wally has deliberately engineered his career so that his own incompetence is contained, and he cheerfully admits his real goal is to be paid while doing work nobody cares about.
summary: Wally plans to land a job near dangerous weapons technology, confident his reputation will ensure he is only trusted with meaningless busywork.

file: 2010/2010-10-22_friend matrix_coworker_sit at computer_computer expert_frisky friend_low standards.gif
title: Friend Resource Matrix Has Gaps

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm updating my friend resource matrix and I have a few gaps.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I already have a friend with a truck, a friend who gives me free tickets, and a friend with tools.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I've got openings for a computer expert friend and a frisky friend with low standards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try the computer one.

situation: A coworker holding a printed chart tells Dilbert he is updating his 'friend resource matrix' and lists the useful friends he already has. He says he has openings for a computer expert friend and a frisky friend with low standards. Dilbert, seated at his computer, chooses to apply for the computer expert role.
punchline: The coworker treats friendship as a resource-allocation exercise, and Dilbert, knowing the other opening is insulting, picks the computer expert slot, which means being used for free tech support.
summary: A man manages his friendships like a spreadsheet of useful assets and invites Dilbert to fill the vacant roles.
themes: being used for free tech support

title: Engineer Defends Veterinarian Nose Job

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I probably shouldn't have gone to a veterinarian for my nose job.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But as an engineer, I value function over form, and the airflow is actually quite good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You might be rationalizing a little.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I pity you with your inefficient nostrils.

setting: Lunch table in a break room or cafeteria
situation: Three coworkers eat lunch together while Asok admits he made a poor choice by having a veterinarian perform his nose job. He defends it by claiming an engineer's preference for function over form, citing improved airflow. When Dilbert suggests he is rationalizing, Asok turns it around and says he pities Dilbert's inefficient nostrils.
punchline: Asok doubles down on a bad decision by dismissing normal noses as inefficient, using engineering logic to rationalize his botched cosmetic surgery.
summary: A coworker defends his animal-doctor-performed nose surgery by boasting of its superior ventilation and mocking everyone else's ordinary nostrils.

title: Engineers Duel With Dueling Links

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How engineers duel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your data are weak.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Make your move!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sending you a link!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm sending you three links!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have time for this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Winner!

situation: Under the heading 'How engineers duel', Dilbert insults a coworker's data and the coworker challenges him to make a move. They trade escalating attacks by texting web links to each other on their phones. Dilbert gives up because he doesn't have time to read all the links, and the coworker celebrates his win.
punchline: An engineers' duel is won not by being right but by burying the opponent in so many reference links that he gives up from lack of time.
summary: Two engineers settle a data dispute by flooding each other's phones with web links until one quits.

file: 2010/2010-05-14_computer_engineer_worst user interface_click_sell social security number_overhead view of cubicle_technology_engineering.gif
title: Random Clicking Sells Your Identity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The world's greatest engineer prepares to do battle with the world's worst user interface.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click click.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope that did something.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Your social security number has been sold.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer, thinking of himself as a great engineer about to take on a terrible user interface. A wide view of his cubicle shows him clicking furiously and randomly. He hopes his clicking accomplished something, and the computer announces that his social security number has been sold.
punchline: Dilbert's blind, desperate clicking on a confusing interface did accomplish something, but it was disastrous, as he unwittingly authorized the sale of his personal data.
summary: A confident engineer mashes buttons on a baffling program and discovers the result is selling his own private identification details.

title: Sarcasm Aimed at Rolling Forecasts

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to move to a rolling forecast.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, the problem is that forecasts are worthless, and your solution is to do more of them?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If my sarcasm is a problem, I can solve that by doing more of it.

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Snork

situation: At a meeting table, The Boss announces he is switching to a rolling forecast. Dilbert sarcastically points out that forecasts are worthless and the boss's fix is to make more of them. The boss misreads the sarcasm as a problem to be fixed and suggests solving it by doing more sarcasm, while a bald coworker snorts coffee in amusement.
punchline: The boss applies the same flawed logic Dilbert just mocked, solving a problem by doing more of it, which makes Dilbert's sarcasm point land even harder.
summary: A manager's plan to produce more of a useless report draws a sarcastic jab, and his reply repeats the very same faulty reasoning.

title: Dogbert Defends Pessimistic Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not right to use your tech support job to trick people into hurting themselves.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I help people take their minds off of hopeless technical problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know a problem is hopeless?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great. So now pessimism is a crime?

situation: Dilbert sits on a stool and confronts Dogbert, who works tech support wearing a headset, about tricking callers into hurting themselves. Dogbert claims he is merely distracting people from hopeless technical problems. When Dilbert asks how he knows a problem is hopeless, Dogbert deflects by accusing him of criminalizing pessimism.
punchline: Dogbert dodges the accusation that he declares problems hopeless to manipulate callers by indignantly defending his pessimism as if it were being outlawed.
summary: A cynical help-desk dog brushes off a coworker's ethical objection by claiming gloomy outlooks should be perfectly legal.

title: Demo Unit Borrowed, Splatter Zone Warning

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: A salesman borrowed the demo unit that you flew across the country to see.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Can I show you something totally irrelevant so this doesn't feel so awkward?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a minute to get out of the splatter zone.

setting: Vendor's office or showroom with a computer on a counter
situation: Dilbert and a woman colleague have flown across the country to see a product demo, only to be told by a salesman that another salesman borrowed the demo unit. The salesman awkwardly offers to show them something irrelevant to ease the tension. Dilbert asks for a minute to get clear of the splatter zone, because his angry colleague is about to explode.
punchline: Dilbert recognizes that his furious coworker is about to erupt at the salesman and politely asks for time to move out of range of the fallout.
summary: After a wasted cross-country trip, a salesman's clumsy attempt to soften the blow leaves Dilbert stepping away from his visibly furious companion.

title: Dilbert Critiques Dogbert's Critic Advice

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A good leader cultivates internal critics so all sides of an argument are heard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For example, I cultivated Dilbert to argue the point I just made.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your premise is that a leader is not qualified to make decisions without the help of critics.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But selecting the appropriate critic is itself a decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There is no reason to assume a leader is any better at selecting a critic than he is at making any other decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your overpaid consultant is recommending that you add randomness to an already flawed process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In summary, this meeting is a waste of time, and your consultant is ripping you off.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How great was that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You owe me $400 for my time.

setting: Conference room during a consulting session, with a projector screen showing the Dilbert logo
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that good leaders cultivate internal critics, and says he cultivated Dilbert to argue his point. Dilbert then logically dismantles the advice, pointing out that choosing a critic is itself a decision and that the consultant is wasting the Boss's time and ripping him off. Dogbert then cheerfully bills the Boss $400 for the demonstration.
punchline: Dogbert planted Dilbert as a critic to attack his own consulting advice, and then charges the Boss for the meeting that proved it was worthless.
summary: A consultant stages a debate in which his own colleague trashes his advice, then bills the manager for the privilege.

title: False Memory Of Marketing Sign-Off

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told you to get a sign-off from Marketing before you sent this around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How vivid is your false memory of that conversation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's plenty vivid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were unicorns involved?

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert for sending out a document without getting Marketing's sign-off, claiming he had told him to do so. Dilbert insists no such conversation took place and suggests the Boss is remembering something that never happened. When the Boss says his memory is vivid, Dilbert asks whether unicorns were part of it.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss's vivid recollection is as imaginary as a fantasy creature, mocking his tendency to blame others for instructions he never actually gave.
summary: Accused of skipping an approval step he was never told about, an employee gently suggests his manager invented the instruction in his own head.

title: Brainstorming Customer Trust, Rejecting Honesty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can we rebuild the trust of our customers? Let's brainstorm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could stop using misleading benchmark tests to sell shoddy products that have hidden costs.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I heard someone say "lie." Let's write that one down.

setting: Conference room with a flip chart
situation: The Boss leads a meeting at a flip chart headed "Trust" and asks for ideas on rebuilding customer trust. Dilbert raises his hand and suggests the company stop using misleading benchmarks to sell shoddy products with hidden costs. The Boss mishears this as the word "lie" and eagerly writes it on the chart as a brainstorming idea.
punchline: The Boss turns an honest suggestion to stop deceiving customers into a proposal to lie, showing that management thinks deception is the way to build trust.
summary: A manager asking how to win back customer confidence hears a plea for honesty as an endorsement of fibbing and adds it to the list.

title: Hoping a Slug Will Hurry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My success depends on you doing your role in a timely and energetic manner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People say you're a big, fat slug, but I have confidence in you. I'll stick this to your slimy face and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to think I'm a pretty good judge of character.

situation: Dilbert sits at a desk facing a large, lumpy slug and tells him that his own success depends on the slug performing his role quickly and energetically. He acknowledges the slug's reputation for being fat and lazy, then sticks a sheet of paper to the slug's slimy face and hopes it gets done. He closes by saying he considers himself a good judge of character.
punchline: Dilbert's claim to be a good judge of character is ironic, since he is entrusting an important task to a creature famed for being slow and slimy, which implies he is setting himself up for failure or has no better option.
summary: A man hands an important task to a notoriously sluggish slug and optimistically trusts his own instincts about who deserves his confidence.

file: 2010/2010-04-01_feedback_website design_computer_eyes wide_psychopath_photo wall_toe fungus_despair_yell_mouth open_scared_pain_satan_licking_brain_tone down_hair stand up_technology.gif
title: Brutally Honest Website Design Feedback

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I need your honest feedback on our new website design.

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I'll say, "Needs work."

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It feels like Satan is licking my brain!

situation: A coworker asks Asok for honest feedback on the company's new website design. Asok launches into vivid, brutal insults about the layout and colors. He then says he will tone it down and just say it needs work, while visibly staring in horror at the screen and shouting an even worse description.
punchline: Asok claims he is toning down his criticism to something polite, but his shouted inner reaction shows the design is truly horrifying.
summary: A coworker begs for candid opinions on a website redesign and gets a scathing review that is only a diplomatic version of the real horror.

title: Booking Every Room to Skip Meetings

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I propose an unholy alliance.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Assistant
transcript.text: You have my attention.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reserve every meeting room under my name for the year. That way you won't need to do any scheduling, and I won't need to attend any meetings.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't panic; that strange feeling is you falling in love with me.

transcript.speaker: Administrative Assistant
transcript.text: It feels like I'm eating cheese!

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, proposes a deal to his administrative assistant: she books every meeting room in his name for the whole year. That spares her from scheduling work and spares him from attending meetings. She is delighted, and he tells her the strange feeling is love.
punchline: The Boss smugly interprets her delight at doing less work as love for him, while she cheerfully compares the feeling to eating cheese, showing how easily laziness is dressed up as a favor.
summary: A manager and his assistant strike a cheerfully lazy bargain that lets both of them dodge meetings and scheduling for a whole year.

file: 2010/2010-04-15_nose job_question_art department_veterinarian_dog nose_snout_artistic statement_hot_airflow_sit in chairs.gif

transcript.speaker: Asok

situation: Asok visits the art department, where a female artist with a bird perched on her head studies his nose. She asks whether it is a botched nose job or a bold artistic statement. Asok replies that it began as a mistake but he is keeping it because it improves his airflow.
punchline: Asok tries to spin an accidental disfigurement as a deliberate, practical choice, hoping the artist finds it attractive, while her only concern is whether it counts as hot.
summary: An artist sizes up a coworker's odd-looking nose and wonders whether it is an error or a statement, and he awkwardly claims it as a feature.

title: Pirated Copy of Boss's Quote Book

setting: Conference room table during a lunch meeting
situation: Wally announces that his book of the Pointy-Haired Boss's quotes will soon be published and make him rich. Dilbert cheerfully says he looks forward to getting a pirated copy, and Wally suggests he could just buy it. The Boss, sitting between them, is confused because he thought the work was a book.
punchline: The Boss doesn't realize he is the source of the quotes, and his remark suggests his own statements are so foolish that he doesn't recognize them, while Dilbert jokes about pirating rather than paying for the book.
summary: A coworker's plan to profit from compiling the boss's foolish sayings meets a casual vow to steal it and a clueless reaction from the boss himself.

title: Handsome Translator Makes Dilbert Sound Better

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The translator will repeat everything you say, word for word, but he'll say it more handsomely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What's he jabbering about?

setting: Boss's office, then a conference room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the customer is an attractive young woman, so he must bring a handsome man along to translate. The translator is supposed to repeat Dilbert's words exactly but deliver them more handsomely. At the meeting, Dilbert simply says hi and the customer asks the translator what he is jabbering about.
punchline: The customer can't understand Dilbert at all, since the translator is meant to be a good-looking mouthpiece for a language she already speaks, and she clearly treats Dilbert as irrelevant in favor of the handsome man.
summary: A manager sends a good-looking stand-in to speak for his engineer in a sales meeting, and the customer ends up ignoring the engineer entirely.

file: 2010/2010-04-10_powerpoint proboscis_medical condition_nose grows_long nose_lie_pinocchio_garbage man_advice_corporate whistle-blower_nose through garbage bag.gif

situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man that his nose grows whenever his co-workers lie. The garbage man jokes that it might whistle and calls Dilbert a budding corporate whistle-blower. When Dilbert asks if the garbage man is lying, the man admits it, and Dilbert's nose grows long enough to poke through the garbage bag.
punchline: The garbage man lies on purpose just to watch Dilbert's nose grow, turning the whistle-blower pun into a real demonstration.
summary: A trash collector teases a man with a lie-detecting nose, then fibs deliberately to see the nose stretch.

transcript.text: I can't justify changing my priorities without one.

transcript.speaker: Woman

punchline: The manager hands out placebo 'stress pills' that make employees forget his bureaucratic obstruction, claiming they solve 20% of his problems, which means he fixes his own problems by pacifying people rather than by fixing the process.
summary: A stonewalling manager calms an angry coworker with fake pills that wipe her memory of his red tape, then admits the trick only partially works for him.

title: Chain Letter Panic Over Friends

transcript.text: Oh no. If I don't forward this e-mail to fifty friends, I'll die within a week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't have that many friends! I need to make more friends, and fast!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you sending him now?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm upping it to sixty friends.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss reads a chain e-mail claiming he will die within a week unless he forwards it to fifty friends. He panics because he doesn't have that many friends. Dilbert asks Wally what he is sending the Boss, and Wally reveals he is raising the demand to sixty friends.
punchline: Wally is the one behind the chain e-mail and is deliberately escalating the Boss's gullible panic by increasing the required number of friends.
summary: A gullible manager frets over a superstitious forwarded message while a coworker cheerfully tightens the screws on him.

title: Satisfaction Doubles By Firing Smart People

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yeff!!!

punchline: Employee satisfaction only 'doubled' from a tiny 1% to 2%, and the supposed cause is firing smart people, which leaves the survivors safe and cheerful while the brilliant Asok is the one in danger.
summary: A manager brags about a trivially small satisfaction increase and attributes it to purging the intelligent staff, leaving the brightest intern terrified.

title: Boss Doesn't Worry About Others' Jobs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wouldn't worry about losing your job after the merger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because you put in a good word for me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's more of an observation that I don't worry about other people's jobs.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, stops by Dilbert's cubicle and tells him not to worry about losing his job after the merger. Dilbert hopefully assumes the Boss has recommended him to someone. The Boss clarifies that he simply doesn't worry about anyone else's job.
punchline: The Boss's apparent reassurance is really an admission of indifference to his employees' job security, not a promise of protection.
summary: A manager's seemingly comforting words about an upcoming merger turn out to mean he just doesn't care what happens to his staff.

title: Empowered Intern Fires Boss Instantly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I want you to make decisions as if you owned the company.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Clear out your desk, you worthless bag of meat!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sorry. The fake power went to my head for a moment.

situation: The Boss tells Asok, the intern, to make decisions as if he owned the company. Asok immediately points at The Boss and orders him to clear out his desk, insulting him. Realizing what he has done, Asok apologizes, saying the fake power went to his head.
punchline: Being handed pretend authority instantly corrupts even the humblest employee, and Asok's reaction shows how hollow and intoxicating empowerment talk from management can be.
summary: A manager's encouragement to act like an owner prompts his intern to abruptly fire him before sheepishly backing down.

title: Devil Ombudsman Goes to Helen Fry

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Helen, we're looking for a new ombudsman. Your experience in the afterlife makes you an ideal candidate.

transcript.speaker: Helen
transcript.text: I'll take the job. But call me Mrs. Fry.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I have an issue with management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go to Helen Fry.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Yes, I know it's an old joke.

situation: The Boss offers a red devil named Helen the job of company ombudsman, citing her experience in the afterlife. She accepts but insists on being addressed as Mrs. Fry. Later, an employee complains about management and the Boss sends him to Helen Fry, with a caption admitting the joke is old.
punchline: The pun on 'Go to hell, fry' is delivered via the devil's name, and the strip acknowledges with a caption that it is a well-worn joke.
summary: A demon is hired as the company complaint handler, and her name turns a gripe about management into a classic insult.

title: Tweeting the Boss's Hypocritical Priorities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our highest priority is satisfying our customers... except when it is hard... or unprofitable... or we're busy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click click click click click click click click click click

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you tweeting my quotes?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Book deal! Cha-ching!!!

situation: The Boss lectures his team that customer satisfaction is the top priority, then lists a string of exceptions. The employees quietly start typing on their phones, and when the Boss asks if they are tweeting his quotes, one gleefully replies that he sees a book deal in them.
punchline: The Boss's self-contradicting statement about customer service is so absurd that his employees see it as perfect material to publish, mocking how routinely companies say customers come first while acting otherwise.
summary: A manager's hollow pledge to prioritize customers is cheerfully live-tweeted by his staff, who sense a profitable collection of ridiculous quotes.

title: Boss Stuck in Ductwork Machine

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Boss is stuck in the ductwork.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The turbo blower kicks in after the lubricant cycle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're sure he's already dead, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Help!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Arguably, the real crime here would be building a machine this cool and not using it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can anyone hear me?

setting: A maintenance area next to a large machine with a ventilation duct
situation: The Boss is trapped inside a ventilation duct while Alice and Dilbert stand beside a machine with a turbo blower and lubricant cycle. Dilbert asks whether the Boss is already dead, and the Boss calls out for help from inside the duct. Alice argues that the real crime would be leaving such a cool machine unused.
punchline: Alice and Dilbert callously ignore the Boss's cries for help, preferring to treat him as dead so they can enjoy running their cool machine on him.
summary: Two employees eye a fancy machine that could flush their trapped manager out of the air duct and decide that leaving it idle would be the greater wrong.

file: 2010/2010-03-03_victor_project_goat head_upset_angry_awful_slap_help_ask_wind up_stand on one leg_cringe_hard hit_dolphin head_change species_seeing stars_messy hair.gif
title: Slapping a Goat Into a Dolphin

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice, a horrible accident has given me a goat head. I need you to slap me so hard that I change species from the neck up.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hold still, Asok. This might take a few tries.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two hours later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dolphin is close! One more should do it.

situation: Asok, who has a goat head after an accident, asks Alice to slap him so hard that his head changes into another species. Alice agrees and kicks him, warning it may take several tries. Two hours later Asok has a dolphin head and Alice says one more hit should finish the job.
punchline: Alice treats slapping a coworker into a different species as a routine task and, after two hours of repeated violence, happily reports progress even though the result is only a different animal head.
summary: A coworker with an accidental animal head enlists a colleague's violence to cycle through species, and she cheerfully keeps at it for hours.

title: Wally Blames Boss for Lost Inspiration

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, have you made any progress coding your module?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Progress is difficult to measure in the software realm.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You could measure the lines of code I produce, but that would reward inefficiency.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The art of this job is binding the rare moments of inspiration to knowledge and machines.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: In fact, just a minute ago I could feel the inspiration welling up inside me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But then you interrupted me with your naive question and the moment was lost.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe you should go back to your office and reflect on the damage you've done here today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There goes the one person who has less of a real job than I do.

setting: Wally's office cubicle area (Sunday strip with a title banner showing Dilbert presenting the logo on a screen)
situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he has made progress coding his module. Wally, holding his coffee mug, gives a pompous speech about how progress can't be measured in software and claims the Boss's question destroyed his moment of inspiration. The Boss grits his teeth and leaves, thinking that Wally has even less of a real job than he does.
punchline: Wally dodges accountability by turning a simple progress check into an accusation, and the Boss, grudgingly impressed, admits that Wally has an even more pointless job than his own.
summary: A lazy engineer turns his manager's routine status question into a lecture on creative genius and blames him for ruining the muse.

title: Dogbert Sells Customer Data, Fake Name

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert consults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your customer data is worth a fortune.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll find you some buyers if you give me 25%.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What about privacy?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's not a problem. I never use my real name.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that his company's customer data is extremely valuable and offers to find buyers in exchange for a 25% cut. When the Boss raises the issue of customer privacy, Dogbert dismisses it by saying he never uses his real name.
punchline: Dogbert treats privacy as only his own concern, protecting his identity while happily selling everyone else's personal data.
summary: A consultant dog offers to sell a company's customer information for a commission and brushes off privacy worries by pointing out he personally stays anonymous.

file: 2010/2010-05-18_raise_face front_budget_better than nothing_annoyed_yell_mouth open_close eyes_shake fist_angry.gif
title: Raise Offer With Budget Loophole

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you help bring in a new account, I'll give you a raise, unless there's no money in the budget then for raises.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please don't say what I think you're going to say next.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better than nothing.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: No it isn't!

situation: The Boss promises Alice a raise if she helps land a new account, but adds that there will be no raise if the budget has no money for raises. Alice, anticipating a feeble justification, begs him not to say it, and he says it's better than nothing. She shouts back angrily, shaking her fist.
punchline: The raise is conditional on money that probably won't exist, so the offer is effectively worthless, and the Boss's 'better than nothing' defence is the exact cliche Alice dreaded.
summary: A manager dangles a conditional pay bump that may not exist, and his frustrated employee explodes at his lame defence of it.

file: 2010/2010-04-24_good news_raise fist_wireless network_bad news_knowledge_lack of understanding.gif
title: Winning Bid Without Wireless Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news! We won the bid to build a nationwide wireless network!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bad news! We don't know how to build a nationwide wireless network!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's wireless. How hard could it be to not install wires?

situation: The Boss approaches Dilbert's cubicle and announces that the company has won a bid to build a nationwide wireless network. He then admits the company has no idea how to build one. He dismisses the problem by claiming that the job is simply a matter of not installing wires.
punchline: The Boss trivializes a complex engineering project by reducing it to the absence of wires, showing he has no grasp of what the work involves.
summary: After landing a huge contract his company is unqualified to fulfil, a clueless manager brushes off the difficulty by joking that all you do is leave out the cables.

title: New Boss Cancels Predecessor's Projects

transcript.speaker: New Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to cancel your project because my predecessor supported it.

transcript.speaker: New Boss
transcript.text: And I'll need a list of any children he fathered with the staff. It's best if you don't ask why.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think he. . .

transcript.speaker: New Boss
transcript.text: We all do. It's how we let off steam.

setting: A manager's office with a large desk and high-backed chair
situation: A newly installed senior manager tells the Pointy-Haired Boss that his project is being cancelled simply because the previous manager backed it. He then asks for a list of any children his predecessor fathered with employees, and when the Boss tries to object, he casually says that everyone in management does this to let off steam.
punchline: The new boss's petty, purge-the-old-regime project cancellation escalates into a casual admission of workplace misconduct, which he dismisses as a normal stress-relief habit.
summary: A freshly arrived executive scraps a project out of spite for his predecessor, then shockingly requests a tally of the former boss's workplace offspring.

title: Therapist Profits From App Addiction

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't stop buying phone apps that I don't need. Am I crazy?

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Yes, you are totally batspit crazy. You'll need many sessions.

transcript.speaker: Therapist (thought)
transcript.text: Steve Jobs isn't the only one who can do marketing.

situation: A woman lying on a couch tells her therapist she compulsively buys phone apps she doesn't need and asks if she is crazy. The therapist enthusiastically declares her totally crazy and says she will need many sessions. In his private thought, he compares his sales tactic to Steve Jobs' marketing.
punchline: The therapist exaggerates her diagnosis to sell her more sessions, using the same manipulative marketing that gets people to buy unneeded apps.
summary: A shopaholic for apps seeks help, and her therapist cunningly turns her worry into a long-term paying arrangement.

title: Crime Scene Cleaner at Singles Mixer

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I love your tie-dyed overalls. That's a bold look.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, my job is cleaning crime scenes. I didn't have time to change.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The singles scene is all about how you look.

setting: A crowded singles mixer with a bar, then Dilbert's living room
situation: At a singles event, a woman compliments Dilbert's colorful tie-dyed overalls. Dilbert explains that the stains are from his job cleaning crime scenes and that he had no time to change. Back at home, Dogbert sits on the couch and tells him that appearance is everything in the singles scene.
punchline: Dilbert's 'tie-dye' overalls are actually stained with the residue of crime scenes, which will sink his dating prospects since singles culture is judged on looks.
summary: A flattering remark about a flamboyant outfit turns grim when its wearer reveals the stains come from his gruesome day job, leaving his dog to deliver a blunt verdict on his romantic odds.

title: Asok Volunteers as Buzzword Idiot

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tradition requires that every meeting has one buzzword-babbling idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have no naturals today, so Asok has graciously agreed to fill the role.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Good job. You're totally selling it.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We need a multi-platform application strategy!

situation: Dilbert explains to the meeting that every gathering needs someone spouting buzzwords. Since nobody there is naturally suited to the role, he announces that Asok has agreed to play the part. Asok then blurts out a jargon-filled demand, and Alice compliments how convincingly he does it.
punchline: Asok's fake buzzword nonsense is indistinguishable from the real thing, which shows how common meaningless jargon is in meetings.
summary: A meeting gets a designated jargon-spouter, and the volunteer's performance is so authentic that it earns praise.

title: Honest Estimate or Happy Lie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will it take to fix the bugs in our control management software?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want a realistic estimate that will ruin your day, or a lie that will allow your ignorance and your happiness to lock arms and square dance to the next cubicle?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That second option sounds festive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a pleaser.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long it will take to fix the bugs in the control management software. Dilbert offers him a choice between a realistic estimate that will upset him or a comforting lie. The Boss cheerfully picks the lie, and Dilbert happily obliges.
punchline: The Boss knowingly prefers a comforting false estimate over the truth, and Dilbert sarcastically presents his dishonesty as being helpful.
summary: Offered the choice between a grim honest schedule and a cheerful fabrication, a manager happily opts for the fib.

title: Scanner Breaks When Documents Matter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you scan this document for me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it important?

transcript.speaker: Alice
