transcript.text: If it isn't important, you shouldn't bother me. If it is, the scanner will malfunction.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there no room for hope?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I keep mine in this empty candy jar.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, Alice, to scan a document for him. She says she'll only do it if it's unimportant, because the scanner always malfunctions on important documents. When Dilbert asks if there is any room for hope, she holds up an empty candy jar and says that's where she keeps hers.
punchline: Alice's hope is literally an empty jar, showing how thoroughly office equipment's failures have crushed her optimism.
summary: A coworker explains that the office scanner only breaks when a task truly matters, then sardonically admits her hope is stored in an empty container.

title: Human, Squirrel, or Anvil Comprehension

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, explain to Logan the technical issue in terms he can understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure. What's his comprehension level? Are we talking human, squirrel or anvil?

transcript.speaker: Logan
transcript.text: Which one am I?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't make this awkward.

transcript.speaker: Logan
transcript.text: Did the squirrel go to a community college?

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to explain a technical issue to a coworker named Logan in terms he can understand. Dilbert sarcastically asks whether Logan's comprehension level is human, squirrel or anvil, and Logan sincerely asks which one he is. The Boss tells them not to make it awkward, and Logan then asks whether the squirrel went to community college.
punchline: Logan is so oblivious that he misses the insult and, even when it's implied he's below human level, only wonders whether the squirrel is better educated than he is.
summary: A sarcastic offer to dumb down a technical explanation backfires into an awkward exchange when the target takes the insult literally and fishes for where he ranks.

title: Non-Standard Means Useful, Wordsmith

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My software is so old that I can't open any files that people send me.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I can't upgrade your computer because then it will be non-standard.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And by non-standard, you mean useful?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Be gone, Wordsmith!

situation: An employee tells Mordac, the head of information services, that her software is so outdated she cannot open files sent by colleagues and asks for an upgrade. Mordac refuses, claiming an upgrade would make her computer non-standard. She points out that non-standard seems to mean useful, and Mordac angrily dismisses her.
punchline: The employee sarcastically exposes that IT's insistence on standardization really means preventing anything useful, and Mordac can only respond by shooing her away.
summary: An IT gatekeeper denies a needed computer upgrade to keep everything standard, and an employee's sharp retort about usefulness gets her thrown out.

title: Wooden Stakes at the Funeral

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you think he's really dead?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I brought a wooden stake just in case.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Me too, just in case the afterlife rejects him.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's legal, right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Spouse?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did anyone think to bring a mallet?

setting: A funeral viewing next to an open casket
situation: Coworkers stand around an open casket at a funeral, quietly doubting whether the deceased, apparently The Boss, is really dead. Several of them have brought wooden stakes to be sure, and when they realize they lack a mallet, Alice asks if anyone brought one.
punchline: The coworkers treat their boss like a vampire and come to his funeral armed to make sure he stays dead, revealing how much they dislike him.
summary: Mourners at a funeral each bring a wooden stake to make sure the dead manager never returns, then realize nobody packed a mallet.

title: Extra Staff Make Projects Slower

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How long will your project take if I add two people?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Add one month for training, one month for the extra complexity, and one month to deal with their drama.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But after all of that . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They'll be as useful as this meeting.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long his project would take if two more people were assigned to it. Dilbert lists three months of added delays: training, complexity, and dealing with the newcomers' drama. When the boss asks about the end result, Dilbert says the new staff will be only as useful as the meeting they are in.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically says that after three extra months of delay, the added people will be about as useful as this pointless meeting, implying both are a waste of time.
summary: Dilbert explains that adding headcount to his project only piles on delays and then insults the meeting itself as equally worthless.

title: Crime Scene Cleanup Cross-Selling Advantage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got transferred to our crime scene cleanup subsidiary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a competitive advantage because I have the customer lists from our other subsidiaries.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, we haven't had any deadly computer explosions here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll check back in an hour.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, then a customer's doorway
situation: Dilbert, dressed in coveralls and holding a push broom, tells Dogbert he has been transferred to the company's crime scene cleanup subsidiary. He explains that he has the customer lists from the company's other subsidiaries and then goes door to door soliciting business, asking a man whether anything deadly has happened. The man says there have been no deadly computer explosions, and Dilbert cheerfully says he'll check back in an hour.
punchline: Dilbert's cross-selling approach treats the company's other products as a lead generator for cleanup work, implying that the company's computers regularly explode and kill people, so he expects fresh customers any time now.
summary: A transferred employee uses his company's customer database to hunt for cleanup jobs, assuming the firm's own products will soon create the mess he is paid to scrub.

title: Permission to Fake Test Data

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We added a new performance test, but learned that the test itself is flawed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now our product fails our own tests and our customers are asking to see the test results.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I have permission to fake the test data?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't even know data can be real.

setting: The Boss's office, with a building exterior shown in the middle panel
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that a new performance test is flawed, so the product now fails the company's own tests while customers are asking to see the results. Dilbert asks for permission to fake the test data. The boss responds that he never realized data could be real.
punchline: The boss's remark reveals he assumes all data is routinely made up, so faking test results is business as usual and not even an ethical question for him.
summary: Faced with a failing product and customers demanding proof, an engineer asks to fabricate results, and his manager is startled to learn data is ever genuine.

title: Pay Stub Proves Time Is Worth More

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you review the document I emailed?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't read attachments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Attachments say you don't care enough about my time to summarize a document.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I brought my pay stub to prove that my time is worth more than yours.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well-played.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker at a meeting whether he reviewed an emailed document, and the coworker says he doesn't read attachments. Dilbert argues that sending an attachment is a way of saying you don't value the other person's time. He then hands over his pay stub to prove his time is worth more than the coworker's.
punchline: Dilbert wins the petty status argument over whose time matters more by literally comparing salaries, and the coworker concedes defeat.
summary: A man who refuses to open emailed files gets shut down when his colleague whips out proof of a higher paycheck.

title: Sold Data to Identity Thieves

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Customers are complaining that we sold their personal data.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: And apparently all of the buyers were identity thieves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's impossible. We checked every buyer's ident. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh.

situation: A bald, mustachioed employee in a white shirt and red tie stands before the Boss's desk and reports that customers are upset because the company sold their personal data. He adds that all the buyers turned out to be identity thieves. The Boss confidently insists that every buyer's identity was checked, then realizes the flaw in his own claim.
punchline: The Boss's boast that the company verified every buyer's identity falls apart when he realizes that identity thieves would easily pass an identity check, since they are impersonating real people.
summary: A manager defends his company's buyer vetting process right up until he notices that checking identities is useless against people who steal identities.

title: Talent Retention Via Display Case

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I found a way to keep our best talent from leaving.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! You found a way to interface a human brain with a robot body to get the best of both!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it's just a cool display case, but your thing would be good too.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has found a way to stop the best employees from leaving. The Boss assumes he has merged a human brain with a robot body, but Dilbert explains the person is simply inside a display case. Dilbert adds that the Boss's imagined idea would also work.
punchline: Dilbert's real solution is to literally trap the best employees in a display case, and he happily endorses the Boss's even more extreme idea of turning them into brain-powered robots.
summary: A cheerful retention scheme turns out to involve keeping a prized worker on display like an exhibit.

file: 2010/2010-07-29_public relations_statue of liberty_destroy_new york harbor_weapon demo_remorse_fake_glasses_fake tears_water_flood.gif
title: Fake Tears Flood the Press Conference

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Public Relations Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The public won't forgive you until you fake some remorse.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: These glasses have a hose that leads to a pumping station and a huge reservoir of fake tears.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If we have another press conference, we should crack open a window.

setting: The Boss's office, which ends up flooded
situation: Dogbert, acting as a public relations consultant, tells the Boss he must fake remorse to win back public forgiveness. He shows off special glasses connected by a hose to a pumping station and a huge reservoir of fake tears. In the last panel the Boss wears the glasses and the office is flooded, with Dogbert treading water and a hand waving from the water.
punchline: The fake crying device works so well that it floods the room, so Dogbert dryly suggests opening a window next time, treating the absurd excess of insincere remorse as a routine PR problem.
summary: A PR consultant equips his client with a tear-producing gadget that inundates the whole office with artificial sorrow.

title: CMMI: Frameworks Without Training Budget

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going to use CMMI. It's a model for developing a process to create a framework.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or it might be a process for creating a framework to make a model.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no budget for training, so we'll be relying on guessing more than usual.

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: The Boss announces to the team that they will adopt CMMI, but his explanation is circular and vague, describing it as a model, process and framework for making each other. He then admits there is no training budget, so the team will have to guess even more than they normally do.
punchline: The Boss cannot explain what the process methodology actually is, and then refuses to fund the training that would help anyone learn it, so the whole initiative will run on guesswork.
summary: A manager rolls out a maturity-model initiative with a hopelessly circular description and then withholds any money to teach it.

title: Dilbert Rejects Salesman, Accepts Attractive Woman

transcript.speaker: Salesman (phone)
transcript.text: Let's have lunch so I can tell you about our products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like meeting new people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every person I meet chips away at my freedom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I have lunch with you, I'll feel an obligation to return your pestering phone calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My lunchtime is the only chance I get during the day to scrape off the leeches.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing personal.

transcript.speaker: Woman (phone)
transcript.text: Do you want to have lunch and discuss our new product line?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure!

transcript.speaker: Salesman (phone)
transcript.text: Carl, you are totally in the wrong profession.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, on the phone
situation: A salesman phones Dilbert and invites him to lunch to pitch his products. Dilbert refuses with a series of increasingly elaborate reasons about hating new people and avoiding obligations. When a woman then calls with the same lunch offer, Dilbert immediately accepts, and the rejected salesman realizes he should have been a woman.
punchline: Dilbert's lofty excuses for avoiding sales lunches were just a cover; he turns down the male salesman but eagerly accepts the same invitation from an attractive woman, revealing his shallow motives.
summary: After giving a pompous list of reasons to dodge a sales pitch lunch, Dilbert happily agrees the moment a woman asks, leaving the rebuffed caller to rethink his career.

title: Smooth Sailing, Except the Goat Head

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you having any problems taking over Victor's project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nope. Smooth sailing so far.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Smooth??? It gave me a goat head!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He asked if I had any problems. Wait for your turn, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Sorry.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert and Asok whether they are having problems taking over Victor's project. Dilbert says everything is going smoothly, but Asok, who has apparently been turned into a goat-headed creature by the project, shouts in outrage. Dilbert calmly tells him to wait his turn since the question was directed at Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert dismisses a literal bodily transformation as a mere interruption of his turn to speak, treating the horrifying side effect as a problem to be reported later in line.
summary: Inheriting a predecessor's project has horrifyingly transformed one coworker, yet the other politely insists the questions be answered one at a time.

title: Emailing Through the Boring Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you don't mind if I do email during the boring parts of your meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't want to be dragged into your time suck hole.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You are kind of a time suck hole.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: I'm thorough!

situation: Dilbert sits at a conference table and announces to the meeting leader that he plans to answer email during the boring parts of the meeting. He opens his laptop and says he doesn't want to be dragged into the leader's time sink. A coworker agrees the leader is a time suck, and the leader angrily shouts that he is thorough while Dilbert keeps typing happily.
punchline: Dilbert's polite-sounding excuse for ignoring the meeting is really an insult, and the leader's furious defense of his thoroughness confirms he is exactly the long-winded time waster Dilbert says he is.
summary: A man blithely checks his email through a colleague's tedious meeting, and when called out the host defensively insists his long-windedness is diligence.

title: Brain-Golfing Through the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What's your take on this, Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? Sorry. I was using this time to think about something useful.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe your boss can fill you in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was brain-golfing.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for his opinion during a meeting, but Dilbert admits he wasn't paying attention because he was thinking about something more useful. The irritated coworker suggests Dilbert's boss could catch him up, and the Boss reveals he wasn't paying attention either, as he was imagining playing golf.
punchline: Dilbert's dig at the meeting's uselessness backfires when the Boss admits he too was mentally checked out, daydreaming about golf instead of working.
summary: A coworker who calls out a distracted Dilbert discovers that the boss he points to was just as zoned out, imagining a round of golf.

title: Boss's Nonsense Intelligence Test

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand either of your technical proposals, and I need to pick one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Normally I'd use favoritism, but I don't like either one of you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I'll give you an intelligence test, and I'll approve the proposal of whoever is the smartest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you shoot an arrow at a monkey from an airplane. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the monkey throws a coconut at the incoming arrow to stop it, but he misses. . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can you tell what time it is?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's not enough data.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You look at your watch?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The correct answer is "Ask the monkey and hope he doesn't hold a grudge."

situation: The Boss must choose between two technical proposals he doesn't understand, from Dilbert and a coworker, and doesn't like either of them. He decides to settle it with an intelligence test, posing a bizarre riddle about shooting an arrow at a monkey from an airplane. Dilbert says there isn't enough data, the coworker gives a sensible answer, and the Boss announces a nonsensical 'correct' answer.
punchline: The Boss's intelligence test has an absurd, arbitrary answer that makes no sense, showing that his decision-making is baseless and that he can't even judge intelligence he doesn't possess.
summary: Unable to evaluate two proposals, a clueless manager picks a winner with a ridiculous riddle whose supposed answer is pure nonsense.

file: 2010/2010-05-07_evil director of human resources_payroll expenses low_bad reviews_employees_defects_list_faults_alphabetical_business.gif
title: Alphabetical List of Employee Defects

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We can keep our payroll expenses low by giving employees bad reviews.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Use this list of employee defects so you don't repeat yourself. It's less obvious this way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Awkward, bumbling, cowardly, dumb. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My faults are suspiciously alphabetical.

setting: Office and the Boss's desk during a performance review
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, advises the Boss that giving employees bad reviews keeps payroll costs low. He hands the Boss a list of employee defects to draw from so the criticism doesn't repeat. During Dilbert's review, the Boss reads the faults straight off the list in alphabetical order, and Dilbert notices.
punchline: The Boss is so lazy and unimaginative that he reads the defects in the list's alphabetical order, making the scheme to disguise the insincere reviews glaringly obvious.
summary: A scheming HR cat supplies a cheat sheet of insults to justify poor reviews, and the manager's mechanical use of it gives the game away.

title: Dilbert Philosophizes His Way Home Early

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's no objective standard for measuring how much I should accomplish in any given day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nor can we really know if things would have turned out better had I done things differently.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a point?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going home early. See if you can tell the difference.

situation: Dilbert stands before the Boss's desk and delivers a philosophical lecture about how there is no objective way to measure how much he should accomplish in a day, or whether different choices would have produced better results. The Boss impatiently asks if he has a point, and Dilbert reveals he is leaving early.
punchline: Dilbert uses the unmeasurable nature of his productivity as justification for leaving early, daring the Boss to notice any difference in results.
summary: Dilbert builds an abstract argument about unmeasurable productivity only to use it as cover for knocking off work early.
keywords: see if you can tell the difference

file: 2010/2010-03-21_security guard_shout_technical advice_career change_loud_yell_mouth open_reboot_promotion_hobo_sponge bath_lobby fountain_typo_nervous.gif
title: Security Guard's Reboot Advice Career

transcript.speaker: Henry
transcript.text: Try rebooting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you?

transcript.speaker: Henry
transcript.text: I'm Henry the security guard. I'm trying to evolve into a new career.

transcript.speaker: Henry
transcript.text: I'm ignoring my real job while loudly giving technical advice to coworkers.

transcript.speaker: Henry
transcript.text: Eventually, people will start to see me as a valuable technical resource. Promotions will follow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know anything about technology besides "try rebooting"?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Henry, who let the hobo take a sponge bath in the lobby fountain?

transcript.speaker: Henry
transcript.text: Try rebooting! Try rebooting!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To fix a typo?

situation: Henry the security guard shouts "Try rebooting" at Dilbert and explains that he is neglecting his real job to loudly dispense tech advice in hopes of earning a promotion. When Dilbert questions whether he knows anything else about technology, a coworker interrupts to ask who let a hobo bathe in the lobby fountain. Henry panics and starts shouting his reboot advice again, absurdly.
punchline: Henry's career-change strategy depends on the one phrase he knows, and he falls back on it as a desperate distraction while neglecting his actual security duties.
summary: A guard hoping to become a tech expert keeps yelling the same stock advice, even as his neglected lobby duties catch up with him.

title: Product Explodes, QA Director Pinned

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: We should consider doing a recall on our product.

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: When it warms up, it explodes and hurls poisonous spines in every direction.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's the Director of Quality Assurance?

transcript.speaker: Company Lawyer
transcript.text: Pinned to the test lab ceiling.

situation: The company lawyer tells the Boss that the product should probably be recalled, explaining that it explodes and hurls poisonous spines when it warms up. The Boss, seated at his desk, asks where the Director of Quality Assurance is. The lawyer reveals that he is pinned to the test lab ceiling.
punchline: The Director of Quality Assurance found the product's lethal defect the hard way, as its first victim, which darkly shows how dangerous the product is.
summary: A lawyer urges a recall of a product that fires toxic spines when heated, and the missing quality inspector turns out to have been skewered by it.

title: Lazy Coworker Brags About Incompetence

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We've never worked together, so let me tell you how this will go down.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You'll expect me to contribute, and you will be disappointed at every turn. In the long run you will do everything yourself.

transcript.speaker: Man in red shirt
transcript.text: How do you stay employed?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Don't make me call myself a genius.

situation: A new coworker sits down with a colleague and cheerfully warns him that he will contribute nothing and that the colleague will end up doing all the work. The colleague, appalled, asks how he keeps his job. The coworker smugly sips his coffee and implies that his skill at dodging work is a form of genius.
punchline: The slacker treats his talent for avoiding work while keeping his job as a genius-level skill, showing that office politics can reward laziness.
summary: A self-declared slacker lays out in advance how useless he will be, then smugly credits his job security to cleverness.

file: 2010/2010-02-28_meeting_accomplish_week_fantasy_time magazine_entrepreneurial_real job_motion to head_powerpoint slides_horror_real life_kill_business.gif
title: Dilbert's Entrepreneurial Fantasy Life Slips Out

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, what did you accomplish this week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I doubled my sales and made the cover of Time magazine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. Whoops. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For a moment there I confused my entrepreneurial fantasy life with my real job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I run a parallel career in my mind. In that world, I'm the founder of a hot start-up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It keeps my brain from fully realizing the horror of my actual career and trying to kill the rest of my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But to answer your original question, this week I made some PowerPoint slides that have no particular use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! My brain is trying to kill the rest of my body!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Moving on...

setting: Conference room during a weekly status meeting
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert in a meeting what he accomplished this week, and Dilbert absentmindedly claims he doubled sales and made the cover of Time magazine. He explains that he runs a fantasy career as a hot start-up founder in his mind to shield himself from the horror of his real job. When he admits his actual output is useless PowerPoint slides, his brain seems to attack his body, and the Boss just moves on.
punchline: Dilbert's real accomplishments are so meaningless that his mind needs an elaborate fantasy to cope, and when reality breaks through, the Boss callously ignores his breakdown.
summary: An employee blurts out an imaginary success story in a status meeting, then admits his daydream career is all that keeps him sane while his real work is pointless.

title: Donuts Make Boss Stupid Research

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm doing basic research to test my theory that donuts make other people stupid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I expect you to do basic research that will increase our profits this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. It works on the first bite.

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk holding a donut and a coffee mug, explaining that his 'basic research' is testing whether donuts make other people stupid. The Boss responds by demanding that Wally do research that will boost quarterly profits. Wally takes a bite of the donut and observes that his theory is confirmed.
punchline: The Boss's clueless, off-topic demand is taken by Wally as instant proof that donuts make people stupid, which is also a sly insult that the Boss was already stupid or is being instantly dumbed down.
summary: A slacking employee claims his donut-eating is science, and his manager's nonsensical response seems to prove the experiment a success.

title: Welcome to the Limbo Cube

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm glad your project was transferred to my department, Ronald.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is flashy! It's sexy!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it's not worth funding because the revenue projections are puny.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until something changes, you'll be in the Limbo Cube.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll trot you out whenever a customer or an executive visits.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can show your sexy-flashy PowerPoint slides while dreaming of being relevant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you work hard, someday you'll be totally forgotten.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you know that honesty makes people sad?

setting: Office hallway, a cubicle area, and the boss's own cubicle; the opening banner shows Dogbert and Dilbert at a presentation screen
situation: The Boss welcomes Ronald, whose flashy project has been transferred to his department, then explains it won't be funded because its revenue projections are tiny. He assigns Ronald to a cubicle called the Limbo Cube, where Ronald will wait to be shown off to visitors and eventually be forgotten. In the last panel the Boss, holding a coffee mug, glances at a red creature on his desk and muses that honesty makes people sad.
punchline: The Boss delivers a brutally frank description of Ronald's dead-end project and career, then pretends to be mildly puzzled that honesty upsets people.
summary: A manager cheerfully parks an appealing but unprofitable project and its owner in a purgatory cubicle, pulling him out only for show and for visitors.

file: 2010/2010-05-24_invention_gadget_sink attaches to body_faucet on head_running water_work_annoyed_hearing_yell.gif
title: Voice-Activated Sink Drowns Out Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I invented a sink that attaches to my body. The faucet is activated by your voice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, what possible use could this stupid thing have? I need you to do some real work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What? I can't hear you when the water is running!

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Wally sits at a meeting wearing a sink strapped to his head and torso, with a faucet that turns on when it hears a voice. The Boss scolds him for wasting time on a useless invention and tells him to do real work. When the Boss speaks, the faucet runs, and Wally claims he can't hear him over the water.
punchline: Wally's useless invention turns out to have one practical use for him: the voice-activated faucet gives him a built-in excuse to ignore his boss's orders.
summary: An employee's absurd wearable sink becomes the perfect tool for tuning out his manager's complaints.

title: Catbert Reassigns Ted to Acid Vat

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ted, I'm transferring you to a job with a higher risk of industrial accidents.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your job will involve reaching over a vat of acid while wearing no safety harness.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Why do we have a vat of acid?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Because toxic fumes take forever.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Ted he is being transferred to a more dangerous job. The job involves reaching over a vat of acid with no safety harness. A worried Ted asks why the company even has a vat of acid, and Catbert explains it is for a sinister purpose.
punchline: The vat of acid exists because Catbert wants to dispose of employees, and toxic fumes are too slow a method, which reveals that dissolving Ted is the real plan.
summary: An evil HR cat sends a nervous employee to a hazardous post over a tank of acid, then casually reveals that the tank is the company's quick method for getting rid of people.

title: Optimism Looks Like Doing Nothing

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'm on my way to a meeting with a prospective customer.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We have such a long sales gestation period that the value of my efforts won't be known for two years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just remember that optimism looks exactly like doing nothing.

situation: A bald salesman in a red sweater tells the seated Boss he is heading out to meet a prospective customer. He explains that the sales cycle is so long that nobody will know whether his work has any value for two years. The Boss responds that his optimism is indistinguishable from slacking off.
punchline: The Boss points out that a salesman claiming his results can't be measured for two years is, from management's view, impossible to tell apart from someone doing nothing at all.
summary: A salesman leans on a very long sales cycle to excuse his lack of measurable results, and his boss cynically calls it laziness in disguise.

title: Assistant Confesses Calendar Self-Interest

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: For the past five years I've managed your calendar based solely on what would create the least work for me.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: It all started when you told me to use my judgment to set priorities.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: In retrospect, you should have hired someone with low self-esteem.

situation: The Boss's administrative assistant sits at her desk and calmly admits she has spent five years scheduling his calendar purely to minimize her own workload. She explains that it began when he told her to use her own judgment to set priorities. She then suggests he should have hired someone with low self-esteem.
punchline: The assistant blames the Boss's own vague instruction for her self-serving scheduling, and implies that only an insecure employee would be too timid to put her own interests first.
summary: A secretary coolly admits she has arranged her boss's schedule purely for her own convenience for years, blaming his hands-off instruction and his hiring choice.

title: Boss Forwards Hoax E-mail Company-Wide

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The urgent e-mail you forwarded to the entire company is a hoax.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People don't really burst into flames if they use their cell phones during an eclipse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And more bad news: The witless protection program isn't a real thing.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of the Boss's desk and tells him that the urgent e-mail he forwarded to everyone in the company is a hoax. He explains that cell phones don't make people burst into flames during an eclipse. The Boss sits silently at his computer while Dilbert delivers a further piece of bad news.
punchline: The Boss is so gullible that he not only spread a ridiculous hoax to the whole company, but also believed in a 'witless protection program', a pun on witness protection, which Dilbert now has to tell him doesn't exist.
summary: A gullible manager gets gently informed that the chain e-mail he blasted to every employee was fake, and that his other belief was equally mistaken.

title: Reeling In the CEO's Crony

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: This rope is attached to a crony from my last CEO job.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Give it a good yank and reel him in. He's your new boss.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is he qualified for the job?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Like a monkey with a hammer!

setting: CEO's office, with the CEO seated in a leather chair with his feet on the desk
situation: The new CEO hands The Boss a rope and explains that it is attached to a crony from his previous CEO job. He tells The Boss to yank it and reel the man in, since he will become The Boss's new boss. When The Boss asks whether the crony is qualified, the CEO says he is qualified like a monkey with a hammer.
punchline: The CEO's answer admits the crony is completely unqualified, since a monkey with a hammer is clumsy and dangerous, yet he is being installed as a boss anyway through cronyism.
summary: A new chief executive literally hauls in a buddy from his old company to supervise the staff and cheerfully admits the man has no business holding the job.

title: Slow-Motion PowerPoint Torture Session

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I could have e-mailed you my PowerPoint deck, and you could have read it in five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: But I prefer making you sit here for an hour while I read each bullet point in slow motion.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: P-O-I-N-T N-U-M-B-E-R O-N-E...

transcript.speaker: Attendee
transcript.text: Yank this as hard as you can.

setting: Conference room during a project presentation
situation: A presenter standing beside a slide titled 'Project EMU' openly admits he could have emailed his PowerPoint deck, but instead forces the group to sit through an hour of him reading each bullet point slowly. As he drags out the first point letter by letter, one bored attendee holds out a green item and tells a colleague to yank it as hard as they can, implying they want the presenter's tie pulled to end the torment.
punchline: The presenter's deliberately slow, pointless reading is so unbearable that an attendee suggests strangling him with his own tie to make it stop.
summary: A smug presenter chooses to drag a slideshow out for an hour instead of sending an email, and his audience would rather choke him than endure it.

title: Witty Name for Retirement Money

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I finally saved enough money to retire anytime I want.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Someone should invent a witty name for that amount of money.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Perfect! Can I use that?

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug stands in front of the boss's desk and says he has saved enough to retire whenever he wants. He muses that someone should coin a witty name for that sum of money. The boss, seated and annoyed, replies with a string of censored swear symbols, and the coworker cheerfully asks to use that as the name.
punchline: The boss's grumbling curse words, reflecting his anger that an employee can quit at will, are treated by the coworker as the witty name for 'f-you money'.
summary: An employee flush with retirement savings gleefully adopts his furious boss's string of expletives as the name for his newfound financial freedom.

title: Generic Manager Pep Talk Backfires

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the generic manager

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We need more people on the project.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Figure it out. Work smarter not harder. Make a plan. Move some things around. Adjust priorities. Just get it done. Give me a status report.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: That did nothing but make me hate you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can replace you with someone who will pretend to be inspired.

situation: An employee asks his manager, Dogbert, for more people on a project. Dogbert responds with a stream of empty management clichés and tells him to get it done. The employee says the advice only made him hate Dogbert, and Dogbert threatens to replace him with someone who will fake enthusiasm.
punchline: Management doesn't want real solutions or honest feedback, only employees who will pretend to be inspired by hollow platitudes.
summary: A boss answers a request for staffing with a barrage of buzzwords, then threatens to swap out the worker who isn't impressed.

file: 2010/2010-03-17_technical issue_coworker_sitting in chairs_facing each other_software_yell_condescend_stupid_dumb_dense_shout_sitting on couch_touchy_engineering.gif
title: Explaining Software Bugs Like Pidgin

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to explain our technical issue in terms you can understand.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The software, it no worky!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He was dense and touchy. It's a bad combination.

setting: Office, then Dilbert's home or Dogbert's living room
situation: Dilbert is asked to explain a technical problem to a non-technical coworker in terms he can understand. Dilbert shouts a childishly simplified sentence at him, and the coworker takes offense. In the last panel Dilbert recounts the aftermath to Dogbert, who sits on a couch.
punchline: Dilbert's dumbed-down shouting insulted the coworker, who was both slow to understand and easily offended, so the attempt at clear communication backfired.
summary: Told to put a technical problem in layman's terms, Dilbert bellows a baby-talk version at a coworker and later laments that the man was both thick and sensitive.

title: Failure Estimates Built on Hallucinated Assumptions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you get me some failure estimates for our next gen product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can if you like numbers that are based on hallucinated assumptions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I kind of do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we have an under-standing.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert for failure estimates for the company's next generation product. Dilbert says he can only provide numbers built on made-up, hallucinated assumptions. The Boss cheerfully says he likes that kind of number, and Dilbert concludes they understand each other.
punchline: The Boss doesn't care whether the failure estimates are real, and is perfectly happy with fabricated data, which Dilbert recognizes as a shared, unspoken agreement to fake it.
summary: A manager requests reliability figures and is delighted to learn they will be pure fiction, so long as he gets numbers.

title: Boss Models Change by Communicating Poorly

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Header: a Dilbert by Scott Adams title slide, with Dogbert on a stool and Dilbert presenting.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A successful transformation requires employees to feel ownership for the change.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Change? What change?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is there something we don't know?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's important that everyone has clear roles and responsibilities.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What are you trying to tell us? Should we stop working on our projects?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll keep you engaged and energized with my clear communication.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And as your leader, I will role-model the desired change.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If he's our role model, I guess we need to act like morons who can't communicate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need new people.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Fuh fuh fuh fuh fuh fuh

setting: Conference room during a management presentation on organizational change
situation: The Boss gives a presentation on a vague 'transformation', promising clear communication and roles, but his team has no idea what change he means and asks if they should stop their projects. When he says he will role-model the desired change, Alice sarcastically concludes they should act like morons who can't communicate.
punchline: The Boss claims to model clear communication while being utterly unclear, so Alice turns his own logic against him, and he responds by blaming his staff and wanting new people.
summary: A manager lectures his confused team about the importance of clear communication and leading by example, and they gleefully take him at his word.

title: Leadership: Trading Imaginary Promotions for Weekends

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Leadership is the art of trading imaginary things in the future...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For real things today.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If you work all weekend, you might get promoted someday, if there's ever an opening... and no one else is more qualified.

setting: Office, Catbert's desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, explains his idea of leadership to the Boss across a desk. He then demonstrates it by approaching Dilbert, who is working at his computer, and offering a vague, heavily qualified chance at a promotion in exchange for working all weekend.
punchline: Real leadership here means extracting actual weekend labor from employees in return for a promotion so hedged with conditions that it is effectively worthless.
summary: An HR villain defines leadership as swapping hollow future rewards for concrete effort right now, then proves it on a worker.

title: Fake Job Interview for Free Training

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need training to use our new software.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Pretend we have a job opening for a technical expert in that field. Then ask applicants how they would do whatever it is that you need to do.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Does your company provide training?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Provide" is a strong word.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he needs training on new company software. Instead of paying for training, the Boss tells him to stage a fake job opening and interview technical experts so they reveal how to do the task. In the interview, a candidate asks whether Dilbert's company provides training.
punchline: Dilbert's dry reply that "provide" is a strong word admits the company offers no real training and is instead stealing expertise from job applicants.
summary: Rather than fund training, a cheap manager has his engineer interview fake job candidates to extract free know-how, and the engineer wryly concedes that the company hardly supplies any.

file: 2010/2010-09-01_anonymous online employee survey_slip up_look at paper_angry_eyebrows_trust_ironic.gif
title: Anonymous Survey Not So Anonymous

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the anonymous online employee survey, you don't trust management. What's up with that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. Right.

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss reads from a printed survey result and confronts Dilbert for saying he doesn't trust management. In the silent middle panel Dilbert simply stares at him, and the Boss then realizes why the survey response is correct.
punchline: By demanding to know who gave the 'anonymous' answer, the Boss proves the survey was not anonymous and that employees have good reason not to trust management.
summary: A manager tracks down the author of an supposedly confidential survey answer, only to confirm the very distrust it expressed.

title: Honest Opinion Versus Watching Hulu

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new look is a black turtleneck and old man jeans. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You look like a total juice bag.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's good, right?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What answer gets me back to watching my shows on Hulu?

situation: The Boss shows off his new outfit of a black turtleneck and old man jeans and asks Alice for her opinion. She flatly insults it, but he interprets that as a compliment. Alice, uninterested, asks which reply will end the conversation so she can return to watching TV shows on her computer.
punchline: Alice gives up on honest feedback and just wants whatever answer will make the boss go away so she can keep streaming Hulu at work.
summary: A coworker blandly insults her boss's fashion makeover, then admits she only wants whichever reply lets her get back to her streaming shows.

title: Competent People Would Be Overloaded

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And I'll need all of that by tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: No problem. I'll get right on it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is a bad sign. If you were even a little bit competent you would be overloaded with work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I'm putting my trust in a moron!

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Wow. You got there fast.

situation: Dilbert hands a coworker a big assignment due by tomorrow, and the coworker cheerfully agrees to do it. Dilbert reasons that anyone competent would already be swamped with work, so the easy acceptance must mean the coworker is incompetent. He grabs his tie and cries out in dismay, and the coworker remarks on how quickly he reached that conclusion.
punchline: Dilbert concludes the coworker is a moron precisely because he has spare capacity, since competent people in this workplace are always overloaded, and the coworker deadpans at how fast Dilbert reached that judgment.
summary: A worker's calm willingness to take on a rush job convinces the person delegating that he must be hopelessly incompetent.

title: Walmart Knockoff Needs More Greeters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Walmart started selling a knockoff of our product for nine cents apiece.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm looking for ideas. Anyone? Anyone?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They'll need more greeters.

situation: During a meeting, the Boss announces that Walmart is selling a knockoff of the company's product for nine cents each and asks the group for ideas. An exterior shot of the office building shows the Boss repeating his plea with no answer. Wally finally offers a useless remark about Walmart needing more greeters.
punchline: Wally responds to a serious competitive threat with an irrelevant joke about Walmart's store greeters, showing he has no intention of helping and is mocking the question.
summary: Faced with a cut-rate copycat product from a retail giant, a boss begs for ideas and gets only a flippant quip about store greeters.

file: 2010/2010-05-15_customer support_customer service_rodent_talk on phone_creepy personal questions_waste of time_refund.gif
title: Ratbert's Refund-Blocking Customer Support

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert's Customer Support

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're speaking to a powerless rodent.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My job is to prevent you from getting to anyone who is authorized to give refunds.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'd like to begin by asking you some creepy personal questions.

setting: Ratbert's customer support desk, with a phone, computer and office chair
situation: Ratbert answers a customer support call and openly admits he has no authority to help. He explains that his real purpose is to keep callers away from anyone who can approve refunds. He then starts the call by announcing he will ask the caller creepy personal questions.
punchline: The customer support line is deliberately designed to stonewall refund requests and waste callers' time, and Ratbert candidly admits it while adding creepy questions to make the ordeal worse.
summary: A rodent phone agent cheerfully confesses that his whole job is to block refund seekers, then promises to fill the time with invasive questions.

title: Wally's Self-Concealing Optimization Project

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I need to spend the next year optimizing the WDNW system

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've never heard of the WDNW system.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You only hear about the systems that have problems.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If everything goes as planned, you'll never hear about WDNW again.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What does the WDNW system do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It keeps our zeros and ones from accidentally forming tens.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That can happen?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Not on my watch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the "Wally Does No Work" project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The acronym helped.

setting: The Boss's office, then the office coffee area
situation: Wally tells the Boss he needs a full year to optimize a mysterious system called WDNW, and uses vague technical-sounding claims to justify it. The Boss accepts everything without question. Afterward Wally gets coffee and tells Dilbert that the acronym helped him get away with it.
punchline: WDNW stands for "Wally Does No Work," so Wally has gotten his boss to approve a year of doing nothing by hiding it behind a plausible-sounding technical acronym.
summary: A slacking engineer invents an imaginary system with a telltale acronym to win a year of paid idleness from a gullible manager.

title: Defending Certification Against Nobody

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert by Scott Adams, dilbert.com

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: I accomplished nothing this week because I was going through certification.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't ask. Don't ask. Don't ask.

transcript.speaker: Colleague
transcript.text: Certification for... what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plan B: Mount a passionate defense against an argument that no one made.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: How can you say that certification is a waste of time?!

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Without certification, management would be reduced to randomness!

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Do you think you'd be happier just guessing who is qualified to do what? Do you? Do you?

transcript.speaker: Colleague
transcript.text: There's something wrong with you.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Boss
transcript.text: Apology accepted. Next.

situation: At a status meeting, the Boss admits he got nothing done because he was going through certification. A colleague innocently asks what the certification was for, and the Boss responds by furiously defending certification against criticism nobody had voiced. The colleague points out that something is wrong with him, and the Boss treats that as an apology.
punchline: The Boss tries to cover his unproductive week by angrily attacking an imaginary argument, then twists a colleague's insult into an apology he graciously accepts.
summary: Caught admitting he wasted a week, a manager turns the tables by ranting at colleagues over a criticism they never made.

title: Poison Pill: Company Too Awful

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert will describe our "poison pill" strategy for preventing an unfriendly takeover.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It turns out that no one wants to buy a criminally mismanaged quagmire. So you're all set.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe next time you won't skip the pre-meeting.

situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert, a consultant, to explain the company's poison pill strategy against a hostile takeover. Dogbert bluntly says the company is so badly mismanaged that nobody would want to buy it, insulting the executives in the room. The Boss, now irritated, remarks that Dogbert should have attended the pre-meeting.
punchline: Dogbert's honest answer is that the company's terrible management is itself the best poison pill, and he delivers it in front of the very managers he is insulting because he skipped the pre-meeting where the message could have been softened.
summary: A consultant tells a room of executives their takeover defense is simply that their firm is too badly run for anyone to want.

title: Stain Protection Plan for Bad Decisions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's Society for People Who Always Make Bad Decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to thank each of you for choosing the Platinum Stain Protection Plan with your membership dues.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If your reputation gets stained by being in this group, the brochure will teach you how to grow a mustache disguise.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: What if I already have one?

setting: A meeting room where Dogbert addresses a seated audience from a stool
situation: Dogbert stands on a stool welcoming members to his society for people who always make bad decisions. He thanks them for buying the Platinum Stain Protection Plan, which promises to protect their reputations by teaching them to grow a mustache disguise. An audience member who already has a mustache asks what happens in his case.
punchline: The members' bad decisions are shown by their paying for a worthless plan, and the one man who already has a mustache is left with no disguise available.
summary: A scheming dog sells a club full of poor decision-makers a reputation-protection plan that amounts to growing facial hair, which one member already has.

file: 2010/2010-03-25_new vice president of engineering_meeting_introduce_full body_face front_pointy hair_lack of experience_exotic_over selling_mustache_business.gif
title: Exotic Unqualified Engineering VP Introduced

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meet our new Vice President of Engineering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're lucky to have him despite his utter lack of experience in our industry.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Some might call him unqualified, but I call him exotic.

transcript.speaker: New Vice President
transcript.text: You're over-selling.

situation: The Boss introduces a mustached man to staff as the new Vice President of Engineering. He admits the man has no experience in the industry, then tries to spin the lack of qualifications as being 'exotic.' The new VP himself says the boss is overselling him.
punchline: The Boss tries to rebrand total unqualification as an appealing quality, and even the unqualified hire thinks the spin is too much.
summary: A manager presents a clueless new executive as a lucky catch and calls his missing credentials exotic, to the newcomer's own embarrassment.

title: Boss Finds No Good Engineers

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I need you to assign one of your engineers to my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Follow me and I'll show you your choices.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This one is highly capable, but she's in such high demand that you'll be lucky if she ever returns a call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This one is aggressively unhelpful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This one will tell you that all of your plans are impractical and doomed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That one is an intern, so no one takes him seriously.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My management theory is that nature makes everyone useless in their own way.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'm not useless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Said the man who can't find a good engineer.

situation: A manager asks the Pointy-Haired Boss to loan him an engineer for a project. The Boss walks him around the office, dismissing each candidate with a different flaw: unreachable, unhelpful, pessimistic, or just an intern. He concludes that everyone is useless in their own way.
punchline: When the manager protests that he is not useless, the Boss turns his own theory against him, implying the manager is useless too because he cannot find a good engineer.
summary: A boss tours his staff to find a colleague a suitable engineer, rejects every one of them, and then lands a jab at the man doing the asking.

title: Welcome to Matrix Management, Neo

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, would you...?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. I'm doing something important for the Brand Integration Manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe after that you could...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Then I'm doing a rush job for the Director of Sustain-ability.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are those even real people?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Welcome to Matrix Management, Neo.

situation: Dilbert tries to ask Wally for help, but Wally keeps refusing by citing urgent tasks for managers with grand-sounding titles. When Dilbert starts to doubt that these bosses even exist, Wally sips his coffee and answers with a Matrix movie reference.
punchline: Wally uses vague, possibly imaginary managerial roles as an endless excuse to avoid work, and his Matrix quote jokes that matrix management is an illusory system, like a simulated reality.
summary: A cubicle dweller dodges a colleague's request by invoking phantom executives, then mocks the confused questioner with a sci-fi quip about the org chart.

file: 2010/2010-04-04_cpg project_confused_leader_team_face front_back_walk away_flippant_useless_forget_frustrated_angry_comfort_hand on shoulder_shake_clench teeth_hair stand up_business.gif
title: Leading a Project You Never Knew

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the CPG project coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would I know?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're leading that project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am? Since when?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I told everyone on the team two months ago.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not on the team. You never told me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whatever, go tell the team you've been in charge for the past two months and see what they've accomplished.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who is on the team?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forget. I think one had dark hair, and another one was sad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't tell them there's a duplicate project in another division.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll be okay. Just release the caring. Let it go.

setting: Office hallway with coffee mugs, plus a title panel where Dogbert stands on a stool facing a Dilbert projection screen
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how the CPG project is going and announces that Dilbert has been leading it for two months, though nobody ever told him. The Boss orders him to find the team and take charge, but can't remember who is on it, and adds that a duplicate project is running in another division. Dilbert becomes visibly angry and shaky while Wally calmly tells him to stop caring.
punchline: Management assigns responsibility without telling anyone, can't identify the team, and has secretly duplicated the work, so the only sensible survival strategy is to stop caring.
summary: A manager blames an unwitting employee for a project he was never told he led, and the resigned coworker's advice is to give up caring.

title: Public Speaking Class Erases Personalities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending all of you to a public speaking class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They will rid you of your nervous habits... and, with any luck, your personalities too. You will become indistinguishable from robots.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is that as fun as it sounds?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Get out of my head!

situation: The Boss tells his team at a meeting that he is sending them all to a public speaking class. An establishing shot of an office building accompanies his explanation that the class will strip away their nervous habits and personalities, making them like robots. Alice sarcastically asks if that is as fun as it sounds, and Asok reacts with a shocked demand that someone get out of his head.
punchline: The class is openly meant to erase employees' personalities, and the team's sarcastic dread (Asok's horror at the idea invading his mind) shows how dehumanizing corporate training can be.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces mandatory speaking lessons designed to make his staff as personality-free as machines, and they react with sarcasm and alarm.

file: 2010/2010-09-23_pitchman_new product_salesman_block of wood_machine_rays_reality distortion_stand on stool_consumers.gif
title: Dogbert's Reality Distortion Field Pitch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Pitchman

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fire up the reality distortion field as soon as I'm introduced.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our product is nothing but a block of wood, and yet you need three of them.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: I am a creative individual who does as he is told.

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: I can't feel my arm!

setting: A stage and auditorium during a product presentation
situation: Dogbert, working as a pitchman, instructs Dilbert to switch on a reality distortion field machine as soon as he is introduced. Dogbert then stands on a stool and admits his product is just a block of wood that people need three of. The entranced audience obediently agrees, with one man proclaiming he is a creative individual who does as he's told while another complains he can't feel his arm.
punchline: The reality distortion machine makes consumers so suggestible that they will buy three pieces of wood and even ignore their own bodies going numb, a jab at hype-driven product launches.
summary: A talking dog uses a mind-bending gadget to convince a crowd to buy useless lumber in triplicate.

title: Job Applicant's Identity Theft Plan

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: If I hire you, you'll get minimum wage to attend meetings and pretend you're me.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: My plan is to get hired for several jobs and replace myself with low-paid look-alikes in each one.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: My plan is to bury you in a shallow grave and assume your identity.

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: You don't interview well.

situation: A balding manager interviews an applicant and explains the job: attending meetings at minimum wage while pretending to be the manager. The applicant reveals his own scheme of taking several jobs and sending low-paid look-alikes to each. The interviewer then threatens to murder him and steal his identity, and the applicant concludes the interview isn't going well.
punchline: The interviewer's escalating scheme of murder and identity theft tops the applicant's own sneaky plan, prompting the deadpan understatement that he interviews badly.
summary: Two schemers trade increasingly sinister plans in a job interview until one threatens to bury the other and take over his life.

title: Allocated Minute for Wasting Time

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Absolutely.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I allocated one minute today for tasks that are a complete waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This isn't a complete waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bummer. I only allocated time for things that are.

situation: A coworker holding a sheet of paper asks Dilbert if he has a minute. Dilbert, seated at his computer, cheerfully agrees and explains that he budgeted exactly one minute for useless tasks. When the coworker insists his request is worthwhile, Dilbert says he has no time for it.
punchline: Dilbert's rigid time budget only covers pointless tasks, so a genuinely worthwhile request is the one thing he can't accommodate.
summary: A man with a request is turned away by a colleague whose daily schedule only has room for activities that accomplish nothing.

title: Penalized for Saving, Then Told to Help

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You added the savings from my project to the budget for Ted's project.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ted is a serial failer. You've destroyed in advance any hope that I might do something useful.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you could help Ted on his project.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Making it worse!

situation: Carol complains to the Boss that the savings from her successful project were handed over to Ted's budget. She points out that Ted habitually fails, so this wrecks any chance of her work mattering. The Boss responds by suggesting she help Ted with his project, which leaves her in visible distress.
punchline: The Boss answers a complaint about being punished for success by proposing she be assigned to the failing project, which makes her situation even worse.
summary: After her thrifty project's savings are given to a chronic underperformer, a frustrated employee is told by her manager to go and assist that very colleague.

title: Book Deal From Boss's Dumb Quotes

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Good news: I got a book deal based entirely on the dumb things you've said.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It's totally legal because the law only protects "intellectual" property.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Frugga bugga!!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And so began the sequel.

situation: An employee, holding a phone, tells the Boss he has landed a book deal made up entirely of the dumb things the Boss has said. He explains with air quotes that it's legal because the law only protects 'intellectual' property. The Boss angrily spills his coffee and shouts nonsense, which the employee promptly records on his phone for the sequel.
punchline: The employee insults the Boss by implying his remarks aren't intellectual property, then gets fresh material for a sequel when the Boss's angry outburst is itself another dumb quote.
summary: A worker profits from his supervisor's foolish remarks and gleefully gathers more material when the furious supervisor rants.

title: Yawning Elbonians Steal Souls Negotiation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Cultural sensitivity training

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Elbonians believe that if you yawn in their direction, you steal their soul.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: In other words, we can use it as a negotiating tool.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: No, that's not...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Okay, my intern has your soul. Give us a 20% discount or he swallows.

setting: Conference room during cultural sensitivity training, then a negotiation with Elbonians
situation: A trainer explains that Elbonians believe yawning in their direction steals their soul. Alice immediately decides this is a negotiating tactic, and the trainer tries to object. Later, Alice confronts two Elbonian negotiators and claims her intern has stolen their souls, demanding a 20% discount or he will swallow them.
punchline: Alice turns a lesson meant to teach respect for a foreign culture into a means of extortion, which is the opposite of cultural sensitivity.
summary: A training session on respecting a foreign superstition gets weaponized by a colleague who uses it to hold her trading partners' souls hostage for a price cut.

title: Competitors Are Biting Vampires

transcript.speaker: Salesperson
transcript.text: I don't like to say bad things about my competitors, but they're all vampires.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson
transcript.text: And not the sexy kind either. They're more the bitey kind.

transcript.speaker: Salesperson
transcript.text: Our product doesn't even work, and you're still better off buying from us.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: They said you eat babies.

setting: Conference room or sales meeting table
situation: A salesperson pitches to a potential customer and slanders his competitors by calling them vampires. He then admits his own product does not even work but insists it is still the better buy. The customer, holding a paper, replies that the competitors claim his company eats babies.
punchline: Both sides of the sales competition trade absurd smears, and the customer's deadpan reply shows that the salesperson's mudslinging is just as ridiculous as the accusations hurled back at him.
summary: A sales pitch built on monstrous insults about rivals gets a taste of its own medicine when the buyer reveals what the rivals say in return.

title: Boss's Friend Tinkers With Scope

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our scope needs to be calibrated. Do we have a budget for that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can save a few bucks by sending it to my friend, Elrod. He likes to tinker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everything about that idea is bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You should see the car he made from a bathtub.

situation: Dilbert tells the boss that their scope needs calibration and asks whether there is a budget for it. The boss proposes sending it to his friend Elrod to save money, since Elrod likes to tinker. Dilbert objects that the idea is bad, and the boss responds by bragging about a car Elrod built from a bathtub.
punchline: The boss offers a bathtub-car as proof of his friend's engineering skill, which only confirms that entrusting precision calibration to a hobbyist is a terrible idea.
summary: A manager wants to cut costs by handing precision equipment to an amateur pal, and cites that pal's eccentric bathtub vehicle as a credential.

title: Wally's Survey Resembles Unabomber Manifesto

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, we're concerned about the comments you made on your anonymous employee survey.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your comments are disturbingly similar to the Unabomber's manifesto.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He was a good writer.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We have a problem.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it a copyright thing?

situation: Catbert, acting as the human resources representative, confronts Wally about the comments he wrote on his supposedly anonymous employee survey, saying they closely resemble the Unabomber's manifesto. Wally calmly sips his coffee, compliments the writing, and then asks whether the real concern is copyright infringement.
punchline: Wally misses the alarming point that his survey comments sound like a terrorist's manifesto and worries only about plagiarism, while the 'anonymous' survey is clearly traceable to him.
summary: Wally is called out by HR for survey answers that echo a notorious terrorist's writing, and he responds by wondering if he has plagiarized.

title: Arguing Over What Robust Means

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The marketing department has asked us to make our products more robust.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: None of us knows what that means.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we can either cancel this meeting and go ask them. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we can pretend that arguing with each other about the true meaning of "robust" is just as good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: While that option is stupid, it would give us the illusion of doing something useful right now.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Would it be ethical to ignore the long-term interests of stockholders just to feel good about ourselves for a few minutes?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I think robust means it has lots of features.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It means sturdy!

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his team that marketing wants the products to be more robust, but nobody knows what that means. Rather than simply asking marketing, the group chooses to sit and argue over the definition, with one engineer raising an ethics question about wasting shareholders' time before they finally disagree about the word's meaning.
punchline: Instead of taking the simple step of asking marketing for clarification, the team knowingly picks a pointless argument because it feels productive, and the debate ends with each person guessing a different meaning.
summary: A team that has been handed a vague buzzword decides to bicker about its definition instead of asking the people who used it.

title: Integration Layer Boasting Coworker Condescends

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: This week I mapped our applications to our domains and defined the interface between our applications and our software environment.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Whatever you did this week probably seems lame compared to all of that.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
