transcript.text: The stuff I'm doing is way up here in what's called the integration layer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's he been reading?

situation: A bald coworker at a meeting brags about mapping applications to domains and defining interfaces, then belittles what everyone else did that week. He stands and holds his hand high above the Boss's head to show how lofty his work is in the 'integration layer'. The Boss, puzzled by the jargon, wonders what the coworker has been reading.
punchline: The coworker's pompous technical jargon is so buzzword-laden that even the Boss suspects he is just parroting something from a book or article to sound superior.
summary: A smug colleague uses lofty architecture buzzwords to put down his peers, and the Boss quietly suspects he picked it all up from a book.

title: Wally Weaponizes Social Convention Against Favors

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, will you do me a favor?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Absolutely. What are friends for?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: After all, you'd do a favor for me if I asked, right?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Um... sure.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Of course you would.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So do me a favor and don't ask me to do any favors.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow. Okay. I did not see that coming.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're like a wizard who uses the rules of social convention as if they are magic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're Hairless Potter!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't tell Baldemort.

situation: A coworker asks Wally for a favor, and Wally cheerfully agrees, then tricks the coworker into promising reciprocity. Wally then uses that promise to demand that the coworker never ask him for favors. Dilbert, watching, compares Wally to a wizard and dubs him Hairless Potter, and Wally warns him not to tell Baldemort, who turns out to be the balding, horned Boss standing nearby.
punchline: Wally exploits the social obligation of reciprocity to get out of ever doing favors, earning a bald Harry Potter nickname, with the Boss serving as the bald Voldemort.
summary: Wally manipulates a colleague's politeness into a binding promise that frees him from ever helping anyone, impressing Dilbert with his twisted social magic.

file: 2010/2010-03-26_new vice president of engineering_office_lack of experience_revenge_office politics_worry_sabotage_best engineer_4g_skeptical_false information.gif
title: Sabotage by Sending Bad Engineer

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The new VP

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Manager
transcript.text: Don't worry that I wanted your job, or that you have no experience in this field.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Manager
transcript.text: I won't try to sabotage you. In fact, I'll send my best engineer to bring you up to speed.

transcript.speaker: New VP
transcript.text: So... it's called 4G because it's G-G-G-good.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Something like that.

setting: Office of the new vice president of engineering
situation: The Boss, who wanted the VP job himself, visits the new VP, who has no experience in engineering. He promises not to sabotage him and offers to send his best engineer to teach him. The VP then repeats a ridiculous explanation of 4G wireless technology, showing he has been fed false information by the engineer.
punchline: The Boss's promise of help is itself the sabotage, since the engineer feeds the clueless VP nonsense that will make him look foolish.
summary: A passed-over manager pledges support to his inexperienced new superior, then quietly undermines him by supplying a mentor who teaches him absurd falsehoods.

title: Upgrading Your Project From Nonexistent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The people buying our company don't know that your project exists.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you're not allowed to talk to anyone over there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But don't lose hope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm working hard to upgrade your status from nonexistent to unimportant.

setting: Boss's office, with a view of the acquiring company's building
situation: The Boss sits across the desk from Alice and tells her the company's prospective buyers are unaware her project exists, and that she is forbidden from contacting them. He then reassures her that he is trying to raise the project's standing, though only to the level of unimportant.
punchline: The Boss's idea of encouraging news is that his best-case goal is getting her project recognized as unimportant rather than nonexistent.
summary: During an acquisition, a manager offers cold comfort to an employee whose project has gone entirely unnoticed by the buyers.

file: 2010/2010-04-11_beta test_meeting_face front_impractical maintenance requirement_lube_bear's ear_warrant_product_legal_shake fist_justice_sick_hand to mouth_shake_throw up_business_medical.gif
title: Weaponizing Warranty Against Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The beta test went well. Thank you, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I'll have Tina add an impractical maintenance requirement to the manual and we're ready to go.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's standard procedure.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say the user needs to lube the product ten times a day with the wax from a bear's ear.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And say the warranty is voided if the device isn't properly maintained.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that legal?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's better than legal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're using the law to keep justice away!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel sick.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's how you know it's working.

setting: Conference room at a company's office
situation: After a successful beta test, the boss tells the team they will have Tina add an absurd maintenance requirement to the product manual, such as lubing it ten times a day with bear ear wax. The warranty would be voided if customers fail to comply. Dilbert questions the legality, and the boss gleefully admits they are using the law to deny customers justice, while Dilbert and Tina feel queasy.
punchline: The boss treats the nausea Dilbert feels at the company's deliberately unfair warranty scheme as proof that the scheme is working.
summary: A manager plans to hide impossible upkeep rules in a product manual so warranty claims can always be refused, and calls his team's disgust a sign of success.

title: Unverifiable Awesomeness Of The Server Hero

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our servers were about to crash, so I wrote a suite of scripts to keep them running.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your accomplishments are suspiciously hard to verify.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, recapping what we know for sure, you're an inadequate verifier, and you can't rule out the possibility that I'm awesome.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker claims he wrote scripts that prevented a server crash. The Boss says his accomplishments are suspiciously hard to verify. The coworker turns this around, saying the Boss can't verify the work and therefore can't rule out that he's awesome.
punchline: The coworker twists the Boss's skepticism into a logical loophole, claiming that the Boss's inability to verify his work means he can't disprove that he's awesome.
summary: A worker flips his manager's doubts about unprovable results into an argument that his greatness can't be disproved.

title: Learning to Listen to Idiots

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Communication skills training

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Today you will learn how to listen to idiots without snorting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Break into groups of two, with one idiot and one non-idiot in each pair.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you want to be my partner?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um. . .

setting: Corporate training room during a communication skills class
situation: Dogbert, standing on a stool as the trainer, announces a lesson on listening to idiots without snorting. He then tells the class to pair off, one idiot and one non-idiot per pair. A coworker asks Dilbert to be his partner, and Dilbert hesitates awkwardly.
punchline: Dilbert's hesitation reveals he has instantly recognised the coworker as the idiot of the pair, and he is dreading the assignment.
summary: A dog leading a workplace seminar splits the class into pairs by intelligence, and one man's invitation leaves his chosen partner wincing.

title: Wally Plans to Hide Monday

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, I'll need your load calcs by Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Remind me on Monday.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're hoping I won't remember to remind you. Then you'll say it's my fault.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But I will remember, and I will remind you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Good luck. Monday is my hiding day.

situation: Alice tells Wally she needs his load calculations by Tuesday, and he asks her to remind him on Monday. She sees through the ploy, realizing he wants to blame her later for any missed deadline, and vows to remind him anyway. Wally calmly replies that Monday is the day he hides, so she won't be able to find him.
punchline: Wally has a scheduled hiding day, showing he deliberately avoids work and responsibility and has planned around even Alice's determination to hold him accountable.
summary: A coworker cuts off a slacker's blame-shifting scheme, only to learn he has already arranged to be unreachable.

title: PowerPoint Coma Prank Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. My audience has fallen into a PowerPoint coma.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only thing I can do now is put them in funny poses and leave.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: It looks like his finger hit brain.

situation: Dilbert gives a presentation and realizes his audience of coworkers has gone catatonic from boredom. He decides to arrange them in funny poses and sneak away, including jamming one man's finger up his nose. Police later investigate and observe that the man's finger went all the way into his brain, implying he died.
punchline: Dilbert's harmless prank of posing the comatose audience turns out to be fatal, since the finger he put in a coworker's nose reached the brain, which a deadpan cop notes.
summary: A presenter whose dull slides have stunned his listeners poses them for a joke and leaves, only for police to find that one of the poses proved deadly.

title: Confidential Project: Dig Your Grave

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to work on a highly confidential project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you're done, I want you to dig your own shallow grave and beat yourself to death with the shovel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why does it feel as if my entire career has been preparation for this project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're welcome.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has a highly confidential project for him. He then casually instructs Dilbert to dig his own shallow grave and beat himself to death with the shovel once finished. Dilbert remarks that his whole career has prepared him for this, and the Boss takes it as a compliment.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic remark implies his career of mistreatment has trained him for self-destruction, but the oblivious Boss mistakes it for praise and says 'You're welcome.'
summary: A manager casually orders his employee to bury and bludgeon himself after a secret assignment, and misreads the employee's bitter quip as gratitude.

title: Marketing Slide Insults The Audience

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: Our ad campaign will portray users of our competitor's products as baby-eating hobos.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Presenter
transcript.text: While our users will be portrayed by the coolest guy in the entire world.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Soon the meeting turned ugly

transcript.speaker: Woman in Meeting
transcript.text: Then why are you showing a slide of a giant @$$#0%*?

setting: Conference room during a marketing presentation
situation: A bearded marketing presenter explains an ad campaign that will depict competitors' customers as baby-eating hobos, while his own company's users will be shown as the coolest guy in the world. The slide for the cool guy is a photo of the presenter himself, and a woman at the table angrily calls him out for it.
punchline: The presenter's idea of the 'coolest guy in the entire world' is a picture of himself, so a colleague insults him with a censored swear word, implying he is an arrogant jerk.
summary: A marketer's ad pitch reveals he has cast his own face as the epitome of cool, provoking an insult from an unimpressed colleague.

file: 2010/2010-03-10_angry_annoyed_complain_feng shui_lobby_mirror_workplace energy_desk_angle_give the finger_flip the bird_chi.gif
title: Feng Shui Complaints From Wally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Who's the idiot that put a mirror in the lobby? That's bad feng shui.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I keep trying to work, but all of our workplace energy is getting reflected right back out to the sidewalk.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And the way your desk is angled is totally flipping me the chi bird!

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, stands in front of the Boss's desk and complains about a mirror in the lobby, claiming it reflects the office's workplace energy out to the sidewalk. He then adds that the angle of the Boss's desk is also bad feng shui. The Boss sits silently at his computer throughout.
punchline: Wally dresses up his habit of not working in feng shui jargon, blaming the office's energy flow and the desk angle for his lack of productivity, and his 'chi bird' pun makes the nonsense complaint even sillier.
summary: Wally blames the office's bad energy flow, from a lobby mirror to an awkwardly angled desk, for his inability to get any work done.

title: Focus Group Job Includes Fire Marshal

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We need someone to run focus groups about our existing products.

transcript.speaker: Frankenstein's monster
transcript.text: What is a focus group?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: In our case, it's like a mob of angry villagers armed with sharp pens.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And you'd also be the fire marshal for the floor. Are you in?

transcript.speaker: Frankenstein's monster
transcript.text: Yeah. It's a tough job market.

setting: Catbert's HR office, with an exterior view of the office building in the last panel
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, interviews a Frankenstein-like monster for a job running focus groups on the company's existing products. Catbert describes the focus group as an angry mob with sharp pens and then adds fire marshal duties for the floor. The monster accepts anyway.
punchline: The job is so unpleasant and overloaded that only desperation in a tough job market would make someone accept it, and the monster, who should be the one scaring people, gets bullied into it.
summary: A fearsome-looking applicant takes a miserable combined focus-group and fire-marshal job because employment is scarce.

title: Boss Claims Credit, Dilbert Lives In Negative Space

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I added my name to your patent application.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I could have stopped you from working on it, but I didn't. I'm like an artist who understands negative space.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you know what negative space is, Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm living in it!!!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has added his own name to Dilbert's patent application. He justifies taking credit by saying that not blocking Dilbert's work was his contribution, comparing himself to an artist who understands negative space. When he asks if Dilbert knows what negative space is, Dilbert shouts that he is living in it.
punchline: The Boss's contribution is merely having done nothing, and Dilbert, feeling like he's stuck in an empty void of being overlooked and exploited, sarcastically declares he is living in negative space.
summary: A manager grabs co-credit for an invention simply by not interfering, and the furious inventor says he already lives in the emptiness the manager is praising.

title: Vampire Fangs Look Like Walrus

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I asked my dentist to put vampire tips on my incisors so I'd be more intimidating.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here comes Alice. Watch me put the fear into her.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You need to lose a few pounds to pull off the vampire look. This is more of a walrus vibe.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he had his dentist fit vampire tips on his front teeth so he would seem more intimidating. He bares his new fangs at Alice, expecting her to be scared. Alice coolly critiques the look instead, saying he is too heavy to look like a vampire.
punchline: Instead of being frightened by his fangs, Alice insults his weight by saying he looks like a walrus, which deflates his attempt at intimidation.
summary: A boss gets dental fangs to scare his coworkers, but one of them just mocks his figure.

title: Elbonian Slave Labor Isn't That Bad

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're getting some heat from the media for using Elbonian slave labor to build our products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been trying to tell the media that it's not as bad as it sounds.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Now I'll be the slave and you be the oppressor!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: No!!! Not yet!

setting: Conference room, then an Elbonian factory
situation: In a meeting, the Boss tells Dilbert and the others that the company is getting bad press for using Elbonian slave labor, and says he has been telling the media it isn't as bad as it sounds. The final panel shows two chained Elbonians at an assembly line, one proposing they play at being slave and oppressor, and the other refusing.
punchline: The Elbonian workers are so enslaved that even their games of role reversal are begged off, which shows the labor really is as bad as it sounds, and the Boss's PR spin is false.
summary: A manager downplays a scandal over exploited foreign workers while the workers themselves are shown chained to an assembly line.

title: Asok Chooses Death Over Change

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't be afraid of change, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Okay. Wait. What?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Your subtle implication is that I should change to be more like you!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bumpy start.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I choose death!

situation: The Boss tells Asok not to be afraid of change. Asok realizes the boss is implying he should become more like the boss himself, and panics. The Boss mildly thinks it was a bumpy start while Asok shouts that he would rather die.
punchline: Asok finds the prospect of becoming like his pointy-haired boss so horrifying that he would rather die than change.
summary: A manager's casual advice about embracing change makes his young employee realize he is being urged to become just like the manager, and he recoils in horror.

title: Dreaming of a Snout Nose

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I must have fallen asleep during your presentation. I dreamed I had an animal snout for a nose. It seemed so real.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you can't tell your dreams from your reality, maybe this is your dream and you really do have a snout.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does anything seem strange or out of place in this reality?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Can we please do some work?

situation: Asok admits he dozed off during Dilbert's presentation and dreamed he had an animal snout for a nose. Dilbert responds by suggesting Asok might still be dreaming and that he really does have a snout, then wiggles his fingers mockingly and asks if anything seems strange. A bald coworker, annoyed by the silliness, asks that they get back to work.
punchline: Dilbert turns Asok's admission of sleeping through his presentation into a spooky mind game, and the exasperated coworker just wants the pointless teasing to end so they can work.
summary: After a colleague confesses to napping through a talk, the presenter retaliates by trying to convince him he is still dreaming and has a snout.

title: Personality Disguised as Communication Skills

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I signed you up for a class to try and get rid of that thing you have.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What thing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The thing. You know. The thing that makes you the way you are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My personality?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Exactly. But we call it communication skills because it sounds less rude.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, tells Dilbert he has enrolled him in a class to get rid of 'that thing' he has. After vague hints, Dilbert realizes the boss means his personality. The boss confirms it and explains the class is labeled 'communication skills' to sound less rude.
punchline: The company's 'communication skills' training is really an attempt to eliminate employees' personalities, and the polite name is only there to avoid insulting them.
summary: A manager sends an employee to training meant to erase his personality, but dresses it up with a more polite name.

file: 2010/2010-03-07_quality tester_version 2_engineer_overpaid_appear_performance review_office politics_raise_arms out_plan_strategy_wave folder in face_angry_bug eyes_grit teeth_insubordination_engineering.gif
title: Dilbert Resists Quality Testing Duty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I need you to help with quality testing on version 2.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm an engineer, not a quality tester.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I do quality testing, even temporarily, it will make me appear grossly overpaid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That impression could work against me during my next performance review.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A one percent difference in pay, compounded over the rest of my life, is big money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Obviously my best strategy here is to offer resistance that's just short of insubordination.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So move on, little man! Scat! Go!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too much?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to help with quality testing on version 2. Dilbert refuses, arguing that doing lower-level work would make him look overpaid and hurt his next performance review. He explains his calculated plan to resist without quite being insubordinate, then shoos the Boss away with a folder and asks if he went too far.
punchline: Dilbert carefully calculates how much defiance he can get away with, then overshoots, and the Boss's furious face shows he crossed the line into insubordination.
summary: An engineer weighs his long-term salary prospects and decides to stonewall his manager's request, only to find he has pushed the brush-off a little too far.

title: Dilbert Introduces Meeting Attendees Rudely

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And this is Ellen. She has no legitimate reason for attending this meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I assume she's just nosey, or maybe it's a networking sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this guy is a total waste of protein.

transcript.speaker: Ellen
transcript.text: Maybe next time we should introduce ourselves.

situation: Dilbert gestures toward a woman at the meeting table and introduces her to the group by announcing she has no legitimate reason to be there, guessing she is nosey or networking. He then points at a man beside him and calls him a total waste of protein. Ellen, looking annoyed, suggests that next time people should introduce themselves.
punchline: Dilbert's brutally candid introductions of his colleagues are so insulting that Ellen sarcastically proposes everyone introduce themselves in the future.
summary: A blunt coworker narrates who everyone in the room is, trashing each attendee's worth, until one of them snaps back with a sarcastic suggestion.

title: Boss Thinks Work-Life Balance Means Thinking About Work

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I need to get some of that work-life balance I keep hearing about.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I thought about work all last night at home, so what do I do now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not too late to get in on this.

setting: Conference room table in an office meeting
situation: At a meeting table, a bald, green-shirted coworker says he wants some work-life balance, then explains that he spent the previous night at home thinking about work. Dilbert sits beside him while the Pointy-Haired Boss looks on, and in the last panel the Boss clenches his teeth as Dilbert replies.
punchline: The coworker has completely misunderstood work-life balance, believing that thinking about work at home counts as the 'life' part, and Dilbert's deadpan reply that it's not too late to join in underscores how clueless he is.
summary: A colleague seeking better work-life balance proves he has no grasp of the concept by describing a night spent mentally working at home.

file: 2010/2010-06-05_quality metric_bid proposals_magic powers_sarcastic_silly_joke_serious_hand paper_muggles_harry potter_men in black.gif
title: Dilbert Wipes Competitors' Memories

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your quality metric for next year is to win 30% more bid proposals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. I'll use my magic powers to control how much our competitors bid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I worry that you're not taking this seriously.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If the Muggles find out, I'll wipe their memories.

situation: The Boss sets Dilbert a quality metric of winning 30% more bid proposals next year. Dilbert sarcastically replies that he will use magic powers to control competitors' bids. When the Boss says Dilbert isn't taking the goal seriously, Dilbert holds up a small device and says he'll wipe the memories of any 'Muggles' who find out.
punchline: Dilbert answers an unrealistic, externally dependent target with a sarcastic Harry Potter and Men in Black fantasy, showing the goal can only be met by magic.
summary: Handed a performance goal that depends on factors he cannot control, an employee jokes that he will solve it with wizardry and a memory-erasing gadget.

title: Annoyance Before Dishonor Flashlight Ritual

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I cannot meet your arbitrary deadline, so the engineer's code requires me to kill myself with a lightsaber.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But lightsabers haven't been invented yet. The best I can do is annoy myself with a flashlight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Could you do this in the hall?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Annoyance before dishonor!

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he can't meet an arbitrary deadline and, following an imagined 'engineer's code,' says he must ritually kill himself with a lightsaber. Since lightsabers don't exist, he substitutes shining a flashlight in his own face. The boss, unmoved, just asks him to do it in the hall.
punchline: The boss's only concern is that Dilbert's melodramatic ritual suicide-substitute be done out of his office, showing total indifference to the employee's distress over an unreasonable deadline.
summary: An engineer parodies samurai honor by blinding himself with a flashlight over a deadline he can't meet, and his manager only wants him to relocate.

title: Proofreader Mangles Technical Acronyms

transcript.speaker: Proofreader
transcript.text: I proofread your technical document despite not understanding a word of it.

transcript.speaker: Proofreader
transcript.text: I couldn't tell the acronyms from the typos, so I changed them all to whatever felt right.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You say we should migrate our lemon flutes to a hard flea?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not all at once.

setting: Office cubicle and a manager's office
situation: A proofreader tells Dilbert she edited his technical document without understanding it, replacing every acronym she mistook for a typo with whatever felt right. A horned manager then reads the garbled recommendation, asking about migrating 'lemon flutes' to a 'hard flea', and Dilbert can only respond weakly.
punchline: The nonsense-filled document is taken seriously as a real technical proposal, and Dilbert's deadpan 'Not all at once' treats the gibberish as if it were a legitimate migration plan.
summary: An editor who understood nothing of a technical paper scrambled its jargon, leaving the reader to puzzle over a bizarre migration proposal.

title: Thanking Audience For Utter Apathy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's my plan. I'd like to thank all of you for your utter apathy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A few of you stayed awake, and I think I got some accidental eye contact once when the A.C. made a noise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In conclusion, I hate my job, I hate my coworkers, and I hope feral cats eat every one of you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you taking questions?

situation: Dilbert finishes presenting his plan in front of a screen reading 'The End' and thanks his audience for their complete lack of interest. He notes that few stayed awake, then concludes by saying he hates his job and coworkers and hopes feral cats eat them. He then casually asks if anyone has questions.
punchline: Dilbert delivers an openly hostile, insulting conclusion to an audience too apathetic to notice, then cheerfully opens the floor for questions as if nothing unusual was said.
summary: After an unengaged audience sleeps through his talk, a presenter sarcastically thanks them, voices his hatred for everyone, and politely offers to answer questions.

title: Fiddling With Boss's Life Support

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: He survived because his pointy hair cushioned the impact.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Please resist the urge to fiddle with the cool machines that keep him alive.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Maybe we can make him smarter.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What's this do?

situation: A doctor explains to Dilbert, Alice and Wally that the Boss survived an accident because his pointy hair cushioned the impact. He warns them not to play with the life-support machines, but Alice suggests making the Boss smarter and Wally starts poking at the equipment asking what a control does.
punchline: Despite a warning not to touch the equipment keeping the Boss alive, his coworkers immediately start tinkering with it, showing they care more about experimenting than his wellbeing.
summary: Coworkers gathered around the Boss's hospital bed ignore a doctor's plea and start experimenting with the machines keeping him alive.

file: 2010/2010-04-12_nose job_health insurance_surgery_cloth over nose_good deal_veterinarian_dog nose_squirrel_medical.gif
title: Cheap Nose Job From Veterinarian

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our health plan doesn't cover nose jobs, so I used the market system to bargain for a good deal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I learned that a veterinarian is just like a doctor, but cheaper.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you smell a squirrel?

situation: Wally, with a bandage over his nose, tells Dilbert that his health plan wouldn't cover a nose job, so he shopped around for a cheaper option. He reveals he had a veterinarian do the surgery, then asks Dilbert if he smells a squirrel.
punchline: Wally's bargain-priced vet surgery has apparently given him a dog's sense of smell, so he is now sniffing out squirrels.
summary: A man saves money on cosmetic surgery by visiting an animal doctor and ends up with unexpectedly canine senses.

title: Death Ray Gets North Korean Interest

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: We're getting a lot of interest in your death ray invention.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not a death ray. It's a portable brain scanner with a popcorn microwave option...

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: We have an RFQ from North Korea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. That's a death ray.

situation: The CEO tells Dilbert that his company is getting a lot of interest in his death ray invention. Dilbert insists it is merely a portable brain scanner with a popcorn microwave feature. When the CEO adds that a request for quotation has arrived from North Korea, Dilbert abruptly concedes that it is a death ray after all.
punchline: Dilbert's insistence that his device is harmless collapses the moment a notorious rogue state wants to buy it, revealing he knows it is really a weapon.
summary: An inventor downplays his weapon as a kitchen gadget until a request from a hostile regime makes him drop the pretense.

title: Boss Told to Live in Ductwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, my security clearance was accidentally canceled. I need your help.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe you could live in the ductwork, and forage for stale donuts after dark.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I fit in there?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Try foraging as effectively as you manage.

situation: The Boss tells Asok that his security clearance was accidentally canceled and asks for help. Asok sarcastically suggests he live in the ductwork and scavenge for stale donuts at night. When the Boss asks how he could fit, Asok replies that he should forage as effectively as he manages.
punchline: Asok insults the Boss by implying he manages poorly, saying he should forage as effectively as he manages, meaning not very well.
summary: After losing his building access, a clueless supervisor gets a snide suggestion from his subordinate to become a vent-dwelling scavenger.

title: Herding Drunk Cats on Social Media

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: As the marketing manager for social media, my job is to use these two words a lot.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Marketing through social media is like herding cats. And just to make it interesting, many of the cats are drunk and stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Burn.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am totally defriending that witch.

situation: A social media marketing manager presents to a meeting, pointing at a whiteboard that reads only 'Facebook' and 'Twitter'. She explains her job is to say those two words a lot, then compares social media marketing to herding drunk, stupid cats. Dilbert, Dogbert and the Boss sit at the table, and Dogbert reacts to her insult by announcing he is defriending her.
punchline: The manager insults the very people social media marketing targets, and Dogbert responds with a social-media-style retaliation by defriending her, showing how shallow and petty the whole field can be.
summary: A social media marketing expert belittles online audiences as intoxicated felines, prompting an immediate online-style snub from Dogbert.

title: Boss's Browser Shrunk By Toolbars

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Whenever my browser asks me if I want to install a toolbar, I'm afraid to say no.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now my browser window is only one inch tall.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you see anything important on the Internet, could you write it down for me?

situation: The Boss stands by Dilbert's desk holding a coffee mug and admits he always agrees to install browser toolbars. Because of this, his browser window has shrunk to a sliver one inch tall. Instead of fixing it, he asks Dilbert to look at the Internet for him and write down anything important.
punchline: The Boss's habit of blindly accepting every toolbar has made his browser unusable, yet rather than remove the toolbars he delegates his web browsing to Dilbert.
summary: A boss who accepts every toolbar offer ends up with a nearly useless browser and simply outsources his internet use to a coworker.

title: Buzzword Assessment Plan Sells Out Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And of course we'll assess our progress along the way.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Will you be using an enhanced assessment methodology?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I hope that means something. All I did was string together some words I heard in the hallway.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I'll be assessing... by measuring... and um...

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I'd better get in on this.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I can't support this project until I see your advanced assessment methodology plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have it in ten minutes, assuming you don't know what it's supposed to look like.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Very good.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll be in the shower trying to wash my soul.

setting: Conference room during a project presentation, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert presents a project and mentions assessing progress. A coworker asks if he'll use an 'enhanced assessment methodology', a phrase he improvised from hallway buzzwords. Rather than question it, a manager demands an 'advanced assessment methodology plan' before supporting the project, and Dilbert agrees to bluff one together, then goes home to shower and feel clean again.
punchline: Meaningless buzzwords are so convincing to management that Dilbert has to fabricate a plan for something that doesn't exist, and he feels morally dirty about it.
summary: A throwaway phrase made of overheard jargon convinces a manager that a nonexistent methodology is required, forcing the presenter to fake it and then scrub away his guilt.

title: Endless Updates Excuse for Not Working

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Every time I update my software, it tells me I have to reboot.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And every time I reboot, I get another message to update something else. It's all I've been doing since October.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you worked in September, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I admire your optimism about the past.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: At a meeting, Wally explains that software updates and reboots have consumed all his time since October. The Boss hopefully asks whether he at least got work done in September. Dilbert dryly comments on the Boss's optimism.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that Wally has never really worked at all, so the Boss's hope that he did something productive in September is naive.
summary: A lazy employee blames an endless loop of software updates for months of idleness, and a coworker mocks the boss for assuming he ever worked before that.

title: Dogbert Reboots Dilbert's Brain

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's tech support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The problem is in the part of your brain that handles intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can reboot you, but I won't lie: it's going to hurt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We need to talk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you near stairs?

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk in an office
situation: Dilbert consults Dogbert's tech support, and Dogbert diagnoses the fault as being in the part of Dilbert's brain that handles intelligence. Dogbert offers to reboot him but warns it will hurt. When Dilbert says they need to talk, Dogbert asks if he's near stairs, implying he intends to push him down them.
punchline: Dogbert's 'reboot' of Dilbert's brain is a thinly veiled threat of violence, with a push down the stairs as the fix for his stupidity.
summary: A tech support dog tells a customer his intelligence is faulty and hints that the cure involves a painful tumble down some stairs.
keywords: turn it off and on again

title: Ghost Writer Lost A Knife Fight

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert Publishing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm assigning a ghost writer to tighten up your first draft.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Technically, he's not a ghost yet. He's just a guy who lost a knife fight.

transcript.speaker: Author
transcript.text: How long do I have to wait?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you're in a hurry, steer him toward the window.

situation: An author sits across a desk from Dogbert, who runs a publishing house, and is told a ghost writer will polish his first draft. The ghost writer turns out to be a man with a knife stuck in his head who is still alive. Dogbert suggests nudging him toward the window if the author wants him to die faster.
punchline: Dogbert takes the term 'ghost writer' literally and suggests hastening the stabbed man's death so he can become an actual ghost.
summary: A publisher offers a writer a ghost writer who is not yet a ghost, then casually proposes a way to speed up the process.

title: Paper Bag Over Dilbert's Head

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our best sales guy asked for you to accompany him on a sales call.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the secret of being a good sales person?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: You need to give customers the information they need...

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: ...without getting in their faces so often that you become a nuisance.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: For example, a customer would get sick of your face much sooner than mine.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: So halfway through the sales call, you'll need to put this bag over your head while I close the deal.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It looks as if I win our bet.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: No... wait for it...

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Whoa. How do you do that?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It's called sales. Now you owe me a purchase order.

setting: Office and a customer's conference room
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company's best salesman wants him along on a sales call. The salesman explains that the secret to sales is not annoying customers, and that customers would tire of Dilbert's face faster than his own, so Dilbert must wear a paper bag over his head during the pitch. At the meeting, the customer is impressed and the salesman claims a purchase order as his winnings.
punchline: The salesman's 'secret' is that he is more tolerable to look at than Dilbert, so hiding Dilbert's face with a bag lets him close the deal and win a bet.
summary: A star salesperson brings Dilbert to a client meeting only to hide his unappealing face under a bag so the sale goes through.

title: Stalker Coworker Declares Love for Wally

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, you helped me avoid work, and now I can't help loving you.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I show my love by a combination of insanity and stalking.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aren't you married?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You owe me an old carpet.

situation: A wide-eyed coworker appears at Wally's cubicle and declares her love for him because he helped her avoid work. She cheerfully admits her affection takes the form of insanity and stalking. When Wally asks whether she is married, she ignores the question and demands that he give her an old carpet.
punchline: Wally's reasonable question gets a non-sequitur demand for a carpet, showing that the stalker's obsession is really about getting something out of him, not romance.
summary: A deranged admirer confesses her stalker-style crush on Wally, then dodges his question about her marriage by demanding a carpet.

title: Alice Isn't Honest, Just Hateful

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I called this meeting because you're the only person I trust to give me honest feedback on my strategy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's great. It's amazing. It's the best strategy in the universe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought you were honest.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's a common misperception. I just hate people.

situation: The Boss calls Alice into a meeting because he believes she is the one person who will give him honest feedback on his strategy. Alice responds with over-the-top praise, and when the Boss points out that she is supposed to be honest, she reveals she is actually just a person who dislikes everyone.
punchline: Alice's reputation for honesty is a misreading of her general contempt for people, and her lavish praise is sarcasm aimed at the Boss's flawed strategy.
summary: A manager seeks candid criticism from the colleague he thinks never sugarcoats things, only to learn her bluntness stems from misanthropy rather than integrity.

title: Dilbert Out-Argues the Boss on Group Size

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll break into small groups to discuss options.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why? Do you think we'll be smarter when we're in small groups?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That way everyone gets more time to talk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: According to your theory, the ideal group size would be one person talking to himself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you also need the knowledge and perspective that extra people bring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would argue for larger groups, not smaller ones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine! Just break into whatever size groups you think make sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like your style, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for noticing.

setting: Conference room during a meeting, with a title panel showing a presentation screen
situation: The Boss announces the meeting will split into small groups so everyone gets more talking time. Dilbert uses the Boss's own logic to show it leads to absurd conclusions, and the Boss's counter-argument actually supports larger groups. Defeated, the Boss tells everyone to pick their own group sizes, and Dilbert ends up alone in the room praising himself.
punchline: Dilbert wins the argument so thoroughly that he ends up as a group of one, complimenting himself and thanking himself for noticing, which is exactly the absurd ideal he mocked.
summary: A manager's flawed case for splitting a meeting into breakout groups gets dismantled by logic, leaving one employee alone in an empty room flattering himself.

title: Interviewee Loves Business Travel, Gets Insulted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The opening is in sales. Do you like to travel?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Yes. It's my favorite thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one likes business travel. You're either an idiot or you've never done business travel.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: How dare you accuse me of not traveling.

situation: The Boss interviews a candidate for a sales opening and asks whether he likes to travel. When the candidate says it's his favorite thing, the Boss insults him, saying only an idiot or someone who has never traveled for business could like it. The candidate indignantly protests being accused of not traveling, choosing the 'idiot' option without noticing.
punchline: Faced with a choice between being called an idiot or inexperienced, the candidate defends his travel experience and thereby implicitly admits to being an idiot.
summary: A job applicant walks straight into a trap when his interviewer says that anyone who enjoys business trips is either foolish or inexperienced.

title: Learning Leadership By Blaming Others

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's taking you so long to fix the control management system?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your leadership has taught me to give you laughably unrealistic timelines, then blame others when I miss deadlines.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're not even doing THAT right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I need more of your leadership.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert why fixing the control management system is taking so long. Dilbert replies that he has simply learned from the Boss's own leadership style: giving unrealistic timelines and then blaming others. The Boss complains that Dilbert isn't even doing that correctly, and Dilbert says he needs more of the Boss's leadership.
punchline: The Boss unwittingly confirms Dilbert's accusation by criticizing him for failing to blame others properly, showing that his 'leadership' consists of exactly the bad behavior Dilbert described.
summary: Dilbert turns his manager's own bad habits against him, and the manager inadvertently admits to them.

title: The Elk Had a Saddle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My hunting trip was a huge success. I bagged an elk.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hmmm...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That's not like you. There's something missing in this story.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It had a saddle.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And there it is.

situation: The Boss stands at Alice's cubicle holding a coffee mug and boasts that his hunting trip was a great success because he shot an elk. Alice senses the story is incomplete, since it isn't like him to tell one without a blunder. He then admits the elk was wearing a saddle.
punchline: The Boss's elk had a saddle, which means he shot someone's riding animal, confirming Alice's suspicion that his stories always hide an embarrassing blunder.
summary: A boastful manager's tale of a triumphant hunt falls apart when he reveals the missing detail that gives away his mistake.

title: Brain Scanner Predicts Murderous Purchase

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My invention can scan a person's brain and predict his buying decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says you plan to buy... a blunt object so you can kill me and claim credit for my invention.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I anticipated that, which is why I included a feature to microwave the offending part of your brain.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Fert!

setting: Office or lab with a desk and a leather chair
situation: Dilbert, in a lab coat, demonstrates a handheld brain-scanning device on The Boss, who sits behind a desk. The scan reveals The Boss intends to buy a blunt object to kill Dilbert and steal credit for the invention. Dilbert says he anticipated this and zaps the boss's brain with a built-in microwave feature, making smoke puff from his ear.
punchline: Dilbert's invention not only reads the boss's malicious intentions but preemptively punishes them by microwaving the offending part of his brain.
summary: A scientist's mind-reading gadget exposes his superior's murderous plot to steal the invention, then fries the guilty brain tissue on the spot.

title: Crime Scene Cleaning Assistant Offer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ratbert, would you like to be my assistant in the crime scene cleaning profession?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Me?!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You had me at "brains and squeegees."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't say any of those words.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Would it kill you to say them now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it does, you can clean me up.

setting: A small workspace with a desk, Dilbert wearing overalls
situation: Dilbert, dressed in overalls, offers Ratbert a job as his assistant in crime scene cleaning. Ratbert eagerly claims he was won over by words Dilbert never actually said, then asks him to say them anyway. Dilbert responds with a dark quip about Ratbert cleaning up after his death.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan reply that Ratbert can clean him up if saying the gruesome words kills him is a grim joke fitting the crime-scene-cleaning job.
summary: A dark-humored career offer turns into a morbid joke when a too-eager assistant asks his boss to repeat words he never uttered.

file: 2010/2010-06-03_open door policy_office_look over shoulder_suspicious_core systems_key processes_pointless question_act randomly.gif
title: Open Door Policy Meets Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's more important — our core systems or our key processes?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If there's no clear answer to that question, I'll continue to act randomly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get out of my office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The open door policy probably looked good on paper.

situation: The Boss, holding a paper, asks Dilbert (who is holding a coffee mug) whether core systems or key processes matter more. Dilbert replies that without a clear answer he will keep acting randomly, which gets him thrown out of the office. He remarks on the way out that the open door policy looked good only on paper.
punchline: Dilbert shows that management's open door policy is hollow, since honest, sarcastic feedback gets him expelled from the office immediately.
summary: A manager's loaded question draws a candid, sarcastic reply, and the employee is kicked out despite the supposedly welcoming management policy.

title: Alice's Diplomatic Incident Flashback

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm sending you to cultural sensitivity training before we meet with the Elbonians.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Last time you almost started a war.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I made one little mistake.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flashback

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And here's another way the women in my country are different.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW!!!

setting: Boss's office, then a flashback to a meeting with Elbonians
situation: The Boss tells Alice she must attend cultural sensitivity training before meeting the Elbonians, reminding her she nearly started a war last time. Alice dismisses it as one little mistake, and a flashback shows her punching an Elbonian delegate while explaining how women in her country are different.
punchline: Alice's "one little mistake" was physically punching a foreign diplomat mid-meeting, a spectacular understatement of her diplomatic blunder.
summary: A manager sends a combative engineer to etiquette classes after her previous meeting with foreign visitors ended in a punch to a delegate.

file: 2010/2010-02-25_new account manager_boring job_problem solver_introduce_shake hands_first day_toys.gif
title: Meet the Bored New Account Manager

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, meet our new account manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His job is solving a hodgepodge of problems that would bore a normal person to death.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We think his parents didn't let him have toys.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first day is the easiest.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to a new account manager and describes Dilbert's job as solving tedious problems that would bore normal people to death. He then speculates that Dilbert's parents never let him have toys, which is why he tolerates it. As the account manager shakes Dilbert's hand, Dilbert grimly remarks that the first day is the easiest.
punchline: The Boss's insulting introduction implies Dilbert's tedious job is endured only because of a deprived childhood, and Dilbert's reply warns the newcomer that things only get worse from here.
summary: A new colleague gets an unflattering preview of the dull work awaiting him, delivered by a boss who mocks Dilbert's childhood while Dilbert offers a bleak warning.

title: CEO Shares His Fortune: Wine Sales

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO wants to share his good fortune with all employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He invites all of you to visit his winery and buy his non-award-winning wine at nearly retail prices.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He asks that you not park your helicopters near his human chess board because it frightens the dwarves.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting, with a final shot of the company building
situation: The Boss reads an announcement from a sheet of paper to the assembled employees, including Alice and Dilbert. The message sounds generous at first but turns out to be a sales pitch for the CEO's mediocre wine. It ends with a request aimed at employees who supposedly own helicopters, showing how out of touch the CEO is.
punchline: The CEO's so-called generosity is just a chance to sell overpriced, unremarkable wine to his staff, while his messages assume employees are as wealthy as he is, with helicopters and a human chess board.
summary: A manager reads out a memo in which the boss's supposed generosity turns into a wine sales pitch and a bizarre request about helicopters and dwarves.

title: Avoiding Low Priorities Takes Everything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, did you finish the vendor comparison?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm proud to say I did not.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You told me to focus on my highest priorities, and that wasn't one of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... when can I expect it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Logically, that would be never.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If that task ever became the most important thing I was doing, you'd eliminate my position.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: True. But at least you're getting the high priority stuff done, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So far, it's taking all of my energy to avoid doing the low priorities.

setting: Office hallway, with a Sunday-strip header showing a projector screen
situation: The Boss asks Wally whether he finished a vendor comparison, and Wally proudly says he didn't because it isn't one of his highest priorities, as the Boss himself instructed. Wally argues that if the task ever became his top priority, the Boss would eliminate his position. When the Boss asks if the high-priority work is at least getting done, Wally admits he spends all his energy avoiding low-priority tasks.
punchline: Wally turns the boss's instruction to focus on top priorities into an excuse for doing nothing, since his entire effort goes into dodging the low-priority work.
summary: A slacking employee uses his manager's own priority advice to justify skipping a tedious task, and admits that avoiding it is his real full-time job.

title: Interviewing Napping Applicant for Sleepy Company

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Interview this applicant and tell me if he's right for our company.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Tim, we don't set the bar as high as we used to.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: In our golden days, we insisted on employees who could work tirelessly through the night.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: As business slowed, we were happy with anyone who put in eight hours a day.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Then our best people left.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Now our cubicles are mostly used for napping.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: So my question is this: would a ringing phone wake you up?

transcript.speaker: Applicant
transcript.text: Probably.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: He comes across as a braggart.

setting: Office interview room and hallway, with a projector-screen banner at top
situation: The Boss asks Tim to interview a job applicant. Tim, acting as interviewer, explains how the company's hiring standards have fallen from tireless overnight workers to people who merely work eight hours, and that cubicles are now used for napping. He asks whether a ringing phone would wake the applicant, and when the applicant says 'Probably,' Tim reports back that the man seems like a braggart.
punchline: The company's standards have sunk so low that an applicant claiming he would probably wake up to a ringing phone is treated as boastful.
summary: A decaying company's interviewer judges a candidate's confidence as arrogance after lowering the bar to simply staying awake.

title: Leader Trusts Gut, Not Process

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A good leader uses a process for making decisions.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I take this one?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Make us proud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: If making a decision is just a process, why can't a computer do it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because sometimes I have to rely on my gut.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which part of your gut is the smart part? Is it the stomach lining, or maybe the colon?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm talking about instinct. It's an indefinable leadership quality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the indefinable thing like a superstition?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Or cooties?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a process!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that your colon talking?

setting: Conference room during a meeting presentation
situation: The Boss lectures the team on using a process for decisions. Dilbert asks why a computer couldn't make decisions then, and the Boss claims he sometimes relies on his gut instinct. Dilbert mocks the idea, asking which part of the gut is smart and comparing instinct to superstition, until the Boss loses his temper.
punchline: The Boss's contradictory claim that leaders follow a process but also trust an undefinable gut instinct falls apart under questioning, and his angry shouting prompts Dilbert to say it must be his colon talking.
summary: A manager praising structured decision-making gets cornered into defending his own mysterious gut feelings, and snaps when his team pokes fun at it.

title: Basic Research Excuse Meets Lab Report

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: I'm exhausted from all of the basic research I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: It's too bad that the value of my work won't be quantifiable for another ten years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to see your lab report.

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: So... the new rule is that we write down stuff?

setting: Conference room table in a research lab office
situation: A scientist at a meeting claims to be worn out from doing basic research, adding that its value can't be measured for ten years. The Boss, seated beside Dilbert, asks to see his lab report. The scientist is startled and asks whether documenting your work is now a requirement.
punchline: The scientist has been using 'basic research' as an unverifiable excuse to avoid work, and he's thrown by the idea that he might have to produce any written evidence of it.
summary: A researcher hides behind the vague promise of long-term science until his manager asks for something on paper.

title: Boss Starved in the Ductwork

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where's our Pointy-Haired Boss?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Dead.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I canceled his security clearance, so he went into hiding in the duct-work. By now he's probably gotten stuck and starved to death.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I plan to cremate his remains, but it might take a while; the thermostat only goes up to 85.

situation: Dilbert asks Alice where the Boss is, and she bluntly replies that he is dead. She explains she canceled his security clearance, he hid in the ductwork, and he has likely starved after getting stuck. She then deadpans that she intends to cremate the body using the office thermostat, which only goes up to 85 degrees.
punchline: Alice casually admits to causing the Boss's death and then treats disposing of the body as a mundane facilities problem limited by the thermostat's maximum temperature.
summary: Alice calmly reports that her paperwork move drove the boss into the vents to die, and plans to dispose of him with the office heating.

title: Business Strategy Is Biased Guesswork

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What do you get when you combine cognitive bias with inaccurate information?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our business strategy! Haha-hahahaha!!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I guess I should keep my day job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good luck with that.

situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug tells Dilbert a joke: cognitive bias plus inaccurate information equals the company's business strategy. He laughs at his own punchline while the Boss, standing nearby, scowls angrily. The coworker admits he should keep his day job, and Dilbert wryly wishes him luck with that.
punchline: The coworker's joke insults the company's strategy in front of the Boss, so Dilbert sarcastically implies his day job is now in jeopardy.
summary: A man jokes that his company's strategy is just flawed thinking built on bad data, not noticing his furious boss listening in.

title: Alice Insults Coworker, Refuses Coffee Run

transcript.text: Nope. Don't have time.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And no one else is qualified, so you might as well give up and look for a new job.

situation: A coworker asks Alice to review a document for technical accuracy, and she curtly says she has no time. He then tells her she should quit because no one else is qualified to do it, and Alice responds by insulting him and telling him to fetch her coffee.
punchline: Alice turns the coworker's attempt at an insult back on him, pointing out that the only useful thing he could do is bring her coffee.
summary: A man's dismissive jab at Alice backfires when she fires back with an even sharper put-down and a demand for coffee.

title: Boss Accidentally Fired, Carol Calls Security

transcript.speaker: Carol

situation: The Boss complains to his assistant Carol that she filled out Ted's termination paperwork with the Boss's name as the fired employee. He lists how his access, phone and passwords have all been cut off and tells her to fix it. Carol instead picks up the phone and calls security to report that she has found the fugitive.
punchline: Carol deliberately wrote the Boss's name on the form and now gleefully turns him in to security as an escaped fugitive, getting revenge on him instead of fixing the error.
summary: An assistant's paperwork slip leaves her manager officially terminated, and rather than correcting it she happily phones security to report him.

situation: A marketing manager shows off her finished promotional video, and Dilbert and the Boss say they will send comments. punchline: The only engineering review of the video was Wally's approval, given because he misunderstood the request as a question about humor, so the technically inaccurate claims went unchecked.
summary: A marketing video full of false technical claims slipped through review because the lone engineer who replied thought he was rating its comedy.

title: Evil Cure for Incompetence

transcript.text: We realized our project can't work even if we execute it perfectly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our boss' plan is to go over budget, attract attention, and hope an executive cancels our project for his own political reasons.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now do you agree that evil is the cure for incompetence?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't make me say it.

setting: Outdoors on a walking path in a grassy park area
situation: Dilbert walks outside with Dogbert and explains that his team's project is doomed even if executed flawlessly. He reveals that the Boss's plan is to overspend and draw attention so that an executive will cancel the project for political reasons. Dogbert, standing on a tree stump, asks whether Dilbert now agrees that evil cures incompetence, and Dilbert reluctantly refuses to say it.
punchline: The Boss's incompetent project can only be saved by a scheming, politically motivated executive, which makes Dogbert's claim that evil is the cure for incompetence uncomfortably plausible, as Dilbert's unwilling reply admits.
summary: A doomed project can only be rescued by a cynical executive's political cancellation, leaving Dilbert unwilling to concede that Dogbert's pro-evil philosophy has a point.

title: Bandaged Tester Swears About Shipping

transcript.text: Is our new product safe enough to start selling?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did that sound like "ship" to you?

situation: The Boss introduces Rodney, a tester wrapped head to toe in bandages, as the person in charge of product safety testing. When asked if the new product is safe enough to sell, Rodney flails and lets out a string of cursing. The Boss ignores the obvious signs and asks Dilbert whether the outburst sounded like the word "ship."
punchline: The bandaged safety tester is clearly injured and angry from testing the product, but the oblivious Boss deliberately misreads his swearing as approval to ship it.
summary: A mummy-like injured tester answers a safety question with furious profanity, and his boss chooses to hear it as a green light for release.

title: Dogbert Pitches Merger Bribe Book

transcript.text: I'll arrange an unwise merger so you can cash out while I collect an obscene commission.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's like a bribe, but instead of going to jail, a stranger will write a best-selling book with your name on it.

transcript.speaker: CEO

situation: Dogbert, acting as an investment banker, tells an incompetent CEO that he can engineer a bad merger so the CEO can cash out while Dogbert earns a huge commission. He compares it to a bribe, except the CEO gets a ghostwritten best-selling book instead of a jail sentence. The CEO's only question is whether he can read the book.
punchline: The CEO is so unaware and incurious that, after hearing the plan is essentially corrupt, his only concern is whether he gets to read the book supposedly written under his name.
summary: A dog financier cheerfully admits to an incompetent executive that a harmful merger will enrich them both, and the executive just wants to know if he can read his own ghostwritten bestseller.

title: Failing Project Needs Strategic Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should I stop buying stuff?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert tells his colleagues that the math proves their project can't succeed. The Boss admits canceling it themselves would be embarrassing, so he proposes acting dumb and hoping upper management kills it over budget. Dilbert asks if he should stop buying supplies, and the Boss tells him to buy double.
punchline: The Boss would rather deliberately waste money to trigger a budget-driven cancellation than admit the project is doomed and cancel it himself.
summary: Rather than own up to a hopeless project, a manager schemes to make it so costly that someone higher up has to kill it.

title: Brusque Email Versus Brevity Apology

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You owe me an apology.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're making it worse!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why am I so happy?

situation: A female coworker with arms crossed complains to Dilbert that his e-mail was rude and demands an apology. Dilbert reframes his curtness as conciseness and then offers a mock apology that insults her instead. She gets angrier, and Dilbert cheerfully points out that her anger hasn't bothered him at all.
punchline: Dilbert's non-apology is a deliberate insult, and he gleefully admits that her getting more upset only makes him happier.
summary: After being scolded for a curt message, Dilbert issues a backhanded apology that enrages his colleague while delighting himself.

summary: A consultant briefs a client on the absurd fallout of wrecking a national monument, but the client daydreams about sightseeing from his luxury aircraft.

situation: Dilbert is walking outdoors with a date who tells him she likes it when a man cooks for her. punchline: Dilbert cooked for his date out of affection, but she merely wanted a free meal, and he sarcastically states this mismatch as 'wanting different things' after the date fails.
summary: A woman's enthusiasm for being cooked for makes Dilbert suspect she's after a free meal rather than a relationship, and the date goes nowhere.

punchline: Dilbert dismisses the obvious creepiness of his invention by comparing himself to Edison, a self-serving rationalization that ignores how unsettling the shoulder head really is.
summary: An inventor presents a bizarre shoulder-mounted phone designed to look like a tiny elderly head and brushes off criticism by likening himself to a famous genius.

situation: Dogbert, working as a tech support agent, asks a caller to email him a list of everything they've already tried. He then explains he'll make them repeat every step, sometimes several times. He adds that they should take their time because he's busy reading a good book online.
punchline: Dogbert's tech support deliberately wastes the customer's time with pointless repeated troubleshooting while he entertains himself, mocking the unhelpfulness of real support lines.
summary: A smug support agent plans to make a customer redo every failed fix over and over while he enjoys some leisurely online reading.

punchline: Catbert deliberately delivers the good news first so Alice celebrates a promotion that is really just twice the work, and then gloats about his manipulation.
summary: A promotion turns out to be a trap when the HR cat saves the bad part for after the celebration.

situation: Dogbert announces a support group for people who always make bad choices, and Ratbert eagerly signs up. Dogbert then makes Ratbert the organizer and adds demands that everyone wear uniforms and chant his name, which Ratbert finds more and more appealing.
punchline: Ratbert is the perfect recruit because his habit of making bad choices keeps him enthusiastically joining what is clearly a cult, and he is delighted by each warning sign.
summary: A scheming dog sets up a self-help circle for poor decision-makers and a gullible companion happily volunteers to run what turns into a personality cult.

He then demonstrates it by ignoring an angry audience member who demands an answer to his question. Dogbert tells Beverly, who is busy typing on her phone, to keep going because the man doesn't exist.
punchline: Dogbert illustrates his rude-equals-efficient thesis by pretending a furious questioner doesn't exist so that he and Beverly can keep working uninterrupted.
summary: A pint-sized seminar leader proves his theory of productivity by cheerfully refusing to acknowledge an enraged attendee.

summary: A dreaded forced software upgrade drives an employee to protest in a primitive caveman outfit, which only irritates the unsympathetic IT enforcer.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company assigns people to careers based on their looks. Dilbert is transferred to the art department, where an artsy coworker welcomes him and says he envies the snout.
punchline: The company's absurd policy of matching careers to appearance sends Dilbert to the art department, where his deformity is admired as a daring creative statement.
summary: A boss reassigns an engineer to the art department because his odd-looking nose no longer fits the profession's look.

punchline: The Boss is so convinced that software is made by magical elves that Alice's lesson about real engineering effort only convinces him his imaginary elves are acting up.

When a coworker then asks him for the revised budget estimate, Wally deliberately garbles the request and uses it as his excuse for not having it.
punchline: Wally immediately demonstrates the scam by absurdly mangling the words 'revised budget estimate' to justify not doing the work, shamelessly proving his own point.
summary: A slacker coworker openly confesses that faking bad hearing gets him out of tasks, then promptly puts the trick into practice on an unsuspecting colleague.

summary: The sinister HR chief justifies slashing perks with a questionable poll, then piles on a ridiculous extra conclusion that reveals the data is invented.

situation: Wally tells The Boss that futurists predict a labor shortage once baby boomers retire. summary: A coworker's snide remark about a bad cosmetic surgery result gets answered with a jab at his faith in horoscopes and alternative medicine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: That's terrific.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
