setting: Mom's kitchen or home with a table and potted plants
situation: Dilbert tells his mother, who is potting a seedling, that his company is moving to a web-only business model. She sarcastically asks about phase three and whether it exists only in his imagination. When he asks her to be nice, she retorts by asking him to help grow her plant back into a seed.
punchline: Dilbert's mom sarcastically implies his company's web-only strategy is an unrealistic fantasy with no real plan, and compares it to the absurdity of reversing a plant's growth into a seed.
summary: A mother gardening at home responds to her son's news of a web-only company strategy with cutting sarcasm about its dubious planning.

title: Handover: A Mysterious Glowing Box

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Victor quit. I need you to take over his project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did he leave any documentation?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but it's obviously some sort of glowing box. That should be enough to get you started.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you finish it by Monday?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If it's a nightlight, I can finish it by today.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a coworker named Victor has quit and that Dilbert must take over his project. With no documentation, the only starting point is a small glowing box that the Boss hands over. The Boss asks for it to be finished by Monday, and Dilbert has no idea what it actually is.
punchline: Dilbert has to guess what the project even is from an unexplained glowing box, and sarcastically notes that only if it's a simple nightlight could he finish it that fast.
summary: A departed employee leaves behind nothing but a mysterious glowing box, and the boss expects the replacement to figure it out and deliver by the deadline anyway.

file: 2010/2010-08-27_skill assessment_lazy_bad worker_morning person_sleepy_afternoon_sell stock_stand on chair.gif
title: Catbert Interviews Lazy Candidate, Sells Stock

transcript.text: I get sleepy in the afternoon. And I'm not a morning person.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm at my best for about an hour in between, which explains why I'm an exceptionally good lunch eater.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's the workforce skills assessment going?

transcript.text: I just sold all of my company stock.

setting: Office conference room and Catbert's office
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, conducts a workforce skills assessment by interviewing Wally across a conference table. Wally cheerfully admits he is useless in the morning and the afternoon and is only good at eating lunch. When the Boss later asks how the assessment is going, Catbert replies that he has just sold all of his company stock.
punchline: Catbert's assessment reveals such a bleak view of the workforce's skills (as typified by Wally) that he dumps his company stock, implying the company is doomed.
summary: After hearing a staffer describe himself as productive only at mealtime, the HR chief reports his progress on evaluating employee skills by cashing out his shares.

title: Carbon Footprint Book for Triplets

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I barely know her.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: She's having triplets. Try to bring an appropriate gift for once.

transcript.speaker: Kim
transcript.text: It's a... book on how to lower my carbon footprint?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're killing us all.

setting: Office cubicles and a break room table at a baby shower
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert about a baby shower for Kim, who is expecting triplets, and warns him to bring an appropriate gift for once. At the shower, Kim unwraps Dilbert's present and finds a book on lowering her carbon footprint. Dilbert bluntly tells her she is killing everyone by having so many children.
punchline: Dilbert's gift is a pointed, passive-aggressive criticism that having triplets is environmentally irresponsible, and he says so outright.
summary: Told to bring a proper present to a colleague's baby shower, Dilbert instead hands over an eco-guilt book and accuses her of harming the planet.

title: Success Is Attendance Plus Luck

transcript.text: Dogbert the Empire Builder Consultant

transcript.text: Success is just attendance plus luck.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You always want to be in the general vicinity when something good happens.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. I just doubled the bit rate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Present!

setting: Office, with a lab-style workstation in the final panel
situation: Dogbert, wearing a crown and acting as an empire builder consultant, tells the Boss that success is just attendance plus luck and that you should be near wherever good things happen. In the last panel Dilbert, in a lab coat, announces he has doubled the bit rate. The Boss pops in from the doorway, waving his hand and shouting that he is present.
punchline: The Boss immediately applies Dogbert's advice by showing up the moment Dilbert achieves something, so he can claim a place in the success without having done any of the work.
summary: A crowned consultant's cynical theory of success is put into practice when the Boss barges in just as an employee's achievement is announced.

title: Asok's Stomach Leaps Into Mouth

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, I need you to help Alice give a presentation to 500 sales reps.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: GMPH!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that your stomach?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Yeth.

situation: The Boss tells Asok, who is holding a coffee mug, that he must help Alice present to 500 sales reps. Asok is so terrified that he spills his coffee and his stomach comes up into his mouth. The Boss calmly asks if that is his stomach, and Asok confirms it.
punchline: Asok's fear of public speaking is so extreme that his stomach literally jumps out of his mouth, and he answers the Boss's casual question with a lisp because of it.
summary: A young employee is so frightened by the prospect of a huge presentation that his stomach pops out of his mouth.

title: Ritual Sacrifice Improves Google Ranking

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We can improve our Google search ranking with key words, inbound links and...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: ...ritual sacrifice of a...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I think it's down to you or me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What are you implying?

situation: At a meeting about improving the company's Google search ranking, Asok lists key words and inbound links, then casually adds that ritual sacrifice is part of the plan. Looking around the table, he concludes the victim must be either himself or the one coworker, who reacts with alarm and asks what he is implying.
punchline: Asok is so matter-of-fact about the need for a human sacrifice for search ranking that he calmly picks who should die, and the coworker is the only one who finds that alarming.
summary: A junior employee treats a human sacrifice as just another item in the search-engine optimization checklist and then starts working out who should be the victim.

file: 2010/2010-02-21_cost estimate_deny_numbers_manipulate_decisions_hurt_typing at computer_humming noise_annoy_go away_angry face_home_sitting on couch.gif
title: Humming Away Cost Estimate Requests

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I don't trust you with numbers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the kind of guy who will remove useful qualifiers and distribute a figure as if it is true in all cases.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Decisions will be made. People will get hurt.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For everyone's sake, the safest thing I can do is make an annoying humming sound until you go away.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hummmmm-mmmmmmmmm-mmmmm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Half of life is making people go away.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Humm-mmmm

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for a rough cost estimate for the design phase. Dilbert refuses because he expects the number to be stripped of its caveats and treated as fact, and he warns of the damage that will follow. He then hums annoyingly until the coworker leaves, and at home he tells Ratbert that half of life is making people go away.
punchline: Dilbert's solution to the risk of his estimates being misused is to avoid the conversation by humming until people leave, a tactic he treats as a life skill.
summary: Rather than risk his tentative figures being taken as gospel, an engineer drives off a questioner by droning, then reflects on the value of dismissing people.

file: 2010/2010-04-09_powerpoint proboscis_medical condition_nose grows_long nose_lie_pinocchio_close eyes_grit teeth_nose through face_pain_sting_clench fists.gif
title: Sympathetic PowerPoint Proboscis Nose Growth

transcript.speaker: Salesman

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please stop.

transcript.speaker: Salesman

situation: Dilbert tells a visiting salesman that he has a condition in which his nose grows whenever other people lie. The salesman keeps making insincere claims, Dilbert's nose grows longer and he grimaces and asks him to stop. In the last panel the nose has grown so long it is jammed into the salesman's face.
punchline: The salesman's lies make Dilbert's nose grow so long that it pokes him in the face, so he cheerfully warns that pulling it out might sting, which shows how automatic and oblivious his dishonesty is.
summary: A man whose nose lengthens whenever others lie is skewered by a salesman whose insincere patter makes the nose grow right into his own face.

title: Garbage Man's Soul-Swapping ShamWow Scheme

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Souls are totally fungible. Use this ShamWow to absorb someone else's soul while you suck on the other end.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Why does this suddenly seem so wrong?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slurp

setting: An alley beside a trash bin, then a conference room
situation: Asok, who has lost his soul, approaches a garbage man who claims to know how to get it back. The garbage man hands him a ShamWow towel and says he can absorb someone else's soul by sucking on the other end. In the final panel Asok is in a meeting with a towel over a colleague's head, sucking on it while Dilbert and The Boss look on, and he suddenly has second thoughts.
punchline: Asok only realizes how wrong it is to steal another person's soul after he is already doing it, a dig at how people rationalize unethical acts until they are in the middle of them.
summary: A desperate intern follows a shady street tip to reclaim his missing soul by siphoning one from a coworker with a miracle cleaning cloth, only to question his ethics mid-slurp.

title: Conference Room Goes to Highest Rank

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need this room for my meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't it make more sense for you to get a different room since we're already here?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of the conference rooms are booked.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, then I guess we should compare the importance of your meeting versus this one.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not how it works.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Conference rooms go to the highest ranked manager.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took me months to schedule this meeting!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Scram.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The goal of this meeting is to figure out why nothing ever gets done around here.

situation: The Boss barges into a conference room where Dilbert is holding a meeting and demands it for his own. When Dilbert points out the other rooms are booked and suggests weighing the importance of the two meetings, the Boss says rooms go to the highest ranked manager and kicks Dilbert's group out. The Boss then opens his meeting in the commandeered room.
punchline: The Boss bumps a meeting that took months to schedule, then uses the room to discuss why nothing ever gets done, never recognizing that his own rank-pulling behavior is the cause.
summary: A manager commandeers a hard-won meeting room by pulling rank, then convenes to ponder why the company is so unproductive.

title: Dinosaur Purchasing Director's Fossil Fuel Revenge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Bob is the director of purchasing. He's here to describe our new procurement process.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Our system divides products into two categories: things you don't want, and things you're not allowed to buy.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It's my way of saying thanks for lubing your SUV with my dead ancestors.

situation: The Boss introduces Bob, a dinosaur who is the director of purchasing, to explain a new procurement process. Bob says the system sorts items into things employees don't want and things they aren't allowed to buy. He then reveals the policy is deliberate payback for humans burning fossil fuels made from his dead ancestors.
punchline: The procurement process is deliberately useless because Bob, a dinosaur, is taking revenge on humans for using oil and gasoline, which are made from dinosaur remains.
summary: A dinosaur running the purchasing department designs a purchasing system that blocks every request as payback for humanity fueling its cars with ancient dinosaur remains.

transcript.speaker: Amber

setting: Office break room by the coffee maker
situation: Dilbert asks his coworker Amber, who is holding a coffee mug, if she would like to celebrate New Year's Eve with him. She answers 'maybe' and openly admits it is so he can't make other plans while she waits for a better offer. She gestures at him dismissively as she explains she can get away with it, and Dilbert glumly agrees.
punchline: Amber brazenly admits she is stringing Dilbert along as a backup option, and Dilbert resignedly accepts that his unappealing appearance and status let her treat him that way.
summary: A coworker bluntly confesses that her noncommittal reply to a date invitation is a way to keep him on hold while she shops for better options.

title: Dilbert Escalates to Talking Over Others

situation: Dilbert sits on a rock beside Dogbert and announces that he is stepping up his antisocial behavior from simply not listening to actively talking over people. Dogbert asks how he can enjoy conversation without listening, and Dilbert's reply is printed overlapping Dogbert's, demonstrating the talking-over in the lettering itself. Dilbert concludes that listening was never the fun part of conversation.
punchline: The overlapping, jumbled speech balloons visually demonstrate Dilbert talking over Dogbert, and his conclusion that listening isn't the fun part reveals the self-centered logic behind rude behavior.
summary: A smug Dilbert explains to his dog that he now interrupts people on purpose, since hearing others was never the enjoyable bit of chatting.

title: Role Model Who Does It Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think you're doing your part wrong.

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's cubicle holding a coffee mug and announces he is there to be Dilbert's role model. He says his actions speak louder than words and invites Dilbert to observe him. Dilbert, unimpressed, tells him he is doing his part wrong.
punchline: The Boss offers himself as a model to emulate, but Dilbert points out that the boss is so incompetent that he is not even playing the role of role model correctly.
summary: A manager volunteers to lead by example, and the employee deadpans that the manager is failing at even that.

title: Mental Gifting Goes Straight to Insults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Stupid sweater.

setting: A table in a break room or kitchen, on Christmas
situation: Dilbert, wearing a bathrobe, proposes that he and Dogbert exchange imaginary Christmas gifts. Dilbert imagines giving Dogbert a sweater that doesn't fit, and Dogbert imagines giving Dilbert a tool he already owns. Dilbert wishes him a Merry Christmas and Dogbert grumbles about the imaginary sweater.
punchline: Dogbert is so petty and ungrateful that he complains about a gift that exists only in imagination, which shows that even pretend gift-giving cannot escape the awkwardness of bad presents.
summary: Two friends swap pretend presents that are every bit as disappointing as real ones, and one of them still sulks about it.

title: The Dutch Sandwich Tax Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... that would transfer our tax burden to people who can't afford tax attorneys.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah... Their sandwich has a less appealing name.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a tax consultant, offers to cut the company's corporate taxes with a loophole strategy called the "Dutch Sandwich." The Boss works out that the tax burden would simply be shifted onto people who cannot afford tax attorneys. Dogbert agrees and quips that their sandwich has a less appealing name.
punchline: Corporate tax avoidance pushes the burden onto ordinary people, and the joke implies their "sandwich" would be something like a "crap sandwich," which is far less appealing than a Dutch one.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a cleverly named tax loophole and cheerfully admits that ordinary taxpayers end up paying for it.

title: Dilbert's Dismal Date Pitch

situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman on a date and tries to sell himself by admitting he has less to offer than other men. He describes his job as clinging to his cubicle walls while a vortex of failure consumes him. When she asks about his long-term prospects, he says he will probably choke to death on an olive.
punchline: Dilbert's honest self-assessment is so relentlessly grim, from a doomed career to a ridiculous death, that it makes the worst possible dating pitch.
summary: On a dinner date, a man keeps listing bleak facts about his career and future, making himself sound like the least appealing partner imaginable.

title: Flawed Test Results Used Anyway

transcript.text: Thanks to your input, the test had nothing in common with how things work in the real world.

transcript.text: So I wasted two weeks of my life on a test that is not only meaningless. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . but also dangerously misleading.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This slide shows the gap between the test results and reality.

transcript.speaker: Manager

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Why's he so cranky?

transcript.speaker: Coworker

situation: Dilbert presents the results of a technology test and sarcastically thanks the people who set its parameters, explaining that the test bore no resemblance to real-world conditions. He shows a slide of the gap between results and reality, but management says they'll use the results anyway because it's the only data they have. Dilbert wishes them dead and the attendees wonder why he's so cranky.
punchline: Management knowingly bases decisions on admittedly meaningless and misleading data simply because it's the only data available, and then dismisses Dilbert's justified anger as mere crankiness.
summary: After exposing a worthless test, an engineer watches his bosses cheerfully adopt its bogus numbers and then puzzle over his bad mood.

The delighted employee cheers that crime pays, and Catbert explains the company hopes he can lie as well as he steals.
punchline: The employee's slacking on Facebook is treated as qualification for a social media marketing job, and the promotion is justified by his talent for lying, with 'steal' referring to his stolen work time.
summary: A wasteful worker is promoted to a social media marketing role because his time-wasting supposedly proves his suitability, and his gloating gets undercut by an insult.

title: Recalibrating Faith in Humanity Online

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks Dogbert what he is doing at his computer. Dogbert explains he is recalibrating his lack of faith in humanity by reading message board opinions. Before he finishes explaining, he is already so enraged by what he is reading that he slams his fist and shouts an insult at the screen.
punchline: Reading online message board comments instantly drives Dogbert into a rage, proving that the activity reliably confirms his low opinion of humanity.
summary: Dogbert cheerfully describes a quick routine for confirming his distrust of people, then loses his temper at the very first online comments he reads.

title: Goatee Gets Brutally Honest Review

The coworker, unbothered, replies that the flea is resistant to soup, implying food is trapped in his facial hair.
punchline: The coworker casually admits his goatee is so messy that soup residue clings to it and even a flea survives there, confirming Dilbert's insult.
summary: Fishing for a compliment about his new facial hair, a man gets a candid dismissal and then cheerfully confirms how unkempt it is.

title: Punished for Being Happy at Work

punchline: The supposedly unspeakable infernal punishment for workplace happiness is simply a tedious, mundane office meeting task, implying that ordinary corporate drudgery is a kind of hell.
summary: A devil-costumed Phil punishes a cheerful Dilbert by hauling him off to a meeting where the torment is a dull photo-editing chore.

title: Can Versus Should: Doing His Job

setting: Office, across a desk in a meeting
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he can put one system onto a particular network, and Dilbert confirms that he can. Dilbert then warns that what an engineer is able to do is rarely what he ought to do. When the Boss asks what he should do, Dilbert says he should be doing the Boss's job.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the Boss is incompetent and that engineers end up doing his work for him, which is why he does things he technically can do but shouldn't have to.
summary: An engineer agrees to a technical request but tells his manager that engineers often get stuck doing work that belongs to someone else, namely the manager.

title: Promoted Into Limbo

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you've been such a good intern that I've decided to promote you.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Your new status is called limbo. You will exist in a plane between the living and the damned.

transcript.speaker: Asok

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: (thought) Great. It went right to his head.

situation: The Boss tells Asok, his intern, that he is being promoted. The promotion turns out to be a new status called limbo, a plane between the living and the damned. Asok is overjoyed just to be told he will exist, and the Boss privately grumbles that the praise has gone to his head.
punchline: Asok is so starved of recognition that merely being told he will exist counts as a triumph, and the Boss, who gave him nothing real, resents the pride he caused.
summary: A boss rewards a hardworking intern with a promotion to an in-between state of non-being, and the intern is thrilled anyway.

title: Man Who Couldn't Summarize Earth History

transcript.text: It all started 4.53 billion years ago during the Hadean Eon.

transcript.text: I hope you don't mind if I skip over the part where the Earth formed by accretion from the solar nebula.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hours later

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: ... and that formed what we call the Moon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll just ask someone else what time it is.

situation: Dilbert asks a man a simple question, such as the time, and the man begins a lengthy history of the Earth starting 4.53 billion years ago. He proudly offers to skip one part, then continues for hours, reaching the formation of the Moon. Dilbert finally gives up and decides to ask someone else.
punchline: The man believes he is being concise by skipping one small detail of a cosmic history, while Dilbert just wanted a quick answer and gives up after hours of rambling.
summary: A chatty colleague turns a quick question into an epic lecture on planetary origins, leaving his listener exhausted and seeking help elsewhere.

title: Loofah and Bread in Clean Room

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm getting a lot of complaints about you eating your lunch in the clean room.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: And people don't like it when you use your loofah in there.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's my French bread. And I can't help it if my back itches.

situation: Catbert, the HR director, tells the Boss that coworkers are complaining about him eating lunch in the clean room. He adds that people also object to the Boss using his loofah in there. The Boss defends himself, claiming the loofah is his French bread and that he can't help his itchy back.
punchline: The Boss tries to justify scrubbing his back with a loofah in the clean room by absurdly passing it off as a loaf of French bread.
summary: An HR cat scolds a clueless manager for grooming habits in a sterile workspace, and the manager's excuse only makes things worse.

file: 2010/2010-12-30_competitor from future_terminate company_issue_time travle_robot building skills_zombies.gif
title: Time-Traveling Robots Crunchier Than Zombies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A competitor from the future is sending robots back in time to terminate our company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far it's not much of an issue because their time travel technology is way ahead of their robot-building skills.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is that as fun as it looks?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Totally. They're like zombies, but crunchier.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk and a hallway
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that a competitor from the future is sending robots back in time to destroy the company. He reassures him that the threat is minor because the attackers' robots are poorly built. In the hallway, a coworker holding a coffee mug asks Alice if fighting the robots is as fun as it looks, as she holds a broken robot upside down.
punchline: The future competitor has mastered time travel but cannot build a decent robot, so the terminators are flimsy and easily smashed, making them like zombies that crunch.
summary: A rival from tomorrow dispatches sloppy killer machines to wreck the firm, but their shoddy construction turns the attack into a crunchy novelty.

title: Website Launch Already Obsolete and Crashed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We launched our revamped website today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All of the technology we used is already obsolete and every vendor we hired is out of business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and it just crashed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I miss the days when we had brief windows of success.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that the revamped website has launched, but the technology used is already obsolete and all the hired vendors have gone out of business. He then adds that the site just crashed. The Boss responds wistfully that he misses when they at least had brief windows of success.
punchline: The Boss's nostalgia for 'brief windows of success' implies the company's projects now fail immediately, with no success at all, not even a short-lived one.
summary: A freshly launched website arrives outdated, orphaned by bankrupt vendors, and promptly broken, leaving the boss longing for the good old days of fleeting wins.

title: CEO Pep Talk Meets Silent Audience

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO pep talk

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I want to know I can count on every one of you!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Wordless panel: the employees sit silently in the audience.)

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: What's wrong with these people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well... I fired that guy this morning. His last day is tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That one retires at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Those three are contractors. I didn't renew their contracts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The rest of them believe that motivation is how the powerful steal from the dumb.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Tell them I hate their guts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did that in the pre-meeting.

setting: Company auditorium during a CEO's pep talk, with a Dilbert logo on the projection screen in the header
situation: A CEO gives a pep talk and asks to be able to count on everyone, but the audience sits in stony silence. The Boss explains why: one person was just fired, one is retiring, three are contractors who were not renewed, and the rest are cynics who see motivation as exploitation. The CEO then asks the Boss to tell them he hates their guts, and the Boss says that was already covered.
punchline: The workforce is disengaged because management has fired, retired and dropped most of them, and the CEO's idea of motivation is so insulting that the Boss already delivered the hatred message in advance.
summary: A chief executive's rousing speech falls flat because the crowd is mostly on their way out or too cynical to be inspired, and the leader's own contempt for them was already announced beforehand.

title: Safe Risks, Punished Mistakes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My job is to create an environment where employees feel safe taking risks.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My other job is punishing employees who make any kind of mistake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My point is that I'm glad I don't have YOUR job.

situation: The Boss sits in his big chair while Dilbert stands in front of his desk. The Boss explains that he is supposed to make employees feel safe taking risks, then admits he is also responsible for punishing any mistake. He wraps up by saying he is glad he doesn't have Dilbert's job.
punchline: The Boss's contradictory duties mean employees can never safely take risks, yet he somehow believes Dilbert's job is the harder one.
summary: A manager describes two conflicting responsibilities, encouraging risk-taking while punishing every error, then congratulates himself on not being in his employee's shoes.

title: Blocking Wally's Escape Routes

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, do you have a minute?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nope. I'm far too busy.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm blocking the only exit. You have no choice but to answer my question.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I blocked the air vent too.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Well played.

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: A coworker approaches Wally at the coffee maker with a question, and Wally claims to be too busy to talk. The coworker blocks the only exit so Wally has to answer. Wally is then seen trying to escape through an air vent, only to learn that the coworker has blocked that route too.
punchline: Wally, famous for dodging work, is so determined to avoid a simple question that he tries to crawl into an air vent, and he graciously concedes when the coworker anticipates even that.
summary: A persistent coworker corners the work-averse Wally by sealing off every escape route, including the ventilation shaft.

title: Boss Names His Heir Mistakenly

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Assemble the Supreme Leadership Board. I am ready to name an heir to succeed me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't have a Supreme Leadership Board, and this isn't a hereditary dictatorship.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's crazy talk.

transcript.speaker: Flying Monkey
transcript.text: Ignore him, Daddy.

situation: The Boss announces he wants to convene a Supreme Leadership Board to name his successor, with a winged monkey in a bellhop-style hat sitting on his desk. Dilbert points out that no such board exists and that the company isn't a hereditary dictatorship. The Boss dismisses this as crazy talk, and the monkey, who calls him Daddy, tells him to ignore Dilbert.
punchline: The Boss treats the company like a royal dynasty and plans to hand it to his monkey son, and the monkey is happy to back him up against Dilbert's reality check.
summary: A boss with grand ideas of dynastic succession plans to crown his winged monkey offspring, brushing off an employee's objections.

title: Dilbert Lists Career Options Boss Won't Like

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need this class to update my skills. Will you approve the expense?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where's the analysis of alternatives?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When you ask for funding, you need to tell me what my options are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, okay. That seems logical.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option two: Do nothing while I become increasingly unqualified for my job.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Option three: Replace me with someone younger who earns less than I do and already has the skills.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Options are only good when other people don't have them.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss to approve funding for a training class. The boss demands an analysis of alternatives, so Dilbert lays out the boss's options, which are to do nothing and let Dilbert's skills decay or to replace him with a cheaper, younger, already-skilled worker. The boss realizes he's out of good choices, and Dogbert comments on the nature of options.
punchline: By presenting the boss's 'options' honestly, Dilbert shows that the only sensible choice is to approve the training, and Dogbert notes that options only benefit those who hold power.
summary: A worker turns his manager's demand for alternatives into a gentle threat that leaves approving the training class as the only real choice.

title: Confusopoly Pricing Explained to Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or is your pricing intentionally confusing?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: It's intentionally confusing.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: That way you can't compare our prices to our competitors' prices.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our competitors do the same thing. It's called a confusopoly.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We all get our fair share of confused customers and we don't need to lower our prices to compete.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: We use the profits from our anti-competitive behavior to fund innovation.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: So don't ruin a good system by trying to understand what you're buying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That almost sounds reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Now spank yourself and thank me!

setting: A vendor's office, across a desk
situation: Dilbert, holding a price sheet, asks a salesman whether the company's pricing is deliberately confusing. The salesman cheerfully admits it is, explaining that the whole industry does it so customers can't compare prices and nobody has to compete on price. He claims the profits fund innovation, and Dilbert finds this almost reasonable.
punchline: The salesman openly admits to deliberate price obfuscation and then absurdly orders Dilbert to spank himself and thank him for it, showing how brazen anti-competitive behavior can be.
summary: A vendor frankly confesses that his industry muddles its pricing on purpose to dodge competition, then demands gratitude from the customer who questioned it.

title: Facial Recognition App Misidentifies Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, my name is...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Don't bother.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My app does facial recognition and searches all social media to give me your full biography.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's that working out?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: You're either Bart Simpson or a huge dry-erase marker.

situation: Dilbert tries to introduce himself to a coworker, but she cuts him off and snaps his photo with her phone. She explains that her app uses facial recognition and social media searches to learn everything about a person. When Dilbert asks how it is going, she says the app thinks he is either Bart Simpson or a giant dry-erase marker.
punchline: Dilbert's bald head, flat hair and odd upturned tie make him so cartoonish that even a sophisticated facial recognition app identifies him as a cartoon character or a whiteboard marker.
summary: A woman's face-scanning phone app can only match Dilbert's distinctive look to a cartoon kid or a stationery item.

file: 2010/2010-12-03_work_depressed_cubicle_take off jacket_sit at computer_powerpoint slides_happy_devil_giant spoon_prince of insufficient light.gif
title: Dilbert's Fantasy Interrupted by Happiness Police

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What fantasy will I use today to stave off madness?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll be "The man who changed an industry with his PowerPoint slides."

transcript.speaker: Prince of Insufficient Light
transcript.text: I have a report of unauthorized happiness inside of a head.

situation: Dilbert arrives at work and, while hanging up his jacket, thinks about which daydream he will use to cope with the day. He picks a fantasy of becoming famous for his PowerPoint slides. Once he sits at his computer, a devil-costumed figure carrying a giant spoon shows up to report that someone is enjoying themselves.
punchline: Even a small, harmless daydream of happiness at work is treated as a violation, with a devilish enforcer sent to stamp it out.
summary: A worker's modest escapist daydream about slideshow glory is promptly policed by a demonic figure who treats cheerfulness as contraband.

title: Cheering Up With Worse-Off Comparisons

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel like a failure. Say something to cheer me up?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Happiness comes from comparing yourself to a reference group that is relatively worse off.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You're a successful member of the reference group.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And that's not nothing!

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, with him sitting on the edge of his bed
situation: Dilbert sits on his bed feeling like a failure and asks Ratbert to cheer him up. Ratbert explains that happiness comes from comparing yourself to a group that is worse off, then tells Dilbert he is a successful member of that group. Dilbert, oddly satisfied, cheers himself up with the thought.
punchline: Ratbert's 'cheering up' actually places Dilbert among the worse-off reference group, which is an insult, yet Dilbert takes it as a win.
summary: A glum engineer asks his tiny pet for encouragement and receives a backhanded compliment that somehow works.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later that month

transcript.speaker: Coworker with wild hair and beard

A month later, he and another coworker show up with ridiculous, oversized hairstyles and beards, hoping to start a trend.
punchline: Trying to escape being uncool, he adopts an absurd new look and insists it will eventually become fashionable, which only makes him look more uncool.
summary: A man desperate to avoid looking uncool responds by growing outlandish hair and a wild beard, certain the style will eventually catch on.

title: Making Email Front of Mind

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert by Scott Adams, dilbert.com

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You didn't answer my e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't check e-mail often.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The whole point of e-mail is that you check it often.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you an idiot or some sort of digital sociopath?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Sometimes I don't remember to check it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You seem like a visual learner, so let me show you how to keep e-mail in the front of your mind.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is this your smartphone?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: BAM!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Now it's in the front of your mind. Get it?

situation: Alice confronts a coworker in a meeting for not answering her email. He admits he rarely checks it and sometimes forgets. Calling him a visual learner, she slams his face down onto his smartphone on the table to 'demonstrate' keeping email in the front of his mind.
punchline: Alice takes the phrase 'front of your mind' literally and violently, pressing the coworker's face (his front) into his smartphone as a visual lesson.
summary: A furious Alice teaches a forgetful coworker to prioritize email by smashing his face into his phone.

title: Values Are an Engineer's Illusion

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who can define "values"? Anyone?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Values are a type of emotional illusion common to children, idiots and non-engineers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can we pretend values are real?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are we a cult now?

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss stands beside a screen reading "Values" and asks the group to define the word. Dilbert raises his hand and dismisses values as an emotional illusion believed only by children, idiots and non-engineers. The Boss then asks whether everyone can just pretend values are real, prompting a coworker to ask if the company has become a cult.
punchline: The Boss's request to pretend values are real exposes corporate values as empty make-believe, so demanding collective belief in them sounds like cult behavior.
summary: A manager's attempt to discuss company values is met with an engineer's blunt dismissal and a suspicion that the whole exercise is a cult.

file: 2010/2010-12-06_body language_at odds with words_endocrine system_shutting down_interrupted boss_crazy_psychotic episode.gif
title: Boss's Body Language Contradicts His Words

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Am I interrupting anything important?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Oh no. I have seen this before. You are preparing to put your body language at odds with your words!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I always have time for my least important employee.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My endocrine system is shutting down!

situation: An employee in a yellow shirt and red tie interrupts the Boss at his desk and asks if he is interrupting anything important. The employee recognizes the signs that the Boss is about to say something polite while his body language shows the opposite. The Boss then says he always has time for his least important employee, with a twitching eye and clenched teeth, and the employee's body reacts in panic.
punchline: The Boss's friendly words are contradicted by his furious twitching face, and the employee is so unsettled by the insincere insult that his body physically starts to fail.
summary: A nervous worker predicts that his boss is about to say one thing while his face says another, then collapses in alarm when it happens.

title: Boss Is the Problem Maker

transcript.text: Are you running into any problems?

transcript.text: I have too many distractions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have any problems that aren't like that one?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Only in my fantasies.

setting: Alice's office cubicle, at her computer desk
situation: The Boss stops by Alice's desk and asks whether she is having any problems. Alice replies that the only problems she has are the ones he makes worse, and he challenges her to name one. She says his interruptions are distractions, and when he asks about other problems, she says she only has those in her fantasies.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that the Boss is her only real problem, and that a workday free of him exists only as a daydream.
summary: A manager checking on an employee's difficulties is told that he himself is the main obstacle, and that problem-free work is merely wishful thinking.

title: Declining the Masters Forum Invitation

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Would you like to be part of a Masters Forum to share knowledge across disciplines?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. The only people who will be there are the ones who don't have anything better to do. I try to avoid people like that.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm the chairperson.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll get a lot done that day!

situation: A coworker, Tina, stands by Dilbert's cubicle and invites him to join a Masters Forum for sharing knowledge across disciplines. Dilbert refuses, saying such forums only attract people with nothing better to do. Tina reveals she is the chairperson, and Dilbert cheerfully says he will be very productive on the day of the meeting.
punchline: Dilbert's insult about forum attendees backfires on him when he learns he has insulted the chairperson, yet he stays cheerfully unapologetic and turns the rejection into an excuse to skip the event.
summary: A colleague's invitation to an knowledge-sharing club is shot down with a cutting remark, and finding out she runs it only makes him happier about staying away.

title: Boss Says Email Almost Made Sense

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My plan is to act randomly and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perhaps I can be more clear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Dilbert stands before the Boss's desk as the Boss says Dilbert's e-mail almost made sense. Dilbert then says his plan is to act randomly and hope for the best. The Boss offers to be more clear, and Dilbert sarcastically marvels that the Boss can switch clarity on and off at will.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies the Boss has been deliberately unclear all along, since he can apparently choose to be clear whenever he wants.
summary: A manager's offer to communicate more clearly prompts his employee to wonder aloud why that ability was ever optional.

title: Boss Admits Meeting Talk Is Meaningless

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you leveraging our resources to optimize the client value stream?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm just messing with you. Nothing I say in meetings actually means anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why do you talk?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I tried listening once. It was awful.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, asks Dilbert a question full of corporate buzzwords. When Dilbert is baffled, the Boss admits he was only messing with him and that nothing he says in meetings has meaning. Dilbert asks why he talks at all, and the Boss says he tried listening once and found it awful.
punchline: The Boss talks meaningless jargon in meetings simply because he finds listening to other people unbearable.
summary: A manager confesses that his buzzword-laden meeting chatter is empty noise, preferring to talk rather than endure the misery of listening.

title: Dilbert's Stupid-Making Drug Dart

transcript.text: Ow.

setting: Dilbert's lab or living room, with Dogbert on an orange couch
situation: Dilbert, in a lab coat, explains that he invented a drug that makes people do stupid things and dipped a dart in it. He admits he doesn't know why he did it, then Dogbert darts him in the back. Dilbert says 'Ow' and Dogbert, now in control, demands a gallon of the drug for the weekend and tells him to breathe the fumes again.
punchline: Dilbert's own stupid-making drug explains his foolish decision to invent it, and Dogbert exploits him by dosing him again and ordering more of it.
summary: After a scientist boasts of a brain-dulling compound with no sensible purpose, his dog uses it on him to get a bigger supply.

title: Dustbin of History Curb Pickup

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The only things that matter are social networks, games and phones.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not working on any of that, so I arranged for the dustbin of history to do curb pickup.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please! I Twitter!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man

setting: Conference room, then outside at a curb with a dumpster
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells Dilbert and the Boss in a meeting that only social networks, games and phones matter. Since they aren't working on any of those, he says he has arranged for the 'dustbin of history' to collect them. Outside, the Boss pleads that he uses Twitter while a garbage man stands by a dumpster already full of other discarded people.
punchline: The Boss's desperate claim that he uses Twitter is dismissed as too little, too late, since the people who missed the tech trends are literally being hauled away as trash.
summary: A consultant dog declares his colleagues obsolete for ignoring trendy technology and has them literally thrown out with the garbage.

title: Free Security Advice From Dentist

He then recommends pouncing on intruders and shaking them until their fillings fall out. Alice asks what the advice cost, and Dogbert reveals it's free because he works for the dentist across the street.
punchline: The consultant's violent advice is free because it is really a scheme to drum up business for a nearby dentist, whose patients would need work after being shaken.
summary: A consultant's bizarrely aggressive security plan turns out to be a front for a dentist hoping to gain new customers.

title: CEO Grooming Winged Monkey Successor

setting: Office hallway and the CEO's office
situation: Dilbert warns Alice and Wally that the CEO is grooming a winged monkey as his successor. Alice hopes 'grooming' means training. In the last panel the monkey sits on the CEO's desk and notes something moving in its fur, and the CEO happily eats the last bug he picked off it.
punchline: The CEO is literally grooming the monkey in the primate sense, picking bugs from its fur and eating them, rather than mentoring a successor.
summary: A worrying report about the boss's heir apparent turns out to be about literal monkey-style grooming rather than leadership development.

title: Dilbert's Brutally Honest Movie Invitation

transcript.text: I only like movies with superheroes, geeks or robots. You probably only like movies with tears, diseases and weddings.
