situation: Dilbert approaches his coworker Amber and awkwardly invites her to a movie, openly admitting that their tastes are completely incompatible. He lists the genres each of them likes, then asks whether his bluntness is attractive to her. Amber responds by saying she has gone off mammals entirely.
punchline: Dilbert's tactless honesty is so off-putting that Amber sarcastically rejects not just him but his entire species, since humans are mammals.
summary: A socially clumsy engineer pitches a date by stressing how badly mismatched he and his coworker are, and she shuts him down with a deadpan zoological burn.

title: Thirty Years Experience Meets Modem

transcript.speaker: Older Manager
transcript.text: I know what I'm talking about. I have thirty years in this industry!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How does that help you understand technology that is six months old in a youth-oriented culture?

transcript.speaker: Older Manager
transcript.text: Grrr...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Please don't hit me with your modem.

situation: An older, balding manager insists his thirty years in the industry qualifies him to speak on technology. Asok, the young employee, points out that his experience is of little help with technology that is only six months old in a youth-obsessed culture. The angry manager picks up an old modem as if to strike Asok, who flinches and begs not to be hit with it.
punchline: The manager's outdated experience is literally embodied by the obsolete modem he threatens to use as a weapon, proving Asok's point about his stale knowledge.
summary: A veteran employee brags about his long career, and a young colleague's blunt reply about fast-moving tech provokes him to threaten violence with an antique piece of hardware.

title: Shareholder Witnesses Year-End Budget Blowout

transcript.speaker: Stockholder
transcript.text: Hi ho! I'm a common stockholder. I'm here to see how my investment is coming along.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, first on the agenda, we need to blow our budget before year end so we don't get less money next year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many ten-dollar mouse pads can we get for $10,000?

transcript.speaker: Stockholder
transcript.text: I hope this is a panic attack.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: A cheerful stockholder visits a meeting to see how his investment is doing. The Boss opens the agenda by announcing they must spend the entire leftover budget before year end to avoid a reduced budget next year, then asks how many expensive mouse pads $10,000 will buy. The stockholder grows visibly distressed and hopes he is merely imagining it.
punchline: The stockholder sits in on a meeting where management openly plans to waste money on pointless purchases, and his only comfort is the hope that it's just a panic attack rather than reality.
summary: An investor drops in to check on his money just as management plots to burn through leftover funds on overpriced office supplies.
enterprise_concepts: use it or lose it budgeting

title: Alice Insults the Boss's Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What do you think of my plan, Alice?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll bet your left brain is so tiny that you stagger in a clockwise direction.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll ask someone else.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Walk toward the credenza and you'll have a good chance of hitting the doorway.

situation: The Boss asks Alice for her opinion of his plan. Alice responds with an elaborate insult about his tiny left brain making him stagger in circles. When he decides to ask someone else, she fires off a second insult about how he will miss the credenza and hit the doorway instead.
punchline: Alice answers a request for feedback with creative, escalating insults about the Boss's intelligence and sense of direction, implying his plan is hopelessly stupid.
summary: Instead of reviewing his plan, Alice mocks her manager's brain and coordination with two inventive put-downs as he tries to leave.

file: 2010/2010-12-21_attend meeting_request_busy_meet halfway_not showing up_half of life.gif
title: Wally Will Meet Halfway, Literally

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally, can you attend my meeting Friday?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm very busy, but I'll meet you half-way.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What does that mean in this context?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They say half of life is just showing up.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So... you will be...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Doing the other half.

situation: Alice asks Wally to attend her meeting on Friday. Wally holding his coffee mug says he is too busy but will meet her halfway, which he explains using the saying that half of life is just showing up. Alice realizes this means he will skip the meeting, doing only the other half.
punchline: Wally twists the idiom about meeting halfway and the saying that showing up is half of life to mean he will deliberately not show up to the meeting.
summary: A lazy coworker uses a pair of folksy sayings to justify blowing off a colleague's meeting while sounding cooperative.
keywords: half of life is showing up

title: Boss's Staff Become Pudgy Sociopaths

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're doing a great job as a role model.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Half of your employees have already turned into pudgy sociopaths.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And they're quick to anger.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert seated across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits across the desk from the Boss and delivers a performance review of his leadership. He praises the Boss as a role model, then reveals that the Boss's example has turned half the employees into overweight sociopaths who anger easily. The Boss's expression grows increasingly sour as the list of effects grows.
punchline: Dogbert's praise is sarcastic: being a good role model means employees are copying the Boss's worst traits, becoming unhealthy, heartless and irritable like him.
summary: A sly dog advisor compliments a manager's leadership example while revealing it has spread his unpleasant traits throughout the staff.

title: Entrepreneurial Failure Looks Like Idleness

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm taking your advice to be more entrepreneurial at my job.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Failing 90% of the time is very similar to not trying at all. I'm pretty sure you won't be able to tell the difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which one am I doing now?

situation: Wally stands in front of the Boss's desk holding a coffee mug and announces he is taking the Boss's advice to be more entrepreneurial. He explains that failing most of the time looks just like not trying at all, so the Boss won't be able to tell the difference. The Boss, sitting in his chair, can only ask which one Wally is doing at the moment.
punchline: Wally turns the Boss's call for entrepreneurship into cover for his usual laziness, and the Boss is left unable to tell whether Wally is failing or just slacking.
summary: Wally answers his manager's push for initiative by promising a high failure rate that is indistinguishable from doing nothing.

file: 2010/2010-12-18_noisy bag of chips_speaker phone_common sense_wounded ego_guy on speaker phone.gif
title: Crunching Chips Into the Speakerphone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's not a good idea to eat a noisy bag of chips next to a speaker-phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. My common sense has wounded your ego and made you defiant.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crunch! Crunch! Crunch!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Did you really think he would stop?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. I hate the guy who was on the speaker-phone.

setting: Conference room during a speakerphone call
situation: In a meeting, Dilbert tells a coworker it's a bad idea to eat a noisy bag of chips next to the speakerphone. The coworker, feeling his ego wounded, defiantly crunches away anyway. Afterward Asok asks if Dilbert really expected him to stop, and Dilbert reveals he wanted the chips to be loud.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately used reverse psychology, knowing his warning would provoke the coworker into crunching louder, because he dislikes the person on the speakerphone.
summary: A gentle warning about snack noise turns out to be a calculated trick to torment a disliked caller.

title: Meeting Pirate Steals Virtualization Credit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've had reports of "meeting pirates," taking over agendas and pillaging credit.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Pirate
transcript.text: Yaaarg!!! I take yer document, and leave ye scurvy rats adrift!

transcript.speaker: Meeting Pirate
transcript.text: And then I invented server virtualization. Yaaarg!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! That was a good idea.

situation: The Boss warns that 'meeting pirates' have been hijacking agendas and stealing credit. A coworker dressed as a pirate then grabs Dilbert's document in the meeting. He then claims to have invented server virtualization, and the Boss is impressed.
punchline: The Boss is warned about credit-stealing meeting pirates, yet he is immediately taken in when one claims credit for someone else's idea, showing he cannot recognize the theft happening in front of him.
summary: A literal pirate seizes a colleague's paperwork in a meeting and claims the idea as his own while management cheerfully applauds.

title: Choosing Your Path of Failure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The request we got for a quote is vague, and the deadline for our response is tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I ask for clarity, we'll miss the deadline. If I don't, our bid will either be below our cost or too high to win.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Which path of certain failure do you prefer?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like the one that makes you work the hardest.

setting: The Boss's office, with a brief exterior shot of an office building
situation: Dilbert brings the Boss a vague request for a quote that is due tomorrow and explains that every option leads to failure. If he asks for clarification they will miss the deadline, and if he doesn't the bid will be too low to be profitable or too high to win. He asks which failure the Boss prefers, and the Boss picks the one that requires the most effort from Dilbert.
punchline: Faced with a choice between doomed outcomes, the Boss ignores the business consequences and simply picks whichever option makes his employee work the hardest.
summary: With a no-win bid looming, a manager is asked to pick how the project will fail and chooses based on how much extra labor it squeezes out of his subordinate.

title: Paying Amber to Be Facebook Friend

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Amber, I'll pay you $500 a month to pretend to be my friend on Facebook.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you need to do is leave me a public message every once in a while.

transcript.speaker: Amber
transcript.text: That would make me a...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Frienditute. But it's better if we don't name it.

situation: Dilbert offers his coworker Amber $500 a month to pose as his friend on Facebook by occasionally posting public messages on his page. Amber starts to say what that would make her, and Dilbert supplies the awkward made-up word 'frienditute' before suggesting they not name the arrangement.
punchline: Dilbert is so desperate to look popular online that he is effectively hiring a paid friend, and the word 'frienditute' (a play on 'prostitute') exposes how sad and transactional the deal is.
summary: A lonely engineer tries to buy the appearance of social popularity by paying a coworker to act as his online friend.

file: 2010/2010-12-05_design plan_suboptimal_highlighted items_illusion of fullness_olden times_hat_manage like its 1800's.gif
title: Managing Me Like It's 1800

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My design plan is obviously too complex for a manager to understand.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I highlighted a few areas that are intentionally suboptimal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just point to the highlighted items and demand that I fix them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That will give you the illusion of usefulness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pretend this is olden times when bosses knew what their employees did for a living.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To round out the fantasy, wear this hat made from a dead animal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now manage me like it's the 1800's!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have a smaller hat?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Imagine that we're out of candles.

situation: Dilbert gives the Boss a design plan with deliberately flawed sections highlighted, so the Boss can look useful by demanding fixes. He then asks the Boss to pretend it's the 1800s, when managers understood their employees' work, and hands him a fur hat to complete the fantasy. The Boss, wearing the hat, asks for a smaller one.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the Boss's cluelessness by scripting his management role down to pointing at planted flaws, and the Boss is too dim to notice the insult, asking only for a smaller hat.
summary: An engineer plants deliberate flaws in his design so his clueless manager can feel useful, then dresses him in period costume to play a boss who actually understood the work.

title: King of the Two Monitors

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In the land of cubicles, the man with two monitors is king.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I pity my uni-monitored subjects, but I cannot respect them.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, in another corner of the kingdom. . .

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The king is dead. Long live the queen.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk with two monitors and thinks smugly of himself as the king of the cubicle land, pitying coworkers who only have one screen. Meanwhile, Alice grins menacingly in her own cubicle, having just unboxed her own second monitor.
punchline: Dilbert's pride in his dual-monitor status is undermined when Alice acquires her own second monitor, declaring his reign over and herself the new ruler.
summary: A man gloating about his superior screen setup is dethroned the moment a more ruthless coworker gets a matching setup of her own.

file: 2010/2010-12-26_long email_waste of time_deleted_free to tell_contents_without reducing prodcutivity_improving communication.gif
title: Deleting the Email Before Reading

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Did you read my long e-mail?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not yet. What's it about?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I can't say.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If I tell you what I wrote, the effort I put into writing the e-mail will be transformed into a waste of time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just decided to delete your e-mail before reading it. Therefore it is already wasted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are now free to tell me its contents without reducing your productivity.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh. Okay.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was something about improving communication, but I worded it better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should read it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you should.

setting: Office break area near the coffee maker
situation: A coworker asks Dilbert whether he read his long e-mail, but refuses to summarize it because that would make the time spent writing it a waste. Dilbert says he already deleted it unread, so the effort is already wasted and the coworker can explain freely. The coworker's summary is vague, and the two end up telling each other to go read it.
punchline: The e-mail was supposedly about improving communication, yet neither the writer nor the recipient can be bothered to read or recall it, so the communication fails completely.
summary: A man guards the value of his lengthy message until a colleague admits he trashed it unread, leaving both stuck pointing at each other to read it.

file: 2010/2010-11-24_computer_headset_marketing research_social security number_bank pin_maiden name_poverty_identity theft_technology.gif
title: Dogbert's Identity Theft Market Research

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello, this is the Dogbert Market Research Company. May I ask you some totally harmless questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What is your Social Security number, bank PIN number and mother's maiden name?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What exactly are you researching?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Poverty rates. I'm shooting for 100%.

setting: Dogbert's office desk with a computer and phone headset
situation: Dogbert, wearing a headset at his computer, phones Dilbert pretending to be a market research company and asks him for his Social Security number, bank PIN and mother's maiden name. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks what the research is actually about. Dogbert reveals he is studying poverty rates and wants to push them to 100%.
punchline: Dogbert's 'research' is an identity theft scam, and he plans to drain victims' bank accounts until everyone is poor, giving a poverty rate of 100%.
summary: A phone survey that demands a person's most sensitive financial details turns out to be a scheme to impoverish everyone it reaches.

title: Old Johannsen's Job Security Secret

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Old Johannsen has kept his job all of these years because no one else has his critical knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pssspss pss pss psss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's the worst-case scenario right there.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss explains that the elderly Johannsen has stayed employed for years because he alone holds critical knowledge. A bespectacled coworker leans over and whispers to him, and Johannsen then slumps over dead with a wisp rising from his head while the coworker grins. The Boss points to the slumped body as the worst-case scenario.
punchline: The coworker apparently whispered something that killed Johannsen, and now his irreplaceable knowledge is lost, which is exactly the risk of depending on one person.
summary: A manager praises an elderly employee's irreplaceable expertise just before a whispering colleague seemingly finishes him off, proving how risky that dependence is.

file: 2010/2010-12-19_feel empowered_forgot buy in_poorly conceived project_destroy from inside_not empowered_old system.gif
title: Empowered to Destroy the Project

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want all of you to feel empowered on this project.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You forgot to get our buy-in before you empowered us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll get your buy-in later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's far too late for that.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm going to use my empowerment to destroy this poorly conceived project from the inside!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't do that!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... now you're saying we're not empowered to do what we think is best?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can we go back to our old system where we're afraid to make decisions and you're never available?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your eyes say, "Yes."

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: The Boss announces that the team is empowered on a project, but the team points out he never secured their buy-in first. One employee threatens to use that empowerment to sabotage the flawed project, so the Boss reverses himself. The team then asks whether they can return to the old arrangement where they feared decisions and he was never around.
punchline: The Boss's empowerment is so hollow that the staff would rather return to a dysfunctional system of fear and absentee management, and he cannot even bring himself to disagree, leaving him glaring while pretending to read their agreement.
summary: A manager's attempt to empower his team backfires when they threaten to sabotage the project, and he is left stuck with their cheerful request to revert to neglect.

file: 2010/2010-12-22_said same thing_27 times_using different words_stop talking_rude_repeat yourself.gif
title: Repeating Yourself 27 Times in Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me. By my count, you've said the same thing 27 times, using different words.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If I can get sworn statements from everyone here that we understand your point, will you stop talking?

transcript.speaker: Man in Meeting
transcript.text: That's mighty rude of you.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Participant
transcript.text: I don't get your point. Can you repeat it 26 more times?

situation: At a meeting, a coworker points out that a long-winded colleague with big curly hair has made the same point 27 times in different words. The speaker offers to stop if everyone swears they understand, but another attendee calls the interruption rude and the speaker sarcastically asks for 26 more repetitions.
punchline: The long-winded speaker pretends not to understand the point so they can justify repeating it another 26 times, showing that they care more about talking than being understood.
summary: A meeting rambler is called out for endlessly rephrasing one idea, and responds by feigning confusion to keep the monologue going.

title: Salesman Guesses Buyer's Hidden Intentions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can you give me a quote by next week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your demeanor tells me that you will never buy our product. You only want the quote as a point of reference.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or maybe I'm giving you false hope because it's less awkward to end the meeting that way.

transcript.speaker: Buyer
transcript.text: Die! Die! Die!

setting: A conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert, acting as a salesman, asks a prospective buyer for a quote by next week. Dilbert then reads the buyer's demeanor aloud, suggesting the buyer will never purchase and only wants the quote for comparison. He adds that the buyer might be faking interest to avoid an awkward ending to the meeting, and the buyer angrily shouts at him.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt, accurate analysis of the buyer's hidden motives makes the buyer so uncomfortable that he explodes in rage, shouting 'Die! Die! Die!'
summary: A salesman voices exactly what a prospective customer is secretly thinking about the sales meeting, and the customer reacts with fury.

title: Unhelpful Moron or Terminator Robot

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I've noticed that whenever I ask you a specific question by email, you avoid answering it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're either an unhelpful moron or a poorly designed robot sent from the future to terminate our company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did you know it was a robot?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Alice confronts a coworker who never answers her specific emails, and speculates he is either an unhelpful moron or a badly built robot from the future sent to destroy the company. In the last panel she pulls off his head, revealing it is a robot, while Dilbert asks how she knew.
punchline: Alice was merely insulting him with two options, so her accusation of being a robot was a guess that turned out to be true, and she never actually knew.
summary: A frustrated coworker's insult about an evasive emailer accidentally exposes him as an actual killer robot.

title: Telling the Boss About Heart Attacks

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: A Swedish study in 2009 showed that people with bad bosses had 40% more heart attacks.

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: AAAK!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I should warn you that I'll probably tell this story a few times.

situation: At a meeting, Wally cites a Swedish study showing that people with bad bosses suffer 40% more heart attacks. A coworker clutches his chest and cries out, then falls out of his chair with his feet in the air. Wally calmly remarks that he will probably repeat the story a few more times.
punchline: Wally's statistic apparently kills a coworker on the spot, and he casually announces he'll keep repeating the story, implying he may be thinning out the staff deliberately.
summary: A cheerful workplace statistic about bosses and cardiac arrest proves instantly fatal for a listener, and the speaker is unfazed.

title: Alice Rephrases Dilbert's Excuse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sorry, I didn't have time to get the information you asked for.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're saying that for an entire week, every single thing you did was more important than my ten-minute request?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, but the way I said it doesn't make me think of a broomstick.

situation: Dilbert tells Alice he had no time to get the information she requested. Alice angrily reframes his excuse as saying that everything he did for a week outranked her small ten-minute request. Dilbert agrees that is what he means but observes that his phrasing sounds nicer than hers.
punchline: Dilbert concedes that his polite excuse means exactly what Alice accused him of, and his only defense is that his wording sounds less like a witch's broomstick-riding rant, a dig at her irritable temperament.
summary: A blunt colleague unpacks the real meaning of a polite excuse, and the excuse-maker admits it was just better worded.

title: Training the Mailroom Guy, Wally Style

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I need you to train the new mailroom guy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because he's unimportant and you're worthless.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay. I was worried that it was the other way around.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All important messages are sent by e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So your job is to shovel all of the regular mail into recycling bins.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We won't be paying you, but you can use packages and tape to build your own igloo.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Two weeks later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is my desk so clean?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're welcome.

setting: Office hallway, a training room, and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss assigns Wally to train the new mailroom employee, explaining that the newcomer is unimportant and Wally is worthless. Wally teaches the new hire that all important messages arrive by email, so all regular mail should go straight into recycling, and he is not paid but can build an igloo from packages and tape. Two weeks later the Boss wonders why his desk is so clean, and Wally takes credit.
punchline: Wally trains the mailroom guy to throw away all physical mail, which leaves the Boss's desk spotless, and he sarcastically takes credit for the result.
summary: A lazy employee teaches the new mail clerk to bin every letter unread, and the boss's suspiciously tidy desk shows the plan worked.

title: Pencils Instead of Ethernet Switch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob, Director of Purchasing

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I requested an Ethernet switch and you sent me a box of pencils.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sometimes I tweak the non-standard orders so I can use our approved vendors.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You can't tell the difference between a switch and a pencil?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I can tell the difference between your problem and mine.

situation: An employee holding a box of pencils confronts Bob, the dinosaur Director of Purchasing, because he ordered an Ethernet switch. Bob admits he alters non-standard orders so he can buy from the company's approved vendors. When the employee questions his competence, Bob replies that he knows exactly whose problem this is, and it isn't his.
punchline: Bob deliberately substitutes items to suit his own convenience and cheerfully dismisses the consequences as the requester's problem, not his.
summary: A purchasing director swaps a requested network device for office supplies just to stay within his preferred suppliers, then shrugs off the complaint.
